div.p: NArtrg. WHAT DOES IT MATTER? It matters little where I was born, Or if my parents were rich or poor; Whether they shrank at the cold world's scorn, Or walked in the pride of wealth secure; But whether I live an honest man, And hold my integrity firm in my clutch— I tell you, brother, plain as I can, It matters much! - It matters little how long I stay In a world of sorrow, sin and care; Whether in youth I am called away, Or live tilt my bones and pate are bare; But whether I do the best I can To soften the weight of adversity's touch On the faded cheek of fellow-man, It matters much!

It matters little where be my grave, Or on the land or on the sea; By purling brook or 'neath stormy wave, It matters little or nought to me; But whether the Angel Death comes down, And marks my brow with his loving touch, As one that shall wear the victor's crown, It matters much!

MORNING. BY WILLIAM HENRY Goss, F.G.S. Hence on thy shadowy wings, thou Queen of Rest, Enchantress of the night, soft Sleep—away! Hence on thy shadowy wings to the far west", Where shades await thee; haste, the King of Day Is fast approaching to resume his royal sway. But welcome to my chamber, early ray Of morn; hail, sky of azure, gold, and rose: 7 Hail, silent hour, blest harbinger of day! Thou, gorgeous Day-king, hasten to disclose The charms of eager Nature waking from repose. Awake, ye slumbering herds in yonder mead; And joyful lambs, your gambols now renew, - Or in your heaven-provided pastures feed— Your sweet green pastures strewn with pearly dew; Awake, ye flocks and kine, the morning breaks for

you - Ye glancing fishes, hiding from our sight— Silent inhabitants of yonder stream— The morning breaks for you; the genial light Reaches your caverns, and ye too, I deem, Rejoice when from the east morn's splendid glories beam.

As in the water, so beneath the ground, A thousand tribes their habitations hold— In how small Compass wisdom may be found ! The ant, skill'd architect and warrior bold, Hails morning from his dusky city in the mould. Rouse up and hail the day, ye aerial things That slumber in the bosoms of the flowers! Spread in the perfumed air your beauteous wings, And hail the foremost of the happy Hours; Rejoice till in the ruby west the Day-car lowers. The flowers, which droop'd and seem'd to pine for day, Towards the Belt their shapely heads now raise; They own the joyous morn: and who shall say The sweets they breathe are not their silent praise— That they are joyless while on heaven they daylong gaze? See,:while I watch, the influence of:the morn Wakens the flowers to hail the new-born day! Their petals open, and the emerald lawn Below is diaper'd with bright display . Of:starry daisies op'ning while I pen my lay. 0 where can fancy reach or eye survey Through all this scene, but joys and beauties are, And wonders infinite? Stay, Fancy, stay! Lead not my spirit to that waning star; 'Tis vain for human thought to penetrate so far! Of earth—among the astral host a grain— Speck.of that gold-dust sprinkled o'er the sky— Man seeks to grasp the knowledge all in vain. Vain were it then for human thought to try To solve the wonders of the countless orbs on high. Meantime, hail warblings sweet! Released from,Night, A thousand throats welcome the morning rays With songs of gratitude, and sweet delight. 0 Father of the Universe, these lays Are Nature's hymns to Thee—Thy creatures' grateful praise!

Then hail! increasing choir: sweet to mine ear Your morning hymns of praise. 0 all I see, And all beyond surveyance ; all I hear— All nature, Mighty Father, praises Thee, All lovely scenes and sounds, all varied harmony! —*Sunday Magazine.

"How many rods make a furlong?" asked a father of his son, a "fast" urchin, as he came home one night from the town school. "Well, I don't know, boss," was .the reply of the young hopeful; "but I guess you'd think one rod made an acher, if you got such a tanning as I did from old vinegar-face, this afternoon." The parent stood aghast. Two Irishmen were walking along one of the main thoroughfares in Glasgow when they noticed a large placard in the window of a shop with the words " But- ter ! Butter! ! Butter! ! !" in giant type printed on it. "Pat," said Mick, "what is the maning of them big strokes atter the words?" " Och ! ye ignoramus," says Pat, "sure they're meant for shillelahs, to show it's Irish butter!"

BABY. Blue eyes, like skies; Brown hair, very fair, Tiny nose, pink toes, Dimpled feet, so sweet," Cunning ways; some day Cries maybe; that's baby. WORSE AND WORSE.—Penderson, who had ju3t been introduced; "Delighted to meet; you, I'm sure! My friend Jones often speaks of you. It was only the other day that he said, 'Mrs. Louisburg is such a fine motherly lady."—Miss Louisburg, with a faint suspicion of annoy- ance on her smiling face: "How droll! Your friend Mr. Jones was probably speaking.'of my mother. I'm Miss, not Mrs. Louisburg."—Fenderson, much agitated: "Oh, I beg pardon. But really, is it possible you have a mother living ?" A lady riding on a tramcar saw a little boy whom she knew. "So you have a little sister, Willie," she remarked pleasantly. "Is she a pretty baby?" "She looks just like mama," m was the smiling answer. "What do you call her ?" asked the lady. "She's named after mamma," answered tke little fellow promptly. Everybody was smiling, and the lady inquired the colour of the baby's hair. "It's the same colour as mamma's," he responded timidly. A gentleman who had been amused by the dialogue, asked the wee man if the new little sister was a good baby. "Yes, sir," was the prompt reply; "she is just like mamma." The Rev. Dr. —, a prominent New York clergyman, relates witn much gusto the following story about him- self. The present Mrs. Rev. Dr. —, by-the-way, is not the wife of the doctor's youth, nor yet of his early man- hood, but is the lady of his third choice, and as a conse- quence the doctor's set of olive branches spring from diverse maternal ancestry. "Such a condition of affairs," says the doctor, as raconteur," might ,at times become embarrassing except for the thorough amiability of all concerned. I confess, however, to a slightly disconcerted feeling when shortly before my third marriage I was ap- proached by one of my daughters, a girl of nine, and one who called my second wife mother, with, Papa, will you let me go to see you married? I have never been at any of your weddings.' "—Harper's Hagarine. HE WAS 'SCIISED.—Down in the woods of the Chicka- mauga battle-fields rabbits skurry from one brush-heap to another, and the squirrels chatter as they look down from their perches at men wandering from point to point in the openings. We were skirt- ing Snodgrass Hill, when we heard a gun go off, followed by a series of yells and whoops. Push- ing into the woods a few rods, we came upon an old darkey seated on a log, with one pant-leg rolled up. There were four or five tiny streams of blood running , down, and it was plain enough that some scattering shot had struck him. As we reached him, a coloured boy about sixteen years old came out of the bush with a light shot gun in his hands, and the old man looked up end said :—" Julius, look heah ! You has dun shot your fadder in the leg !" "Why, pap, I dun 'sposed you was a rabbit. I seed sumthin' movin' in de bush, an' I blazed away." " Zactly, Julius, I correspond. You dun took an ole nigger weighin' 1801 b. for a little rabbit 'bout a foot long an' jist big 'nuff to make soup fur one! Julius, Tie gwine to show you de difference between a rabbit an' your fadder I" He had been cutting a green limb as he talked, and when he finished he took the boy by the collar and played the " bud " to him until the young man jumped 2ftihigh and sang out like a Salva- tion Army band. By and bye we gently interfered to prevent further punishment,lland the old man held the boy off and asked, "Julius, does you see me ?" "Yes, fodder." "Does you know me from a rabbit ?" "Yes" "Den you:start for hurolan'. pick up dat hoe an' make dat co'nfield ache, an' deinexitime you go huntin' you holler off yer mouf befo' you shoot off yer gun! Gem'len, good mawnin', an' please scuse:dis leetle disrupshun." A Frenchman who took to learning the English lan- ' guage, persevered till he came to the word " a-gue." When told its two syllables might be made one by pre- fixing "p" and "1," and making plague of it, the philo- sopher remarked, "That half bthe English might have the a-gue,' and the other half the pla-gue ;' as for him he wouldn't bother further about it." Tommy was a little rogue whom his mother had hard work to manage. Their house in the country was raised Ia few feet from the ground, and Tommy, to escape a well-deserved whipping, ran from mother and crept under the house. Presently the father came home, and, hear- , ing where the boy had taken refuge, crept under to bring I him out. As he approached on his hands and knees, Tommy asked, "Is she after you, too ?" One day little Alice announced to her father her inten- tion to grow up with as much haste as possible, in order to be a "music man and play on a hand organ." "And what will your poor papa do ?" that fond parent in- quired. "while you are going about with your hand organ far away from home ?" .Miss Alice looked per- plexed. She is very fond of her father. She turned the I matter over in her mind before she made answer; then , she said: "Oh, dat'll be all right. You shall be my monkey, and go and get all the pennies." - INDEcisioN.—Of all wretched characters, the man 1" who can never make up his mind" is the most wretched. A torment to himself, he is the reproach and laughter of others, who frequently suffer in no small degree from his hesitation, delay, and fickleness. There can scarcely be any more fatal censure passed upon a I man than that implied in the patriarch's apostrophe to his son: '6 Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel." The very promise of well doing must be denied to the waverer. THE THOUGHTLESSNESS OF You-ern—ln general, I have no patience with people who talk about "the thoughtless- ness of youth." When a man has done his work, and nothing can anyway be materially altered in his fate, let him forget his toil; but what excuse can you find for wilfulness of thought at the very time when every crisis of the future fortune hangs on your decisions? A youth I thoughtless! when all the happiness of his home for ever depends on the chances or the passions of an hour! A youth thoughtless! when the career of all his days de- pends on the opportunity of a moment! A youth thought- less! when his every act is a foundation stone of future conduct, and every imagination a foundation stone of life or death? Be thoughtless in any after years rather than now—though, indeed, there is only one place where a man may be nobly thoughtless—his deathbed. :s.io thinking should ever be left to be done there.—Ruskin. A LION'S AFFECTION.—Prince, a tame lion on board His Majesty's (.George III.) ship Ariadne had a keeper to whom he was much attached. The keeper got drunk I one day, and, as the captain never forgave that crime, ihe was ordered to be flogged. The grating was rigged 011 the main deck, opposite Prince's den, a large barred- up place, pillars large and cased with iron. When the keeper began to strip, Prince rose gloomily from his couch and got as near to his friend as possible. -_`,'On beholding his bare back, he walked hastily round the den, and when he saw the boatswain inflict the first lash his eyes sparkled with fire and his sides resounded with the strong and quick beating of his tail. At last, when the blood began to flow from the man's back, and the " cot- ted cats" jerked their gory knots close to the lion's den his fury became tremendous; he roared with a voice of thunder, shook the strong bars of the prison as if they had been osiers, and finding his efforts to break loose un- availing he rolled and shrieked in a manner the most terrific that it is possible to conceive. The captain, fearing that lie might break loose, ordered the mariners to load and present at Prince. This threat redoubled , his rage, and at last the captain desired the keeper to be cast off, and go to his friend. It is impossible to describe the joy evinced by the lion. He licked with care the , mangled and bleeding back of the cruelly beaten seaman. caressed him with his paws, which he folded round the keeper as if to defy any man renewing a similar treat- ment, and it was only after several hours that Prince would allow the keeper to quit his protection. TOLD FOR IDA.—Once upon a7,time there lived a prin- cess. She was a very pretty little girl, with eyes as blue as the violets that grow by the meadow brook, and cheeks as pink as wild roses, and hair as golden as sun- shine. And all the people loved this little princess be- cause she was so kind and loving and lovable. But she ; had one great fault, and that was—Pro-cras-ti-na-tion. I Sometimes this little golden-haired princess would be playing with her dolls or reading a story book, when her mamma would say, Ida, dear, run upstairs and fetch me a spool of silk from my table." And Ida would answer, with a sweet smile, "In a minute. mamma." One minute would go by, and another, and a great many more. "Will you get my silk, Ida ?" "Oh, yes, mamma, as soon as I finish this chapter." "Now, Ida." "In just a minute, mamma." But the chapter was sure to be finished, with perhaps another„one, before the silk would be fetched. It was not only once, but all the time. "What can I do ?" sighed the queen, to her trusty coun- sellor. "I must break her off this dreadful habit some way, or, when she comes to rule a kingdom of her own, all will go to wrack and ruin. What can Ido ?" "Teach her a lesson, your Majesty," said the trusty counsellor, gruffly. "Teach her a lesson—a 'good lesson." And one day the queen remembered her trusty counsellor's‘words. The little princess came bounding in, to be dressed for a drive, with her blue:•eyes shining and her yellow hair tossing about her face, and her cheeks pinker than usual, which is saying a good deal. "We're going up to the Mountain Castle for lunch, mamma," cried she, "and home around by the lake! And Lillian says her uncle can't wait but a minute, and won't you hurry, mamma, and get me dressed ?" Mamma, the queen, was reading a book, and she hardly raised her eyes from it, but answered, with a smile, "In a minute, dear." So the little princess fidgeted restlessly from one foot to another for what seemed to her a long, long time. "Won't you, manuna?'l " 06, yes, dear, as soon as I finish what I laimttlerepardiinnces"s beganW asn'tto oakwi likeful? violets 'rh e blueafte erya- esshoofwtehre; dca on, hounrlryy. r ?it w „fißveigmhtinauwteays,,, m, and the voice of the little princess trembled. "But they mamma," answered mamma apinlerna ade,de;al‘m‘ olyh,. But just then the little princess heard carriage wheels rolling down the avenue, and she burst into a cry of grief and dismay. "0, mamrna, they've gone without me! I told them to if I didn't come in five minutes. And they had chocolate cake and jelly tarts for lunch. Oh, dear me !" And then a flood of tears came. Mamma, the queen, couldn't help smiling a little, though she felt very sorry, too. But she hoped this would be the lesson; and she took her little daughter on her knee, and talked to her about that old thief, procrastination, which is, you know, a name for putting-off-till-by-and-by what should be done now. "You will try and do better, won't you, dear ?" said mamma, the queen, very tenderly; and the little princess, when her sobs were stilled, answered that she would try. "But it's very hard to do things right off," said she; "unless it's things you want to do, mamma." .:.," Right there selfishness comes in, dear," said mamma, "and selfishness will unlock the door and let in a host of other bad, bad faults." And then mamma, who could not bear to punish her little girl too much, ordered her own carriage, and away they sped after their friends. Princess Ida is trying yet to do better: she has set a guard over those red lips of hers with strict orders not to let the troublesome words, "In a minute," slip by. And though she isn't perfect yet, we think she is almost as near that as it is possible for any little girl to be. "A. C.," in Youth's Companion.

'The volcano of Colima, in Mexico, is in a state of erup- tion for the third time within a year. Notices were posted at the Festiniog slate quarries on Saturday restricting tke out-put to four days per week.

Another thousand colliers have received notice to ter- minate their contracts in Mountain Ash and Neaves Valley, the trade outlook being very gloomy. At South Shields, on Monday, John Dixon, labourer' was sentenced to nine months' for stealing glass shades from graves in Westoe Cemetery. Shades: had been missed for seine time, and the prisoner was proved to have sold no less than 39.

BURNED TO DHATH.—Michael Murray, an old man, died in Berwick Infirmary, on Tuesday, from injuries received in a singular manner. While drunk he lay on a box of matches, which ignited, and be was so severely burned about the back that he has now succumbed.

"To THE DEADHOUSE."—Mr. Coroner Brighouse was shocked the other day at the ignorance of a boy, nine years old, who was put in the box to give evidence in a drowning case at Bootle. To the Coroner's question, "Do you know what telling the truth is ?" no answer was given. But to the next query, "Do you know where good boys go when they die ?" there came a prompt "Yes." "Where ?" asked the coroner. "To the deadhouse," was the unhesitat- ing reply. LOItD SALISBURY AND THE SCOTCH PROTESTANTS—Re- pIying to the Rev. Jacob Primmer, who, as president of the Townhill Conservative Assoeiation. Dunfermline, angrily protested the selection of a Roman Catholic for the office of Home Secretary, Lord Salisbury states that the ap- pointment of Mr. Matthews involves no shadow of injury or danger to Protestant interests. Mr. Primmer rejoins, " We will certainly prefer our religion and our liberties to our party." PROPOSED IRISH NATIONAL CIEURCII.—Dr. Glynn, Prior of the Augustinian College at Rome, is in Dublin, armed with a letter from the Pope, signed by Cardinal Simioni, favouring the project of building an Irish National Church, dedicated to St. Patrick. in Rome. Dr. Glynn is collecling subscriptions for the movement. Arehbishops Walsh, Croke, and Mc.Evilly, and Dr. Kirky, Archbishop of Ephesus and Rector of the Irish College at Rome, are also supporting it. CHURCH CONGRESS.—On Tuesday the Church Congress at Wakefield formally commenced its proceedings. In the morning the president and members were received by the Mayor in the Town Hall, and welcemed es the first visit of the Congress to the town. Afterwards services took place in three of the principil churches, sermons being preached by the Archbishop of York, the Bishop of Meath, and the Bishop of Edinburgh. The last-named condemned what he termed the wicked talk which would set the masses against the classes. The Bishop of Ripon afterwards delivered his presidential address. A. HOMANTIC STORY.—A policeman in the Bth Arron- dissement of Paris, married in 1883 a young girl who had just left an orphanage, but who had known nothing of her parents. A few days ago, shortly after the birth of a child, the officer received a cheque for 100,0001., together with a letter asking him to kiss his wife and child for the donor ; the communication being signed, "Your Wife's Mother." On the eve of her marriage the supposed orphan received a trousseau and a Bank of France note for 1,0001., and a short letter urging her to be always good and virtuous, and adding that it was her mother who begged it. SHOCKING PARAFFIN LAMP ACCIDENT.—At Woodville

House, South-grove, Highgate, occupied by M iskell and his family, a fire broke out on Saturday, caused by the bursting of a paraffin lamp. There was a nurse in the room when the lamp exploded. She was standing close to the lamp when it flickered and burst. The burning oil ran all over the table and set fire to her dress. She was in dames at once. As she ran out of the room she screamed, and her master and mistress soon came to her assistance. The mats and the carpets in the passage were at once wrapped round her and the flames were put out, but not before she had sus- tained injuries from which sbe died in a few hours.

MIRACULOUS ESCAPE FROM DEATH.—An extraordinary accident is reported from the Vale of Llangollen. Opera- tives fixing telegraph poles between Llangollen and Berwyn, have had to contend with limestone ruck, which has to be blasted in order to insert the poles. At one of these blasts a stone, weighing bib, was hurled through the air over the railway, river Fee, the canal, and road, a dis- tance of 400 yards, and fell upon the roof of the entrance lodge of Sir Theodore Martin's residence, breaking through the ceiling, and smashing a large earthenware mug to atoms. The lodgekeeper was washing at the time of the blasting, and only left the washing on hearing the report, thus miraculously escaping a terrible death. THE SPLIT IN THE GOOD TEMPLAR ORDER.—The con- ference held in Boston, Mass., between representatives of the two Supreme Courts of the Good Templar Order has just concl nded its sittings, with the result, a cablegram an- nounces, that a satisfactory and non-compromising basis for amalgamation has been agreed upon. The split in this temperance association, which has branches in every part of of the world, was occasioned ten years ago by the alleged exclusion of negroes from the lodges of the Americans in the ex•slave States. Since then there have been two orders, the one mainly British and the other chiefly Ameri- can, the respective presidents being Mr. Joseph Melina, of Birmingham. and the Hon. T. B. Fince, of Illinois. A di:1)GB ON WELSH TRUTHFOLNEsS. A Welsh news- paper on Friday published a letter from Mr. Justice :Stephen in which he says ti.at the Welsh appear to him to have more poetry and imagination than the _English, and he has never observed the vulgarity which is a common English defect. As to perjury, his lordship says :—" A farmer who has been muddling over matters with another by word of mouth for years, and who finds himself confronted with an awkward document, is apt to lie to get out of it. Then imaginative people, inwardly very excitable, but outwardly silently and shy, especially when they speak in a langnage not quite familiar to them, are apt to lie in order to win. If, however, I were asked whether a Welshman, as such, was more disposed to perjury than an Englishman, as such, I could not say that he was." COUNTERFEIT MONEY. IMPORTANT ARRESTS. At Shrewsbury, on Friday, Arthur Mees, alias John Rylan, was charged with uttering a number of base coins in Shrews- bury. The prisoner was arrested the day following Shrews- bury races at the railway station after a strong resistance. He had a bag containing 37 counterfeit coins in his posses- sion. He was remanded for communication with the Mint authorities.—The same day Peter Daffy and his wife were remanded at Glasgow on a charge of being manufacturers of base coin. On Thursday the two were discavered in a house in Deanside-lane, Glasgow, on tbe fire in which was a lead boiling pot. In the heuse were found the implements which base coiners employ, namely, chipped pewter spoon, two batteries, two moulds of two-shilling pieces, chalk, plaster of Paris, two bottles of acid, and a counterfeit florin. A SALVATION ARMY PROPERTY LEAGUE. The latest scheme of General Booth's foe raising funds is unique and ingenious. The new undertaking has been designated the "Salvation Army Property League," for which the shares will be available in a few days. It is proposed to enrol not less than 20.000 members, to be called shareholders, at a minimum contribution of is. This will produce £4,000 a year, besides which the General anticipates that large sums will be continually added to the fund by gifts and legacies. The money thus raised is to be devoted to the purchase of new barracks and halls. The league will purchase halls and barracks for divisional corps, and will stand in rela- tion of landlord to the corps. For instance, a corps wanting a barracks will have to raise one-sixth of the entire cost, and the league will find the remainder and build the place, and in case of a building which had cost them £l,OOO they are to charge the corps a weekly rental of 30s. Members are intormed that every penny paid will be representative, as the money will be repaid, and again spent in providing ether barracks. MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND THE "WELL-PAID PATRIOTS." —Writing to a Bolton correspondent who asked why he absented himself from the division on Mr. Parnell's Tenants Relief Bill, the Right Hon. J. Chamberlain says:—" I dis- approved entirely of Mr. Parnell's bill. I considered it a dishonest piece of party tactics intended to divide, if possible, the Liberal Unionist% and to provoke agitation in Ireland. I was in favour of giving some further discretion in dealing with evictions, not because I anticipate that there will be an unfair recourse to evictions during the coming winter, but because I considered that the authority for law would be strengthened when it was made perfectly evident that no man would be evicted without the clearest grounds of right and justice. But Mr. Parnell's bill could have done very little for the honest tenant, whilst it would have thrown the whole system of land tenure once more into confusion. The only people who would benefit would be the well-paid patriots, who have already made such a profitable business out of this agitation. lam glad to think that they are be- ginning to be found out both in America and in Ireland, and I should not be surprised if the influence which they have exercised with such unhappy effect for the past few years should speedily collapse in face of the determination of the people of Great Britain not to yield another inch to the vile conspiracy which relies en outrage and assassination to pro- mote its end. MR. GLADSTONE AND SCOTCH LIBERALS. Mr. Glad- stone has written as follows regarding the manifesto of the National Liberal Federation of Scotland :—" Hawarden Castle, Chester, September 29.—Dear Sir,—l thank you for your obliging communication. lam glad to see that in the manifesto you have taken a stop towards the free and fall consideration in end by Scotland how far the present par- liamentary and governmental arrangements are suited to her wants ; and, generally, I can assure you that I feel grateful for her action in the Irish question thus far. I feel yet more confident as to the direction and efficacy of that action in the future.—l remain, dear sir, your most faithful and obedient servant, W. E. GLADTONE."—Tht, manifesto counsels the Liberal electors of Scotland to in- form themselves upon the real facts of the Irish question, and to read the record of Irish wrongs. The immediate prospect is held to be gloomy in the extreme, and bitterly disappointing, and it is urged that until Ireland obtains a government acceptable to the people, no real union can exist, and no progress can he made towards the greater con- silidation of the empire. The manifesto also counsels the Liberal electors to direct attention to the question of Home Rule for Scetlaed. Scottish bueiness, it says, gets scant justice at Westminster, and social reforms demanded for more than a generation, and now ripe for legislation. can- not be approached so long as the mind and purpose of the nation are smothered by the overpowering Conservatism of England. Scotland cannot quietly submit to be so treated. The true remedy is Home Rule—allowing the Scottish people to manage their own affairs. The crisis through which the country is now passing can be only satisfactorily 'overcome by the resolute application of genuine Liberal principles.
SHOCKING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.
A BARONET'S SON KILLED.

Mr. Edward J. H. Synge' assistant manager of the works of the Lancashire Alkali and Sulphur Com- pany, Widnes, met with his death under most painful circumstances on Saturday night. About half-past ten, the driver of a light engine, which was proceeding to Ditton, felt the engine " jump " when about ten yards below the down platform. He at once stopped the engine and whistled for assistance. A search re- vealed the lifeless body of Mr. Synge lying in the four foot. At first the deceased gentleman was unknown, but his name was discovered on a contract ticket be- tween Runcorn to Frodsham. His identity was estab- lished early on Sunday morning, when Mrs Synge, accompanied by her mother, arrived at the Railway Hotel, where the body had been conveyed. The de- ceased was the third son of Sir Robert Synge, Bart., Paignton, Devon, formerly a captain in the Royal Navy. He was also nephew to the late Sir Edward Synge, third baronet of Leslee Court, Cork.. The deceased gentleman, who was only 32 years of age, was well known in Widnes, and his sad and untimely end is deeply regretted by a large circle of friends and acquaintances. He had recently taken the house at Fa.rnworth, formerly occupied by Mr. Charles Knight, in order that he might be nearer to the works, and had made arrangements for haying the place beauti • fully decorated and fitted up. The melancholy oc- currence was feelingly alluded to by the Ven. Arch- deacon Bardsley at the evening service on Sunday at St. Saviour's, Falkner-square, Liverpool, the deceased having formerly been a member of the congregation. The deceased has left a widow and two young children to mourn his untimely fate. The inquest was held at the Railway Hotel on Tuesday, before Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coronN., and a jury, of which Mr. S. Yarwood was the foremin. Mr. C. R. Copeman, solicitor, of Liverpool, was preLent on behalf of the friends of the deceased; Mr. E. W. Parnell, a director of the Alkali Company, represented the deceased's employ- ers ; and Mr. Ferrand, of the solicitors' department, Lime- street, and Inspector Taylor, of Edge Hill, represented the Railway Company. Inspector Millington conducted the in- quiry. for the police. . . _

- Willoughby- Arthur Pemberton, of 4, Cleveland-terrace, Hyde-park, London, identified the body of the deceased, and said be was 32 years of age. William James &yes, of 1, Greek-street, off Lord-street, Runcorn, said he was ticket collector on the Widnes side of the Runcorn Bridge. He saw the deceased pass on to the bridge from Widnes between ten and eleven o'clock. He bad lately seen the deceased pass on to the bridge at all hours up to 10 o'clock.

James Lambert, of 50, Bentinck-street, Runcorn, deposed that he was ticket collector at the Runcorn side of Runcorn Bridge. He had known the deceased for about 12 years. He did not pass off the bridge on Saturday night. By Mr. Fer- rand : At the end of the stone wall at the Runcorn end of the bridge there was a gate, and anyone getting over that could get upon the line, and walk direct to the station. Per- sons often did so. He had never seen that gate opened, and believed that it was kept locked. In walking to the station, by getting over the gate a couple of minutes would be saved; but a person doing so would be a trespasser. Charles Sage, 21, Elliot•street, Widnes, an engine driver in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company for 10 years, deposed that on Saturday night he was driving a light engine from Halton Junction to Ditton. He passed Runcorn Station about 10-30, at a speed of 15 miles an hour. He whistled as he passed through the station. Just beyond the end of the platform be felt the engine crash over something, and lift as though they had run over somebody. He reversed the engine and went back to ascertain what was the matter. He first found a man's hat in the four-foot, a piece of an arm, and then the body. The body was very much mangled, and was lying in the "four-foot." As his engine was going out of the station the ten o'clock express, Liverpool to Chester, was just drawing up. A By r. Copeman : His engine was "tender first," and he could not see things quite so diatinctly as when going in the ordinary fashion. It was very dark, and he did not see anyone on the line. He could not say whether the lamps were lighted on the right hand side of the platform; they were lighted on the left hand side. He gave a prolonged whistle as he went through the station. Three tender wheels and one engine wheel had not passed over the body. He was of opinion that the Chester train had knocked the deceased into the four-foot, because of the peculiar position of the body. Walter Bray, contractor at the Lancashire Alkali and Sulphur Company, deposed that he parted from Mr. Synge in Waterloo-road, Widnes. at 10-15 on Saturday night. Mr. Synge said he had not mach time in which to catch his train, and should have to hurry. Several jurymen said it was a common occurrence to tres- pass upon the line in the manner described to catch trains, and suggested that several of the offenders should De prose- cuted as a warning. Mr. Ferrand remarked that it was very difficult to catch them.
A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. THE FUNERAL.

At the funeral, which took place on Wednesday, the Von. Archdeacon Bardsley officiated, and after the service in the chapel addressed the large congregation. The chief mourners were Captain Sir R. Synge, Bart., R.N. (father), and Larry Synge, Mr. and Mrs Dupois (London), Mr. Penn Harris, and Mrs Harris (Liverpool.) There were also present Mesrs. Crowe, Kirtlan, F. BankiAr, Simon Gar- diner, C. Bankier, C. R. Copeman, &c. Of those connec- ted with the works were Messrs. E. W. Parnell, J. Simpson (directors). J. M•Mahon (senior chemist), T. Willan (cashier), F. Wilson, R. Jones, P. M‘Guire, T. M‘Guire, T. Rowley, J. Trainor, Oultram, Dawson, C. Smith. Stan- ton, W. Brown, and others. The coffin was covered with wreaths sent or placed by relatives and friends, and bore on the shield the inscription "Edward J. H. Synge; born sth March, 1854; died 2nd Oct., 188 G. At rest."
Mesmerism consists of subjecting the mind of one per- son to the control of another. The less mind a man has, the easier he is mesmerised.

A schoolmaster thus describes a money lender: "He serves you in the present tense; he lends you in the con- ditional mood; keeps you in the subjunctive; and ruins you in the future." An irishman took the train from London to Gravesend. On Jumping from the carriage he remarked that "If he had known he could have made the journey in so short a time he would have walked afoot."

"Why, how tight you wear your corsets !" said one lady to another, as they were dressing for dinner. "I never could enjoy anything I ate if I wore mine as tight as you do." "Grace before meat," the other replied, as she laced herself in.

There are 2,750 languages in the world, and a man feels that all of them put together are inadequate to express his feelings when he gets home from church and finds that he has put a sovereign in the contribution box, mistaking it for a shilling. 0; -7 A boy was asked which was the greater evil, hurting another's feelings or his finger ?" The feelings," he said. "Right, my dear child," said the gratified ques- tioner; "and why is it worse to hurt the feelings?" "Because you can't tie a rag round them" answered the child. 6IIDDEN DEATH AT NEWTON. —On Sunday morning Amy Parker, the infant daughter of John Parker, a labourer, residing in Mercer-street, Newton' was found dead in bed. Deceased had been a healthy child since birth, and she was taken to bed by her mother about half-past eleven on Satur- day night. The child was then asleep, and Mrs. Parker placed it on her left arm. The mother slept until half-past six on the following morning, when she woke, and seeing that something was wrong with her child awoke her hus- band, who called in a neighbour, named Hannah Plant. The infant appeared to be dead. and Dr. Overton, atsistant to Dr. J. W. Watkins. who was called in, certifitd the child to be dead. The body of the child was discoloured about the neck, chest, face, and head, and had the appearance of having been overlain.—An inquest on the body cf the de- ceased was held before Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, at the White Lion Inn, Newton, on Tuesday afternoon.—The jury heard evidence to the foregoing effect, and returned a ver- dict of "Accidentally overlain."

DESTRUCTIVP FIRE AT NEWTON PAPER MILL --£1,400 DAMAGES. On Saturday afternoon a destructive and somewhat mys- terious fire was discovered to have broken out on the pre- mises of Messrs. Gillespie and Mason, owners of the well- known Newton Paper Mill, situate in Mill-lane, Newton, near the railway station. The whole of the hands employed at the mill had left the grounds at about twelve o'clock,:and the place was locked up apparently secure. About a quar- ter past one, however, a girl named McDuff, daughter of the timekeeper at the works, and whose father is also employed as watchman, was passing along Mill-lane, when she noticed flames and smoke issuing from a portion of the works. She at once gave an alarm, and Mr. Bryce, the manager, with several employee, were quickly on the snot. It was then found that the jute-shed, in which over 200 tons of jute, in bales, was stored, was on fire. The jute-shed was an iron structure, consisting of iron pillars supporting a roof of similar material. In a very short space of time the entire stock of jute bales was in a blaze, and an immense volume of smoke arose. Men connected with the works, and other persons who had been attracted to the spot, immediately set to work, and while some pulled away the burning materials, others got the hose pipes belonging to the firm and attached these to four stand pipes about the premises. Fortunately there was a plentiful supply of water, but owing to the extreme diffi- culty of getting to the!seat of the fire, which seemed to b 3 in the centre of the bales, the flames were not suppressed until five or six hours afterwards. Some of the bails con- tinued to smoulder for several hours. The whole stock had been more or less damaged. and the total loss, including the shed and its contents, was estimated at about £1,400. The damage is covered by insurance in the Northern Fire and Life Insurance Company. The origin of the fire is not known. As a singular coincidence, it may be stated that October is considered a somewhat unlucky month at the Paper Mill, as the disastrous explosion resulting in the death of two persons and injury to several others occurred on the 22nd October last year, whilst the tire of last Satur- day was on the second day of the same month.

BAPTIST UNION.-ANNUAL SESSION. The annual autumnal session of the Baptist Union of Great Britain and Ireland was opened on Monday evening at Bristol. The number of delegates present was 1.300. The inaugural meeting took place in Colston Hall, when a large number of delegates and their hosts were received by the Mayor, Mr. Wathen. The President, (the Rev. C. Williams, of Accrington) reminded the meeting that the Mayors of Bristol had not al- ways been well disposed to their denomination. In the year 1663 Sir John Knight was Mayor of Bristol, and on the 4th of October—(laughter)—in that year he committed Mr. Ewens, minister of Broadnaead Chapel, to prison for rioting, the rioting being preaching to a Dissenting congre- gation. Things had greatly changed since then. He ob- served that they would very soon be in the jubilee year of the reign of Queen Victoria. (Cheers.) Baptists had never been suppliants at the footstool of an earthly throne. They sought no favour, and they did not proffer any false- homage; but in all things secular they yielded to none in loyalty, and they had every reason to regard with estedbe, respect, reverence, and grateful love her Majesty the Queen. Iu her time they had seen many great changes. Compulsory Church rates had been abolished, the Universities had been opened to men of all creeds and churches, and he was thankful to say to men of no creed and no church, thus recognising the great principle of religious equality. In ad- dition to that they had seen one State Church totally dis- established and partly disendowed. (Applause.) They had seen their parochial graveyards thrown open to dis- senters as to Churchman, and they were getting at any rate within reach not only of perfected religious liberty, but also of its just and logical complement—religious equality. He knew that they did not owe all that to the Queen. They owed much of it to men like Edward Mien, a man who was not appreciated as he should be, a man of keen intellect and pure motive, a man thoroughly disinterested, and whom he believed had done mere for religious liberty during their time than any other man that could be named. They owed, too, not a little to men like John Bright, the Quaker patriot, to men like Sir Morton Petto, Henry Richard, and the late Mr. Samuel Morley, to whose memory he paid a glowing tribute. —The annual meeting of the Baptist Total Abstinence So- ciety was held simultaneously with the otlicial reception of the Union at the Colston Hall. Nevertheless Broadmead Chapel was well filled, and the audience was enthesiastic.— Mr. Caine, president of the society, was announced to preside, but, being on the Continent, Mr. Handel Cossham, member for one of the divisions for Bristol, took the chair, and recalled the many efforts for the enlightenment and freedom of the nation politically in which the Baptist body had taken a conspicuous part, and urged that the same noble energy should be put forth in battling with the greatest evil which affected the nation. The remedy they proposed was safe, easy, and efficacious, and he urged its adoption. save the £120,000,000 a year now spent upon intoxicants, and more will be done to remedy bad times than any Par- liamentary measures that could be adopted.—The Rev. J.R. Wood, of Holloway, gave an earnest address chiefly con- cerning the bearing of the Baptist temperance movement upon the Congo River and the West coast of Africa.—Dr. Barn, of London, followed by an appeal in favour of legis- lation for the restriction of the liquor traffic in this coun- try, as well as the promotion of the same aims by moral force. More than a thousand Baptist ministers were now pledged total abstainers.—An encouraging report was pre- sented by Mr. Sears, the secretary, There were 300 more abstaining than non-abstaining ministers, and the students in the colleges were almost unanimously abstainers. On Tuesday, the Baptist Mission Conference at Bristol was presided over by Sir Morton Peto, and listened to earn- est addresses on the claims of India, China, and Africa, by the Revs. S. Vincent, of Plymouth, R. Glover, of Bristol, and W. J. Henderson, of Coventry, respectively. In the evening an enormous gathering at Colston Hall, presided over by Mr. Townsend, of Bristol. witnessed the designation of ten missionaries for various foreign stations, and who were commended to the work in a touching address from Dr. MacLaren, of Manchester. At Wednesday's sitting of the Baptist Union, the Rey. C. Williams, of Accrington, delivered his presidential address, the title of which was "A plea for Puritanism." Mr. Wil- liams said he believed it was incumbent upon them to give a Puritan training to the young people of their families and congregations. It was made matter of complaint that chil• dren of rich Disseners went over to the Church of England, but he was sure they gained more than they lost by such changes. The Puritans bad rendered signal services to the world; all that was best in the constitution of the American Republic was due to the early Puritan settlers, and in Eng- land the Commonwealth period made the Victorian era pos- eiWee At the close of the address the Assembly adjourned until the afternoon, when reports on the Baptist Union funds were submitted. The income of the annuity fund, including £2,406 realised by redemption of stock, amounted to £9,315, and the payments to annuitants to £3.705. The total investments to September 30 were £109,738. Thire are 845 beneficiary members and 121 annuitants. There are 142 accepted applications for grants from the augmentation fund.
At the meeting of the Baptist Union on Thursday it was resolved to prep we an address of congratulation to her Majesty for presentation on the occasion of her jubilee.

THE TurrtE WAR.—The farmers at LlantysiliO, in the Vale of Llangollen, have received a reply to the memorial forwarded to the tithe owners, praying for a reduction of 25 ~er cent. Substantial abatement is promised for the present and previous half-year, and it is believed an amicable settle- went will now be arranged.

MR. GLADSTONE AND THE IRISH DEPUTATIONS. On Monday the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone was I presented at Hawarden with the freedom of the boroughs of Cork, Waterford, Limerick, mad Clonmel. The gentlemen who had been empowered to make the presentation arrived at the Castle at noon, and were received by the ex-Premier and Mrs. Gladstone, and conducted to the library, a spacious apartment look- ing on to the flower-decked terrace fronting the man- sion. There was also a deputation of ladies, whose purpose it was to present a declaration in favour of Home Rule, which had received the signatures of several thousands of the gentler sex in the sister isle. A few of the ladies wore costumes of • the Irish na- tional colour, and it was remarked that the walls of the room in which Mr. Gladstone bade them welcome were also of the same hue.—The ladies address having been presented by the Lady Mayoress of Dubliu, the MAYOR of Costa followed with the address of the Cork City Council. He said the Municipal Council desired to acknowledge Mr. Glridstone's great genius as a statesman, and the chivalrous and splendid efforts which he had made to restore to Ireland that heritage of legislative independence of which she was so perfidiously plundered at the beginning of this century. To him had been reserved the signal distinction of being the first British statesman to recognise and give effect to the legitimate aspirations of a generous and high-spirited people. He had justified before the world the political faith that had ever been in Irishmen, and had inspired them with a hope that the goal of their national ambition would soon be reached. Upon Mr. Gladstone, under Providence, they rested their confidence in the realisation of that hope, and earnestly prayed that the health and vigour and the matchless intre- pidity which triumphed over the paltry existences of party might be preserved to him till he should have given them in full measure the great boon of regenerated nationhood for which they had so long sighed anti suffered. The Mayors of Limerick, Waterford, and Clonmel next made their presentations, reading at the same time the addresses which had been adopted by their respective Corportions. In each of these addressee eulogist:c reference was made to the services which Mr. Gladstone has rendered to the Irish nation. In each case also the official record of the acts by which the several municipalities had conferred upon Mr. Gladstone their highest distinction was enclosed in a c isket of lrisb oak. The casket sent by the municipality of Cork was described as "skilfully and lovingly wrought by Irisa hands, and adorned with the most cherished national and local emblems." Mr. Gladstone was asked to regard it as a symbol of that more precious enshrinemeut of his honoured name and incomparable services in the hearts of the Irish people, and especially of the citizens of Cork, which he had so nobly won, and which they were proud thus formally and emphetically to acknowledge. The address from Waterford contained the following passages :—" Your last mighty effort to restore peace and happiness to Ireland has awakened in the hearts of her people the warmest senti- ments of love and appreciation towards you, and they await with confident hope tate not far distant time when they will receive through yoer hands the priceless boon of self- government. We now ask to subscribe your honoured name on the roll of our citizens, where for long ages it will be faithfully preserved. We have encased the title of your citizenship in Irish oak, fashioned and carved by Irish hands, and crowned by the•emblem of your former peace and prosperity, and we trust it will remain with you and your descendants as a lasting memento of the veneration and regard which the people of Waterford will always entertain for their illustrious fellow-citizen." Mr. GLADSTONE, after having thanked them for the hon- our they had done him, briefly referred to the disestablish- ment of the Irish Church, and then proceeded to speak of the present controversy. He said : It has been a controversy purely constitutional and Parliamentary so far as the Irish nation is concerned. It was necessary before a proposal of this nature could properly be made by a responsible Govern- ment that it should tie beyond all doubt, and upon demon- strative evidence, made clear that it was made in accord with the determination and deliberate desires of the Irish nation. But it was also necessary that it simuld be made clear that such a proposal stood within the limits of imperial honour, imperial safety, and imperial welfare. (Hear, hear.) Those aims have been completely attained. But force from you we are sot dealing with. Apprehensions of a civil war and a great conflict have not proceeded from you. (Hear, hear.) But I grieve to think there have unhappily been others, in what I trust was momentary irritation, who have not scrupled to introduce that sad and terrible element into the controversy. It is indeed strange to reflect that the great and in many respects enlightened town of Belfast should at this time of the day, to the grief, I am sure, as well as to the shame of every right-minded man in that town, have allowed a stain to be attached to its name which it will require long years to efface. (Hear' hear.) I rejoice to think that the cause in which you are em- barked is the cause of order, the cause of peace, the cause of legality, the cause of faith and confidence in the power of free discussion and of Parliamentary institutions. Now I will only say one single word upon my own personal position. Ireland is the key to that position. After a long public life and after lengthened services' retirement would have been a course which would have been recommended to me by many considerations; but it was the hope of con- ducing in some small measure to the settlement of this great question—and it is that hope alone—which keeps me where I am. (Cheers.) Speaking of matters as I now see them, I am here to remain or to withdraw simply as may appear to me to be good for the progress of this question. There are those who think that my withdrawal would tend to bring about a satisfactory settlement—cries of "No " and "It would not ")—bat I have not yet been able to see that (Hear, hear.) At the same time, if I did see it I should act upon it. It is not as a separate interest that I am speaking of the interest of Ireland. The interest of England is in my opinion quite as much involved in this question as that of Ireland, and that in many ways. Looking simply on the question of money to be saved—to be saved I admit by Ire- land in a very great degree, but to be saved also largely by the Imperial exchequer—l know of no prospect of saving • so great as the redemption of the expenditure now given to misclaievous and useless waste, and both civil and military are the heads to which I refer. Is it not a disgrace for this country that at this moment the civil government of Ireland upon the Civil Estimates costs every year 16s per head of the population, while the civil government of England and Scotland costs 8s? But it is not only on account of the great economy, civil and military, to which, in my opinion, the war is clear and open that we urge the change ; it is on other and much higher grounds. For example, until Ire- land and Great Britain are thoroughly one the authority of this country in the councils of the wcrld never will reach the height to which it ought to attain. What has become of the work of legislation in England ? For the last 15 years or more that work has been falling into increasing arrear at the very same time that the popular demand and public exigencies require that it should be prosecuted with additional celerity and effect. In my opinion there is no way to put legislation for England, Scotland, and Wales upon a proper footing without a preliminary solution of the Irish question. There is one word which I do not think ever escapes from your lips in your recommendation of this measure, and it is the word "separation." The fact is, this fear of separation is now used unfairly. It is somewhat unscrupulously used by our opponents, for I think they must know that separation is not in the minds of the pro- moters of this Home Rule Bill, that it is not in your minds on the other side of the channel—(hear, hear)—and that it is not in our minds on this side of the 6,leannel. To speak of those who promote the Home Rule Bill ae Separatists is a monstrous misuse of terms, which indicates the extraor- dinary weakness of a case which requires a resort to weapons unknown in ordinary political warfare. (Hear, bear.) Having dealt with the historical aspect of the question, Mr. Gladstone said : Our op- ponents do not seem to understand why it is that this historic argument requires to be opened up. In this connection I wish to refer to Mr. Bright. I recollect with the deepest pain that he has been among the most efficient of our opponents in this cause, yet in former days and when your friends were fewer he has rendered you generous and probably inestimable service. Mr. Bright, speaking of this subject, has said, "What is the use of raking up all these lamentable events? No doubt, if you go back to the history of our country you will find many things are wrong." That shows me he has not the smallest conception of the nature of the argument, which is this, that from 1782 to 1800 Ire- land was a nation with a national existence and a national Parliament independent of all the world, and by the admis- sion of the British Parliament, her Kings, Lords, and Par- liament were alone entitled to make laws. That was her judicial, her Constitutional position. How has she lost it. No people ever could lose a position of that kind except by its own free and its own deliberate act, and that is the im- portance of the argument. It becomes necessary to show whether tbis act was free and deliberate, because ',unless it was so, or unless it has received'the subsequent ratification by the attachment of the Irish people, it has no moral vali- dity. as we are assured by Mr. Goldwin Smith. (Hear, hear.) We have suffered a great defeat, and in Parliament there are now four sections, and two great parties. Let us consider these four sections. The first is that of the Nationalists. , As 'understand, they intend by Parliamentary power and constitutional action to contend for the granting of a measure of self-government. Then there is the Govern- ment, and they appear to me as if they thought that a liberal effusion of money from the ex- chequer would have the effect of turning away the Irish people from their purpose. I do not believe that that will be found to be the case. There is another matter of great importance. They have encouraged the occupiers of land to believe that the judicial rents will be re- vised, and will in some cases be reduced. That is a declaration of very great importance. I consi- der that declaration to be embodied in the speech of Lord Salisbury at the commencement of the session, when he said it was contended in Ireland that the judicial rents could not be paid, and that he did not accept that statement to any great extent. But I will not say more on that point, because I do not wish to say anything that could be reore- sented as being an attempt to bar the way of the Govern- ment before its measures were produced. rtherefore re- serve my judgment upon these measures and upon the wonderful encyclopedia of promises, for so I may describe it, which appears to have been addressed to a meeting of Conservatives by a gentleman of whose performances as yet we know much less than we certainly do now know of his promises. (Lauglster.) The Liberals form the third section of the House of Commons. We have endeavozred, and have done all in Our power, to make an approximation and to meet the wishes of our opponents that did not entrench upon or hamper the main design. We are still in that humour, but I have not gathered from the declarations of

our opponents that there are fresh concessions that can b 3 reasonably made on their side of the question' Now the fourth party in the House is the smallest in number, and they call themselves Unionists. I feel Et difficulty in calling them by that name, because although I understand them to be thoroughgoing supporters, like the Tories, a the incorporating legislative statute, yet as regards the union between the two countries, between the heart of Great Britain so,: the heart of Ireland, I do not understand them to be uhienists at all. (Hear, hear.) i I hope it will not be thought an offence, but I think it s a fair description to call thern Sece4rs or Discontent Liberals. The question between them and us can only b 3 settled hY time. It is a very great issue, and I feel confident that those gentlemen acted upon conscientious conviction. Ahis regards the past, they are a triumphant party; they turn"' the scale; they inflicted the defeat. They have taken the burden of the work, and have saved the Tories the trouble. They have probably done it better than the Tories would have done it for themselves. At any rate, they have done it with great ability, and with immetise and unbounded en- thusiasm, and they not only threw out the hill in the last Parliament, but they have defeated the caese of Home Rule within the limits of England at the general election. Just look at the enormous difference in the facts of the case, Last December there were 85 Nationalists, as they were called, in Parliament, and there were 335 Liberals. Those together wade 420. Un the opposite side there were not more than 250. See what a power there was then in e" tence, had there been unity of mind in the Liberal partY, and you will see now how great is the contrast. Instead of 250 Tories, we have, mainly through the agency of the Dissentient Libera!s, something like 315 or 318 Tome, and we have with them from 70 to 75 Dissentient Liberals, making 390 avainst 280 friends of what we think to be the Irish cause instead of the 420 who might have been in Its favour and 250 against it. And that is the result of the action of the dissentient Liberals, and in the case of some of them like Mr. Goschen and Mr. Trevelyan, they have expiated whatever guilt, if it was guilt, there was in their conduct through the verdict of the Scotch people; others like Mr. Chamberlain have developed very great and con' spicuons Parliamentary powers in what I think I may call an unhappy cause, and above all Lord Hartington, who .ha ms by far a preponderating influence, has led and has organised this body and has attached himself to L in the closest manner. No greater triumph was ever achieved by a small party. That is in the Peet, but wben I think of their present position, and When I think of the future, it does not appear to me so satisfactory. The first article of their creed is that they are Liberals, and .as Liberals they recognise what I believe is the general prin- ciple of Liberalism ; a habit of acting, subject of course, to the restraints of prudence, on the principle of trust in the nation. They, on the contrary, have, through their deep misfortune, been compelled to adopt for their guiding laW of action mistrust of the nation. They are likewise in this position. Some persons have thought that they bold the balance of power. They have told us that they felt theme selves bound to support the Tory Government. not only' upon Irish questions, but upon any question necessary to retain them in office. It is plain that in that view of the case these Dissentient Liberals would become nothing else but a tail to the Tory party. (Hear, hear and laughter.) I belief's there are still a few dreamers who think that on this side of the water the Irish question depends upon my' poor individual existence. If the thread of that existence were broken to-morrow it would make no difference as re- gards the Irish question. I have never known a question taken up with greater conviction and with warmer and livelier enthusiasm. In my judgmentyour cause is now firmly' adopted and enrolled as an article in the creed of the Ll3eral party. (Cheers.) And if you will survey impartially the history of the last fifty years you will find that it is that adoption and that enrolment which in the case of every great subject has formed the uniform promise and precursor of ultimate and in most cases of early triumph. I believe in your triumph. I will venture to say I believe in the early triumph of your cause. I trust that triumph will come in the way in which alone it can be truly honourable and thoroughly satisfactory to England and Ireland, that it will come to us with promptitude, with cheerfulness, and with joy. (Cheers). The deputations were subsequently entertained at luncheon by Mr. and Mrs Gladstone.

div.head: TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSION.
div.p: TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSION.
GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.

On Saturday evening an explosion occurred at the Silkstone pit of Messrs. Pope and Pearsons, colliery proprietors Altofts, near Normanton, resulting in great loss of life. Events seem to indicate the firing of the gas in some parts of the workings. The pit was regarded as an unusually safe one, and it was rarely that as was uiscovered in it. It being Satur- day afternoon, only about 30 men were employed in the mine, and of these 21 have been killed. Several are sadly burnt, recognition in two or three cases being very difficult. The fire appears also to have ignited the stables, and 30 or 40'pit ponies have been killed; others, having escaped from the stables, were running loose about the pit. The explosion was heard at a radius of at least two miles, and quickly the officials connected with the col- liery and the neighbouring pits were present to render every assistance. The firing engineer (Mr. Bramley) and one of the workmen were the first to go down, tied to the end of a rope, and great credit is due to these two men for the courage they displayed, for the pit is 420 yards deep, and the cages were unworkable, the shock having rendered them so. They soon heard signals from the men in the pit, and an exploring party was formed and went down as soon as the cage was righted, headed by Mr. IV. P. Garforth (the col- liery manager), Mr. J. Fisher (the certified manager), Mr. Buxton (the steward), and Mr. Bramley (the engineer). It is fearful to contemplate what would have been the conse- quences had the mishap occurred a few hours earlier, when about 500 men were in the working. It appears that after the men had been down the mine nearly an hour, a most alarm- ing explosion took place, startling the whole district, and sounding almost like a peal of thunder. This was followed instantly by dense volumes of smoke rising from the shaft. The explosion caused intense excitement in the district, which is inhabited almost exclusively by colliers, and the utmost anxiety prevailed amongst the relatives of the men who were known to be at work. Large numbers of persons at once rushed to the place, and up to Monday night the bank was crowded. Seven men were discovered near the bottom of the shaft, some of whom were suffering severely from the effects of the explosion, but had con- trived to make their way to where they were found. These were brought out after the lanse cf some hours, and it was found that some were very severely burnt about the head and arms. Others were able to walk home. The fire in the stables was not extinguished until between eight and nine o'clock on Sunday morning. It was also found that the air crossing had been blown out, and the conductors in the shaft disarranged. The Silkstone seam has always been re- garded as free from gas, and during the 20 years the com- pany has worked it, there has been no serious accident. Indeed, up to the last six months naked lights were used, but since then safety lamps of the most reoeern construction —the bonnetted canny—have been employed. Every im- provement in mining has always been adopted at the col- liery, and water cartridges were about to be introduced throughout the working, having been thoroughly tested in one section. The pit has hitherto been considered one of the safest and best managed in England.

"That is because there is a hole on the other side," answered Bebe, with becoming dignity. BATHING IN WARM WATER.—CIeaHIiHeSS isTnot only essential to good health, but also a mark of good breed- ing. Too frequent bathing, however, is weakening. It may not be advisable to take a bath morning and even- ing, as some medical journals advise; but there should be a good washing frequently enough to keep the body clean. Warm baths will often prevent the most virulent diseases. A person who may be in fear of having re- ceived infection of any kind, should take a warm bath, suffer perspiration to ensue, and then rub dry. He is advised to dress warmly to guard against taking cold. If the system has imbibed any infectious matter, it will be removed by resorting to the warm bath if the latter is taken before the infection has time to spread over the system; and even if some time has elapsed, the drench- ing perspiration that may be induced by hot water will be very certain to remove it. In cases of congestion, bilious colic, inflammation, &c., there is no remedy more certain to give relief than a hot bath. In cases of obsti- nate constipation also, wonderful cures have been wrought. For sore throat, diphtheria, and inflammation of the lungs, a hot compress is one of the most potent remedies.

THE Woopcom—Of the woodcocks which arrive in the British Islands in October a large number remain each year to pair and nest. The late Mr. Lloyd, in his "Scandanavian Adventures," says :—" If in shooting you meet with a brood of woodcocks and the young ones cannot fly, the old bird takes them separately between her feet, and flies from the dogs with 11, moaning cry." One of the brothers Stuart in the second volume of the Lays of the Deer Forest," says that he say' a woodcock rising with a young bird in her feet, her long legs dangling and swinging with her little burden like a parachute. She lighted at no great distance, but as he at once came upon her, she got up. In her hurry young dropped the youn bird. She came to the groune, however, almost at the same time as the young one; running back, she sat upon him and rose again with him in her claws. Mr. C. St. John, in his " Natural History and Sport of Moray." declares "that the ela woodcock carried her young, even when larger than a snipe, not in her claws, but. by grasping the little bird tightly between her feet ;" and further, "that in the spring and summer evenings the woodcocks may be seen so employed, passing to and fro and utterin a gentle cry, on their way from the woods to the marshes, wbere they feed." ---- • • ...••••
