FOREIGN NEWS- -- _ _ THE BULGARIAN QUESTION. - REPLY TO THE RUSSIAN NOTE. -MENACING ATTITUDE OF

GENERAL KAULBARS. ST. PETERSBURG, SATURDAY. To-day's journals anent unfavourably unfavourably upon M. Tisza's reply to the inter- pellations in the Hungarian Diet, dwelling especially upon the passages relating to the independence of the Balkan States and to the question of a foreign protectorate. SOFIA, SUNDAY.—The great meeting organised for to-day to hear the result of the interview on the 29th ult. between General Kaulbars and the deputation led by Dr. Vultcheff took place at eleven o'clock this morning, between 4,000 and 5,000 persons being present. The proceedings opened by Dr. Vultcheff giving an account of the interview in question. During his speech he was continually cheered, and groans were given for Russia. Dr. Vultcheff then proposed a re- solution of confidence in the Government, with an assur- ance of moral and material support so long as it continwed in its present policy of maintaining the independence of the Constitution and the laws of the country.—After this reso- lution bad been carried, amid loud cheers, a Russian in the crowd shouted "Long live the Emperor," "Down with the Government." For this he was somewhat roughly handled, and was only saved from the infuriated populace by the efforts of the police.—General Kaelbars then unexpectedly appeared on tbe scene and mounted the tribune. After a great deal of interruption, General Kaulbar's patience was was exhausted, and, adopting a menaciug tone, he threw the responsibility for the consequences which would arise from not listening to' Russia's advice on the country, and declared that the Bulgarian people as a nation did not desire tbe constitution, but a few men only. At this point the shout- ing became so violent that General Kaulbars had to leave the tribune. A deputation then proceeded to the residence of M. Radoslavoff, the Premier, and read the resolution which had been adopted. al. Radoslavoff, in reply, de- clared that he would always follow the policy hitherto adopted—a policy which was dictated by a desire to main the law and Constitution, and to assure independence and liberty. Amid loud and prolonged cheers the people lifted the premier in their arms. The utmost enthusiasm was shown all along the road from the place of meet- ing to the Premier's house, the National Anthem being sung by the whole crowd. VIENNA, SUNDAY. King Milan. of Servia, arrived here on Friday night. His Majesty e ill remain here several days for the purpose of ascertaining the opinion of diplo- matists in this c .pital with reference to the situation in the Balkans. The King, it is stated, knows how necessary it is that he should be on his guard against Russian designs in his kingdom. A coup de main such as that which cost Prince Alexander of Bulgaria his throne is regarded as no nolikely possibiltiv at Belgrade, and has been rendered the more likely since Russia's designs in Bulgaria have received a check at the hands of Austria. Already the trouble has, according to common report, begun to roll in Servia, where the Panslavists are bueily plying their propaganda. King Milan has take every conceivable precaution against such a surprise as befell his princely neighbour of Bulgaria. PHILIPOPOLIS, MONDAY. Public opinion here is in ac- cordance with the resolutions adopted at the meeting at Sofia yesterday. The Russian Consul is again taking meas- ures for distributing among the people the demands 01 General Kaulbars, his first attempt having been frustrated by the confiscation of the placards by the anthorities. PESTH, Moenesae.—A despetch received from Sofia states that of the foreign representatives in that city the French agent alone openly supports General Kaulbars. Intelli- ligence from Warsaw reports that many Montenegrin and Servian subjects have been enrolled in the Russian army at the Government expense, and will remain with the forces until next spring:. BUCHLREST, MONDAY.—It is rumoured here to-night that revolutions have broken out simultaneously in Sofia and Tirnova Details, which are not yet to hand, are awaited with breathless suspense. It is believed that at least three of the great Powers are in agreement as to the attitude which should be adopted on the Bulgarian question. Should Russia find a pretext to carry out her plans in connection with Bulgaria by force, it is certain that a Joint Note of protest from those three Powers would be at once despatchei to St. Peters-

burg. VinnsA., WRDNESDA.r.--i telegram from Sofia published by the "New Free Press" reports that a sensation has been caused in the Bulgarian capital by the arrest of the Bul- garian Brigadier General Schiwaroff, who had been main- taining clandestine relations with General Ranlhars. RUSTCEMIK, WEDNESDAY.—The Russian Consul here has informed Colonel Riloff, commander of the garrison, that if he released the conspirators he would be made a general and otherwise rewarded on the arrival of the Russian troops in Bulgaria, hut that if he disobeyed General Katabars' orders be would be reduced to the ranks. Colonel Reloff communicated these facts to the troops, who joined enthusi- astically in his refusal to liberate the prisoners. INDIA.—SERIOUS AFFAIR.—MANY NATIVES INJURED.

MADRAS, FRIDAY.—A terrible occurrence in the Madras presidencv is reported. Disastrous floods have inundated the Godavay district, and a large number of villagers attempted to cut the bund in order to free their own vil- lagers with water at the expense of others. The inhabi- tants of these places resisted the attempt, and a fierce fight ensued, inl,which, it is said, nearly 100 people were killed. BOMBA.Y, MONDAT.—The "Times of India" publishes in- telligence of a serious affair which occurred"at Etawah, Ben- gal Presidency; in connection with the Busserah and Muhur- rum festivals. A conflict between the Mahometans and Hindoos seeming inevitable, the local magistrate stopped a train with British troops who were on their way to Burmah. At sight of the troops the mob became infuriated, and rushed straight on the soldiers' bayonets. Many of the natives were wounded in the encounter, some of them mortally. Precau- tions have been taken at Allahabad to prevent.disturbances, and some natives who were seen in the streets after nine in the evening, armed with sticks, were arrested. MADRAS, MONDAY,—The remainder of the troops selected for service with the Burmese expedition have sailed for Rangoon. The "Madras Mail" states that a demon- stration in which a large number of persons took part has been held at Trinchinonoly to protest against the payment of income tax. The shops are closed, and business is at a standstill. The Mahometan members of the community are especially excited. Bomse.y, WRDNESDAY,—A serious riot has occurred at Delhi between a number of [Undoes and Mahometans. The latter having armed thernsrdves with clubs, stopped a Hindos procession, and a fight ensued. The police being unable to quell the disturbance, the military were called out and sestored order. One Hindoo was killed and several Wounded. BURMAH.—SUFFERTNGS OF BRITISH TROOPS. RANGOON, SIINDAY.—The detachment under Major Meacham, which has been surrounded for some time past at Thabvabin by Boshwav's force, was relieved on September 28th by 120 of the South Wales Borderers, commanded by Captain Aldwhrth. The relieuing force was not oppoaed on

its march. Major Meacham's force was found in a terrible condition. Out of 50 of the South Wales Borderers 17 had died of fever, and 32 were sick and disabled, only one man remaining fit for duty. A complement of the 16th Bengal Infantry, which formed the remainder of the force at Tha- byabin, has also suffered from fever, two Sepoys having died and another being disabled. No casualities occurred among the officers. RANGOON, MONDAY.—Intelligence has been received that the pretender to the chiefship of Magoung has been killed. A prominent dacoit leader has been captured at Sagaing, and another at Tayco. The expedition from Kendat has dispersed the rebels in the Chindwin Valley, inflicting upon them a trifling loss. A loyal woon, who had been forced to join the rebels, was rescued. THE RISING IN SPAIN. MADRID SubrDAY.—llnring a bull fight this afternoon a number of spectators suddenly displayed large placards bearing the inscription " Long bee Alphonso XIII., pardon for the prisoners, long live the army, long live the Queen." The demonstration caused considerable excitement, but it was received with applause by the spectators. MADRID. MONDAY—The Supreme Council of War and Marine has concluded its deliberations, and has confirmed the sentence of death passed upon Baigadier General Villa- camps and five others. MADRID, TUBSDAY.—The Cabinet Council, by desire of the Queen Regent, has decided that the sentence of death passed upon Brigadier General Villacampa, Lieutenant Gonzalek, and four eergeants, should be commuted to mili- tary imprisonment for life in the Spanish African posses- sions.

EATHQUAKE IN GERMANY. BERLIN, FRIDAY.—From various parts of central Ger- many, principally Thuringis, news continues to arrive show- ing that on the night of the 271 h, or morning of the 28th ult, there was a series of more or. less violent earthquake, At Gerna and other places in Thuringsa the windows, doors, cupboards, and other movable articles of furniture were violently atitated, shaking and rocking too and fro. I VOLCANIC ERUP [ION IN AUSTRALIA. MELBOURNE, TUESDAy.—A volcanic eruption has occurred on the Island of Niapa, in the Tonga Group. Two-thirds of the island is completely covered with volcanic dust. A steamer has been despatched te the scene. It is believed that no loss of life has occurred, but this is not certain. The island has a population of 500 persons. CAPTURE OF TAMAI. SUAKIM, THURSDAY. At dawn this morning the friend- lies captured by assault Tamai, Osman Digma's old strong- hold, after a desperate fight in which the rebels lost 200 men killed and many wounded. Several more were taken prisoners. Osman Digma's nephew WAS ameng the slain. The friendlies' loss was comparatively slight, being about 20 killed and as many wounded. GREAT COMMERCIAL DEPRESSION IN NEW SOUTH WALES. SYDNEY, THURSDAY.—Sir Patrick A. Jennings has made a statement in the Legislative Assembly, in which he de- clared that, owing to the falling off in the receipts from nearly all sources of revenue, there would probably be at the end of the year a total deficit of £2,000,000. in conclu- sion, the Premier added that be could not recollect the country liaving been in such a depressed state as at present for the last twenty-two years. DEMOCRATIC SUCCESSES IN AMERICA. NEw YORK, TRURSDA.Y.—The Democrats have been vie- torious in Georgia State elections. General J. B. Gordon has been elected Governor, and the Democrats have also re- turned their entire State legislative ticket.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. At Owenduff, about 30 miles from Westport, Charles Moran was fired at on Saturday, and shot through the neck. Three men have been arrested on suspicion. Tbe outrage is believed to be agrarian. The four men who were arrested at Penagh, near Feale Bridge, Kerry, on the 23rd ult., were again charged at Lis- towel on Saturday with unlawfully assembling, armed with revolvers, to terrify inhabitants, and discharging shots at police petrel. Owing to want of evidence they were dis- charged.—Three men were also charged at Listowel on Saturday with conspiring to prevent Mr. Huggard, sub- sheriff of the county, executing his duty on Aeg. 11 and 13, when carrying out evictions. They also were discharged for want of evidence. A Belfast newspaper publishes a summary of the leading events of the riots in the town from June 4, when they broke out, up to the present time. This report states that inquest have been held on 30 persons killed during the riots. Of the 30, only seven—six men and boys and one woman— were Roman Catholics, the remaining 23 being Protestants. Of the seven Roman Catholics three were killed in the affray. The other four were shot by the police. Four of the Protestants were killed in the affray. Nineteen were shot by the police, and one a girl of seven, killed by a re- volver bullet fired frcm the Falls-road direction. The Head-Constable Gardiner, and the soldier Private Hughes, were shot while on duty at the Brickfields at midnight on July 13th. The civilians, Robt. Wylie and &rel. M‘Farland, were killed, the former in the Springfield-roed fight on Aug.' Bth, and the latter in an affray of a similar kind at North , Howard-street on August 15th. Of those killed by the police 10 were men or youths, three women, and six boys under 16. The wounded it would be impossible to number, but they amounted to several hundreds, some of whom are crippled for life. As two emergency caretakers were returning home ma Sunday, not far from Castleisland, a number of men jumped ever the fence from both sides of the road, and hav- ing taken their revolvers, disappeared as quickly as they came. The Dublin Evening Telearaph says: We have reason to believe that a packet of Government despatches, which was being forwarded by post to county Kerry for the guidance of General Buller, have not reached their desti- nation. It is said that they got as far as the General Post-office, but that they have been mislaid, or at all events cannot be found. There is said to be much com- motion in Government circles concerning the missing des- patches. A moonlight outrage of a brutal and cowardly nature oc- curred on Monday Morning near King Williamstown, in the county of Cork. The victims were two young girls named Kate and Bridget Jones, daughters of a respectable farmer living in the district The marauders visited Jones's house about half-past seven, when the inmates were about to breakfast. They pushed open the door and demanded a gun, which was refused. The girls became alarmed, and at- tempted to close the door and prevent the ruffians entering, but they were instantly shot by the raiders, who then took to flight. Both girls were dangerously injured, Miss Kate Jones (who recently returned home from a Roman Catholic convent in London owing to ill-health) being shot over the right eye. Mr. Jones, armed with a loaded rifle, pursued the party, but did not succeed in making a capture. His son proceeded immediately to King Williamstown police sta- tion. The police arrived an hour later, and on entering the house discovered the two young women lying in a pool of blood and iusensible. The only motive assigned for the outrage is the refusal to give up the gen. Jones is a prominent member of the local branch of the National League. Addresses were presented on Monday to the Lord Lieu- tenant in Dublin by the Chamber of Commerce earl by the Belfast Corporation. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach has returned to London from Ireland. It is no secret, it is said, that he expects trouble in Ireland during the approaching winter, and his last visit to Dublin has only strengthened his conviction that exceptional measures will have to be adopted before the new year. A disgraceful case of boycotting was reported, on Tues- day, from King's County. Michael Hill, whose family is boycotted.for working for an unpopular landlord, has been unable to obtain at Edenderry a coffin in which to bury his mother. lie applied to three tradesmen who bad coffins in stock, but they refused to sell him one, aithough supplying him with such• necessaries as could be carried away unob- served by National League spies. THE BELFAST RIOTS. The inquiry by Royal Commission into the Belfasi riots was opened on Monday in the Record Court of County An- trim. Justice Day presided. Mr. Hennessy, secretary to the Conamiseion, read the warrants, and Justice Day imme- diately delivered an address, in the course of which he said the Commission was determined to have as searching and as thorough an investigation as their great powers enabled them to carry out. They were determined to elicit the whole truth in reference to transactions that brought so much dis- credit on their great city, and disturbed social order to such a lamentable extent, and they had confidence in the loyalty of tha citizens of elelfast. Various " interests " were repre- sented by counsel, but his lordship gave them to understand that the conduct of the inquiry rested exclusively with the Commissioners, who, he said, did not recognise the right of counsel to appear on behalf of any person. On the conclu- sion of the Judge's address, the majority of counsel objected I® remain on sufferance. as intimated in his lordship's state- ment. The Judge said he should be sorry if any counsel should leave. He should be glad to have their assistance in the inquiry, but they were not te interfere with its pro- ceedings. After some discussion the bar applied for an ad- journment of 15 minutes, but this was refused.—Town In- spector Carr was then called and examined, whereupon the bar retired from the court, with other persons.—The mem- bers of the bar returned into court during the afternoon with a resolution they bad adopted, protesting against the course which had been pursued with regard to the bar, and adding that they did not think it would be conducive to the inter- ests of their clients or the public.—lt was mentioned that the total number of policemen who had been injured in the riots was 349. The Commission of Inquiry into the Belfast riots was resumed on Theeley, before Mr. Justice Day and his asso- ciate Commissioners. Town Inspector Carr's examination was continued, the main points of his evidence baying special reference to the conduct of the workmen employed in the Qeeen's Island Shipbuilding Works. Commissioner Adams closely questioned the witness with the view of eli- citing that the workmen were the aggressors. The inspec- tor said bolts and other iron m'ssiles undoubtedly were taken from the shipyard, aed said that the threat to close the shipyard by the Mayor of Belfast,who is the proprietor, Lad the most salutary effect. Many of the workmen were connected with the Orange Society, but witness could not say that any ringlerders lathe riots were members of that society. The town authorities had no power to appoint special constables. The better classes did not take part in the riots, although sympathising with certain sections of the mob.—Assistant inspector-General Cullen said the with- drawal of the police from Shankhill-road was at the re- quest of the local magistrates and clergy. When the local magistrates differed from the resident magistrate the police did what they thought best.

Several officers of constabulary were examined before the Belfast Commission on Wednesday. Their evidence was to the effect that the sentences on stone-throwers were fax to. lenient. The magistrates took different views of the cases, being divided as well as the population, and their decisions had been criticised as being biassed rby their religion. Party processions should, they thought, be stopped; and to make it effective the law as to the search for firearms should be amended. _ _ .

r would report at their next meeting, fled the Committee hoped to be able to deal with the case. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were confirmed. SCRODL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE : THE SHIP CLIO. Ate ne”ting of fete above committee the Inspector re- ported that 8,2 cases had been inquired into by the Board of Guardians, aell school fees allowed in $3 cases for 184 chil- dren. That 19 cases were taken before the magistrates, and flu-es inflicted in 14 eases, 1 ordered to be whipped. 1 to the Industrial School, and 3 to the ship Clio. It was resolved that the following estimate of expenditure by this commit- tee for the half-year ending 25th March, 1887, be approved: —lnspectors' salaries. .£9B 10s; maintenance of boys at industrial schools, £4O; sundries, £l5; total, £153 lOs ; and that the Council be recommended to grant a donation of ten guineas to the managers of the ship Clio, in which ship several boys from this borough are being maintained free of charge. 33 cases were brought before the committee and dealt with. Alderman WEBSTER, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said that he had particular pleasure in drawing at- tention to the proposal to contribute ten guineas to the ship Clio. About thirty boys belonging to Warrington were low on board that ship, and he wassorry he had notwith him a number of photographs of the boys which the superinten- dent showed to him, and he thought the Council if they could have seen them would have said that, considering their previous bad surroundings, they were an intelligent and a good looking lot of little fellows. The proposed dona- tion would only be some acknowledgment of the satisfaction of the Council at the manner in which the boys were treated. The speaker then read a letter from the superin- tendent of the ship, which stated that all the boys sent to the ship were sent to sea if they wished to go, and an out- fit was provided for them. About seventy per cent. of the boys went to sea, and the great majority turned out well. He believed that the general character of the boys from Warrington was exceedingly good. The captain of the ship told nim that they set quite an example to beys coming from other places. Alderman Webster then referred to the new schools in Battersby-lane, and said he was delighted to think that the schools were being built and he had no doubt from their position they would rank as high as any in the town. He wished to say that, as the time of the examinations approached, the teachers were anxious that all children should attend school regularly, and he wished to impress upon parents the necessity of sending their children regularly to school, so that their suc- cessful operation might not be interfered with. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Dixon seconded the motion. The Mason, in commenting upon the proposal to give ten guineas to the funds of the Clio, said the members of the Council must hear the proposal with pleasure. Many boys from Warrington were sent to the ship, and it must be a real advantage that they were able to relieve them- selves of boys who otherwise might he a great nuisance to them.. , The minutes were adopted. MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE. At a meeting held on the 10th September, the following return for August was presented :—Visitors to the Museum, 3,005, an increase of 7 per cent.; books issued in reading- room, 1,696. an increase of 37 per cent.; books issued to sub- scribers, 1,403, a decrease of 9 per cent. compared with Aukust, 1885. The Curator reported the following gifts, for which the thinks of the Committee were ordered to be sent to the donors :—From Mr. A. Carnegie (the author). "Triumphant Democracy." From Mr. Stock (the publisher), Tolstoi's "What I believe." From Mr. Beamont, Schedule of Deeds of Hale Hall. From Mr. R. Pierpoint, "Stephani Thesaurus Latina Lingua," 4v. to. (1573). ' Four other books. From Mr. H. S. Lewis, Fossil shell from the °onto, Gloucestershire. From the Field Club, Fossil Footprints (reptilian) from Runcorn Quarries, From the Birmingham Free Libraries Committee, catalogue of Reference Depart- ment, A—E. It was resolved that an order be given for four additional benches, 10 feet long, for the reading- room. The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Alderman WEBSTER., seconded by Councillor GREW/ALL. CEMETERY COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this committee the Registrar reported that the interments for the past four weeks were :—Adults, 33 ; minors, 56; stillborn and premature, 7; and for the corre- sponding period last year: Adults, 20; minors, 43; and stillborn and premature, 5. The receipts for the past four weeks were £76 13s 6d, and fa tbe corresponding week last year £4O 16e 6.1. It was resolved that the following esti- mate of expenditure by this Committee for the half- year ending 25th March, 1887, be approved, namely, 262 10s. . .

At the Belfast inquiry, on Thursday, further evidence was given to show that the police received great provoca- tion before they fired on the rioters. The raising of the question whether the Riot Act had been, read before the constabulary fired led the President (Mr. Justice Day) to remark that people attributed a magic power to the Act, but that while the reading of the Act enhanced the offence of a disorderly mob and increased tha penalty, it had nothing to do with the duty of the police in suppress- ing a riot. District Inspector Grene mentioned a noteworthy fact. On the 9th June he ac- quiesced in a proposal of two Protestant ministers that the police should be withdrawn from the Shankhill-road and that the rev, gentlemen should use their influence with the rioters, but when the witness had with- drawnChisimen some distance they cried out "Let us fire before we go," and though he cried out" Nothing of the sort " the men fired, no ward of command haying been given. " The men," be added, " lost their tempers, and fired up and down the street." fie thought, however, that they were justified in beginning to fire as their lives were In danger. The witness said, in answer to a question, that he himself was a Protestant; but, replying te another question, he admitted that be did not see anything to lead him to believe that the constables were acting under sectarian animosity.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. A. meeting of this Council was held in the Town Hall on Tueniay evening. There were present—the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Aldermen Burgess, Webster, and Holmes; Councillors Greening, Brown Jolley, Roberts, Marth, J. Pierpoint, Mackie, Greenall, Tinsley, Whittle, Francomb, Wright, Bolton, Hutchinson, Dakin, Litton, Dixon, Marsh, Ashton, W. Pierpoint, Fleming; Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), Chorley (borough treasurer). 'WATCH 00MMITTE2.—THE DISMISSAL Or A. CONSTABLE. At a meeting of the above committee, held on the 16th September, it was resolved that the following estimate of expenditure by the committee for the half year ending 25th March be approved, namely, £1,106 12s. 61 The MAYOR moved, and Councillor JOLLEY seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor ROBERTS said be wished, as a member of the Council and as a ratepayer, to ask for information upon a point which be thought was deserving of explanation. He had been informed that a late member of the police force had been dismissed for a very serious offence. If his in- formation was correct, the offence was that the officer to whom he referred robbed a prisoner whom be had taken into custody of the sum of V. They looked upon the police as their protectors, but it seemed to him that the offence in the present case was of so serious a character that the mere die- miesal of a man from the force did lot, in his opinion, meet it. He wished to know whether his information was correct in order to know whether the matter should be carried fur- ther or not. The MAYOR: I think it is a mistake, Mr. Roberts. Councillor ROBERTS: I am informed that he was dis- missed from the force because he had taken the snm of £7. The MAYOR said he was told that the officer was guilty of an irregularity, but it was hardly of inch a character as to say that it approached robbery. It was simply the reten- tion of money in his hands for an unreasonable time. He had certainly no right to do what he had done. He had certainly not been taken on again, end would not be re- admitted to the force. Councillor ROBERTS wished te know whether it was not a regulation that all moneys should be recorded in a book kept for the purpose at the police office. The MAYOR: Yes. Councillor ROBERTS: IS it not a fact that this money has never been recorded, and consequently does it not amount to an absolute theft of the money? The MAYOR replied that it was a question of construction. He was not so intimately acquainted with the details as to be able to say, but he thought Councillor Roberts would be answered if he (the Mayor) told him that the officer had not been taken on again. Councillor ROBERTS said he did not raise that question. What he wished to make clear was that if his information was correct he did not think that mere dismissal from the force was a sufficient condemnation of that offence. The MAYOR said he thought Councillor Roberts would require to know the full details before he would know what course to adopt. The Watch Committee in considering the matter had Mr. Hunt's statement, and hi their wisdom they were pleased to consent to the officer merely being dismissed, after the money had been replaced. Councillor ROBERTS: I don't understand you to say. Mr. Mayor, that my information is not correct BO far as it goes? The MAYOR: I admit that he was guilty of an irregu- larity with reference to a prisoner's money, but I know nothing beyond that. I MAY say that at the time I was not in Warrington, being away on my holidays, and, therefore, I am not acquainted with the details that transpired. Councillor JoLLEY said that being a member of the Watch Committee, he knew the whole circumstances of the case. It did not amount to a theft. There was an irregularity which the Watch Committee thought suffi- ciently serious to visit with disniss,l. The time in which the money was produced was considered to be beyond a reasonable time. Councillor Wurrnz : Only a retention. The MAYOR said that from inquiries he made, he found that there was no attempt at concealment, but that the officer frankly admitted his irregularity, and the money was forthcoming when asked for. Councillor Joramy : It may be right to say that several weeks elapsed before it was brought under the notice of the Watch Committee. Alderman Bustarss : May I ask whether it is not a fact that this is not the first case of the kind in the history of the " gentleman " you are speaking of? The MAYOR: I believe there was a previous case concern- ing a trifling sum, but neither of them amounted to a de- liberate attempt to steal the money. Alderman BURGESS: Am I to understand that £7 and a gold watch is considered a trifling thing? It would secure 114 a poor prisoner placed in the dock perhaps penal servi- tude. (Hear, heir.) The MAYOR: When I used the word " trifling " I referred to the previous case, in which the amount was something like 17s. I should certainly say that £7 and a gold watch was a very grave matter. Councillor TINSLEY asked how many times this officer had committed like offences. The MAYOR said that Niell had only been guilty of two irregularities, including the one for which he was dismissed. It was not the custom ot the Council to excuse offences of that kind, but having regard to the fact that he had been an exemplary officer, and an exceedingly clever and useful man, and that he bad a large family, they thought that the punishment of dismissal was sufficient. Dismissal in his case was very serious, as it entirely precluded him from again entering the police force. The subject then dropped, and the minutes were con- firmed. SANITARY COMMITTEE.—APPOINTMENT OF INSPECTORS.

--;"" These minutes were confirmed on the motion of the Maaron, seconded by Councillor Bnows. TOWN HALL, PARK, AND BATHS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this Committee, which were proposed for adoption on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Coon- JOHN FIBRPOINY, contained the following estimate of ex- penditure :—Town Hall department, £2OT ss; Bank Park department, £350; Baths department, £142 3s 10,1 ; total, £699 81 10i. The bath-keeper reported that the income from the baths for the peat four weeks was £33 lie id; and for the corresponding period last year, £l5 14s. It was also recommended that the sum of £5 be voted for the purchase of shrubs. Councillor FRANCOMB mentioned that the celebrated foot- path in the recreation ground was not yet finished. Councillor DIXON complained of the loud noise made on Sundays by the machinery at the baths. He should have, he said, the Mayor summoned before the magistrates for causing a nuisance on the Sunday bad he known the right course to adopt. The MAYOR: I am afraid his fate wonld have been a terrible one if you bad done so. (Laughter.) Councillor Joerase endorsed the remarks of Councillor Dixon. They had heard of "silent engines," but the one at the baths was by ne means a silent one. It made the founda- tions of the buildiag shake. He was glad that Mr. Dixon had brought the subject forward. Alderman WrosTen said that theengine was a noisy one. This was only one, amongst many reasons, that the commit- tee could adduce, why the baths should be altogether re- modelled. (Hear, hear.) He did not see how the engine could be altered under present arrangements. Councillor WEITTLE said there was no shaking of the foundations. If the question had been one of noise made by the Salvation Army there would have been nothing to say. There were some people who never washed themselves who objected to noise, and because the engine at the baths made a little noise they had all that row about it. There was three times as much noise on a Sunday at the manure depot, and certainly four times as much stink. (Laughter.) Alderman BURGESS remarked that if he was correctly in- formed the water in the baths was of such a filthy character that if it did not stink it should do. (Laughter.) Councillor ROBERTS said that as a member of the Baths Seb-oemmittee he was glad that the question had been raised. The fact was that the whole concern was a disgrace to the town. ('oh.") The complaint that was made was the outcome of the Council sanctioning and permitting to be continued an institution of such a low character. They I had bad several fillips from the Council, but they could not get sufficient power to enable them as a committee to go into the question thoroughly with a view to entire renovation. The sooner they had new baths, with modern machinery, the better, for so long as they had filthy bathe and third-class machinery, so long would they have the nuisance that appertained to such a state of affairs. The MAYOR pointed out that the baths were emptied on a Sunday morning, and had to be filled again through the instrumentality of the pump on Monday. Necessarily there must be some noise caused, however good the engine might be. He remembered that when they purchased the baths they were held out to them as being a most eligible Investment for the public good. A rosy picture was drawn of their usefulness, and the Council adopted them. Councillor JOLLEY said that it was not necessary that the machinery should make the slightest noise. At Stocks Well, the largest pumping station within reasonable dis- tance, they could not hear the machinery working until the engine house door was opened, and the volume of water lifted there was something enormous. The minutes were then approved. MARKETS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee were confirmed, on the motion of Councillor LITTON, seconded by Councillor JOHN FIERPOINT. They contained the following :—Resolved, that the following estimate of expenditare by this commit- tee for the half ,year ending 25th March, 1887, be approved, namely, £578 9s. At another meeting of the committee the total income from all sources was reported to be £282 8s 7d. It was resolved that after the 20:h September no tenant be aillowed to provide his own stall in any of the markets, and that the committee provide the stalls for the use of the tenants. The minutes were adopted. GAS COMMITTEE.—THE PRICE OF GAS. The manager reported to this committee that be had made a careful measurement of lengths, sizes, and mileage of the mains in the town and districts, and found the mile- age to be 39 miles and 1,429 yards. It was resolved that tire sum of three guineas be contributed to the funds of the Association of Sulphate and Ammonia Manufacturers, to- wards the prizes for the best treatise on the use of sulphate of ammonia as a manure, and that a fireproof book store be built at the rear of the general offide, at an estimated cost of .£lOO. The auditor reported that he had examined the books and accounts of the Gas Department for the twelve mouths ended 25th March, 1886, which were correct and satisfactory. The usual course had been followed through- out, being that which, in his opinion, left no item unveri- fied, and rendered the audit in every way complete All cash payments and receipts had been verified, and totals checked and followed through their respective accounts to the profit and loss account and balance sheet. The average illuminating power of the gas for the past four weeks was reported to be equal to 17 76 candles at both works. The confirmation of the minutes was proposed by Alderman HOLMES, and seconded by Alderman WEBSTER. Councillor BOLTON asked if it was possible to find out what were the salaries of the officials of the gas works. He thougVt they ought to be in full possession of such in- formation. The MAYOR: If Councillor Bolton will refer to the pocket- book the town clerk issues each year he will find the salaries in detail. Councillor BOLTON thereupon remarked that he would like to see the salaries published in the accounts of the Cor- poration,or in some way that would enable them to be easily accessible to the public. .Councillor Discos thought more information should be given as to the proposal to contribute to the funds ()Mlle Association of Sulphate of Ammonia Manufacturers. As to the entry referring to the gas works paying, he tilt:slight there must be an error. A report was bung circulated that at the end of 1881 they would

_ This Committee recommended that the tender of Mrs. Charlotte Lunt, of Warrington, for removing ashes and re- fuse from the intercepting depots to Longford Depot for six months be accepted.—At a meeting held on the 15th Sep- tember, it was resolved that the tender of Messrs. Roberts, Dale, and Co. for the supply of brown vitriol for the next six months be accepted, and at a meeting on the 22nd Sep- tember, orders were made for payment of accounts (includ- ing £3OO re Longford depot) amounting to ,£1,055 193 2d. It was recommended that the following estimate of expendi- ture by this Committee for the half-year ending 25th March, 1887, be approved: Scavenging department, £1,339 19s; nightsoil department, £1,638 17s; Longford dep6t department, £697 ss; intercepting department, £245 15s; hospital department, £370 ; total, £4,2911C. At a meeting held on the 29th September, it was resolved that James Powell be appointed sub-inspector of nuisances, smoke inspector, inspector under the Food and Drugs Act, inspector under the Contagions Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878, and inspector tinder the Canal Boats Act, 1877 and 1884, in addition to his present appointment, and at his pre- sent salary. It WaS also recommended that John Church be appointed smoke inspector, inspector under the Food and Drugs Act, inspector under the Contagious Diseases (Ani- mals) Act, 1878, and inspector under the Canal Boats Act, 1877 and 1884, in addition to his present appointments, and at his present salary. The minutes were confirmed, on the motion of Alderman BURGESS, seconded by Councillor SuTTON. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

The estimate of expenditure of this Committee for the I half-year was put down at £2l7lo.—At a meeting held on the 20th September, it was resolved that the tender of Messrs. John Nunnerley and Co., Limited, for the supply of 1,000 tons of breakers for macadam at 5s ad per ton, de- livered at Friars'-green yard, and the the tender of Mr. J. Weir, of Newry, for 500 tons of breakers at 33 per ton, f.o.b. Runcorn, be accepted. Councillor BROWN moved the confirmation of the mi- nutes. Councillor WRIGHT seconded the motion. Alderman HOLMES inquired whether any possible efforts could be successful to get rid of an intolerable nuisance in Folly lane. There was a smell there that came from the sewer er somewhere or other they could not qu'lte under- stand. He had asked Mr. Longdin about it that after- noon, and the answer be gave was satisfactory. He now asked the question in the interests of the ratepayers. If nothing could be done, he was afraid that half of the houses in that neighbourhood would be without tenants be- fore long. The Masou : What is the nuisance? Alderman HOL3IES : I am told that it comes from be- hind the railway embankment, which is full of chemical waste. Councillor BROWN observed that the question had been before the Committee, and they made an effort some few months ago to have it abated. They had not been so suc- cessful as they anticipated. The Railway Company under- took to carry out a scheme which they thought would be successful. They laid down a new sewer which had al- ' , ready been before the Committee. The Borough Surveyor

not have cleared them.elves. He had within the last few I Alderman Burgess, Councillors W. For the motion, 5; against, 10. follows :—" I beg to inform you that the price of gas has, This was all the business. been reduced threepence per thousand feet until further notice. The following will now be the net prices, provided payment is made within the specified time : Consumers be- low 100,000 cubic feet per annum, 2s Gd per 1,000 feet 100,000 to 3,000,000, 2e 3d; 3,000,000 and upwards, 25." Why. it was asked in the letter, were not the prices re- duced in Warrington to what was charged at Widnes? If he were to answer that inquiry he should think of saying that" We have a gentleman as chairman of committee who does not take that amount of interest in the manufacture of gas, or does not interest Limself much in the reduction of the price of gas." (Laughter.) A member of that Coun- cil said to him within the last few weeks that if the gas works had been handled as they ought to have been they ought to have gas for as little money as they had in other towns ; but owing to the works falling into the hands of the committee, there had not been that attention or that de- sire there should have been to reduce the price of gas, and the consequence was that they stood in that very unplea- sant position. Alderman HOLMES said, in reply, that, if it was desired, the salaries of the various officials should be published. With regard to the recommended subscription to the Sul- phate of Ammonia Association, he explained that the As- sociation was one formed for the purpose of obtaining in- formation as to the public sales and quantities of ammonia products in this country, and with the view of seeing at what price it was sold. The price of gas was a subject that has from time to time been discussed in the Council Cham- ber. No doubt the works at Widnes were purchased out of the rates, but the Council had bought the Warrington gas works from the original proprietors, and had not only to pay interest, but out of the 3s per 1,000 charged for the gas they had to pay for the purchase of the works. They were is reality paying for the works without any cost to the rate- payers. (Voices: "No.") They had, he said, reduced the price by 6d since they came into possession, and he thought that Mr. Dixon had no ground for his complaint. LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL ON FUTURE LEGISLATION. Lord Randolph Churchill was present on Saturday afternoon at a great Conservative gathering in Oak- field Park, Dartford, to celebrate the return of eighteen Conservatives and one Unionist member for the county of Kent. The chair was taken by Mr, Miller. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, after referring to the special object of tee meeting, and to the Ministerial measures of the past session, said : Now, let zee turn to the policy of the future. Tbe main principle of that policy and its guiding motive will be to maintain unimpaired the union of the Unionst party. (Cheers.) Everything that we do, either in domestic or foreign affairs, will be subordinated to that cardinal principle, the union of the Unionist party. (Cheers.) We know that we, the present Government, owe much of our existence and much of our efficiency to the Unionist Liberals. (Cheers.) It is our business to attribute te their actions lofty and the most honourable motives, and to believe that thy are actuated by no other desire than to maintain pure and intact their political power and inde- pendence, so as to rescue the great Liberal party—which has sadly gone astray—(cheers and laughter)—from all the heresies and all the terrible errors into which Mr. Gladstone has so often led them. (rear, bear, and laughter.) The first duty of Her Majesty's Government is to restore free- dom to the House of Commons. (Cheers.) Your House of Commons is at the present moment in a state of slavery. It is absolutely enslaved to the caprices of the Radical and Parnellite sections. (A Voice: "Turn them out.") There is no chance of any legislation of any kind being under- taken with any prospect of success until freedom has beee restored to the House of Commons. (Cheers.) The first and chief desideratum in any form of procedure must un- doubtedly be a simple and effective power of clos- ing debate. (Cheers.) Whatever evils or dangers would attach to some simple form of closing debate in Parliament they are not to be weighed with the evils of Obstruction in the House of Commons. (Cheers.) Let us assume that the Government have effected these re- forms in procedure and laid the foundation for future legis- lation, and let us consider for a moment the various subjects of legislation which the present Government ought, in jus- tice te the country, to undertake with interest and energy. (Cheers.) lam bound to say that I think we ought to give a chief place to the legislative requirements of England and Scotland. (Cheers.) It is the decided intention of Govern- ment to introduce into Parliament a measure which should provide facilities, through the operation of local authorities, for the acquisition by the agricultural labourer of freehold plots and allettments. (Cheers.) There is a great agree- ment among all parties as to the main lines of the measure, and I do not in the least wish to detract from any credit which may be justly given to men like Mr. Jesse Collings or Mr. Chamberlain, who undonbtedly were foremost in bringing this eubject before the public mind of England. (Hear, hear.) But my hope is that that will be one of the first subjects dealt with by the present Government in the next session. There is another. measure closely connected with that, and one in which Lord Salisbury—(great cheers) —takes a personal interest, and that is legislation by which facilities should be afforded for the sale of glebe lands. (Cheers.) That is intimately connected with the allotment question. I come now to the question of tithes. (A Voice: "Let the landlords pay them.") Undoubtedly it will be necessary for the Government to consider the general ques- tion of tithes over the whole of England and Wales. (Hear, hear.) I rather expect that legislation on the question will tend in the direction intimated so happily by my friend in the crowd—(laughter)—and without doing any injustice to either the landlords or the clergy it may be possible for a great majority of the landlords of this country to take upon themselves the direct burden of the incidence of tithes. (Hear, hear.) There is another measure which I hope the Government may be able to deal with—l mean the question of railway rates. (Cheers.) The railway rates at the present moment operate in a way which Parliament did not intend when they gave the railway companies their powers. Without doubt they manage to give to the foreign importer and the foreign producer unfair advantages over the home producer. (Hear, hear.) I would say to the railway companies they bad better bear in mind the Scriptural text, " Agree with your adversary quickly while you are in the way with him."—(cheers and laughter) —because undoubtedly, if the present grievances which the commercial, manufacturing and agricultural community complain of regarding the regulation of railway rates are suffered to go on undealt with and are developed, then it is possible that the rights and properties of railway companies may be placed in jeopardy. (Hear.) There ;s another measure which the country requires also, and that is a mea- sure which shall provide for a cheaper method of land transfer—(cheers)—and for a cheaper method of acquiring landed property by the individual, and for the registration of titles. All that I can say upon that point is this—that the Lord Chancellor of the present Government is enthusi- astic on the question, and I understand that he has ideas. (Laughter.) And you may depend upon it that when a Lord Chancellor of England is enthusiastic upon aty question, and has ideas with regard to that que tion, he will be a very bold and a very clever man who will stop the Lord Chan. cellor's way. (Laughter.) Therefore I think you may look forward with some confidence to a satisfactory measure I upon this important question being introduced in the House of Lords early next session. (Cheers.) Well, there is the great question of the establishment in country districts of a genuinely popular form of local government. It is the decided intention of the Government to take it up in earn- est, and endeavour to arrive at a settlement of it. It in- cludes two very large questions—it includes some compre- hensive re-arrangement and readjustment of the incidence of local taxation, and it inclades some methods by which , personal property shall be brought more into the area of ' local taxation, and shall be called upon to contribute a far more complete share than now in the expenses of local gov- ernment. (Cheers.) The question of local government ' also includes another large and thorny question—it includes the licensing question. I will not now enter into the com- plexities of that matter, but I believe it is possible for your loc 1 bodies, if properly constituted, to settle the main difficulties which have arisen around the question of licensing. Of course there is another point upon which I am specially interested. which I cannot omit to THE URINAL QUESTION. notice. MINERAL PIIRPOSHS COMMITTEE. This committee resolved that the plot of land adjoining the Museum be let to Mr. Thomas Fletcher at a rent of L 1 is. per annum, the tenancy to be subject to termination at six months' notice, to be given at any time. Mr. Beamont having requested the committee to cat trenches across the vacant land in Bridge-street to discover, if possible, any relics of the Priory of the Warrington Hermit Friars of the Order of Saint Augustine, it was resolved that the request be acceded to, and the Borough Surveyor be instructed to superintend the operations. The motion that the minetes be confirmed was proposed by the MA/OR, and seconded by Alderman Houras. Councillor WRIGHT was pleased to see the minute re- ferring to the excavations in Bridge-street. He believed that some most interesting discoveries would be made there at a very trifling cost to the Corporation. There were some beautiful things to be seen, and the base of a beautiful column in perfect preservation had been found. He hoped that the work would be caref ally done, and that it might also be carefully guarded at night. Such interesting relics should be taken every care of. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR said be assured Councillor Wright that they were all in sympathy with what had been done through the instrumentality of their old friend Mr. Beamont. who was anxious some experiments should be made to discover whether there were any interesting relics with reference to the ancient priory that stood there. He was glad that there was a prospect of something being discovered, and he considered that the money it required was well spent. The minutes were confirmed,

FINASCH COMMITTEIL This committe recommended that a call be made on the overseers of the townships of Warrington and Latchford, on borough rate account, for the sans of £4,509 7s 4d ; that the Finance Committee be authorised to make an improvement rate for the half year ending March 25th, 1887, at is 84 in the pound, which is estimated to produce about £8,640; and that the Council be recommended to authorise the mak- ing of a sewer rate, for the half year ending March 25th, 1881, at Id in the pound, which is estimated to produce about £496. The summary of the estimates is as follows:— Borough rate: September, 1885, £4,709 11s id: March, 1886, £4,272 18s 3d; Sept, mber. 1886, £4 509 7s 44. Im- provement rate: September, 1885, £8,230 Os Id; March, 1886, £7,643 2s; September, 1886. £8,355 8e 24. General sewers rate : September, 1885, £625 21 ; March, 1886, £550 14s 4d; September, 1836, £473 9s 104. Alderman HomitEs, in proposing the adoption of the minutes. said that the last rate was 154 in the £, but when it was adopted they knew it would not entirely cover the expenditure that would Ue incurred. They were in hopes that they would have received more money than they had done from the sale of manures. The result WAS that they had to ask for a rate of is 64 in the X, which, though not desirable, Was unavoidable; but the sewers rate was re- duced by Id in the 1, so that the aggregate increase in the rates would only be 24 instead of 3d. Councillor GRINNING seconded the adoption of the minutes, and the motion was carried, formal resolutions with reference to the making of rates being passed without com- ment.

maintain the best and the most friendly relations with all foreign States, and to lose no opportunity of offering friendly and conciliatory counsels for the purp,se of miti- gwing national ivairies and of peaceably solving Inter- national difficulties. (Cheers.) But should circumstances arise which from their grave and dangerous nature should force the dovernnaent of the Queen to make a choice, it cannot be doubted that the sympathy and even the support of England will be given to those powers who seek the peace of Europe and the liberty of peoples, and in whose favour our timely adhesion would probably, and without the use of force, decide the issue. (Great cheering.) Our policy in these akxious times, subject always to the car- dinal necessity of maintaining the union of the Unionist party, will pursue an even and ste,dy course, avoiding the dangers of officious interference and unnecessary initiative on the one hand, and an attitude of selfish and timid isola- tion on the other ; and I most earnestly hope that we shall be successful in contributing to the preservation of that general peace and security which, however necessary and advantageous it nr.v be for other nations, is to my mind absolutely essential to the progress and prosperity the British Empire. (Loud cheers).

THE ELECTIoN OF A GUARDIAN FOR GRAPPENHALL. ANOTHER, LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY. On Monday Mr. Stevens, assistant Local Govern- ment Board Inspector, held a second inquiry in the Boardroom.Warrington Workhouse, as to the recent election of a guardian for the township of Grappen- hall. It will be lemembered that at the recent triennial election of guardians the representation of the township of Grippenhall was contested by Mr. W. Darbyshire, the late guardian, and Mr. A. Woods, the result being that Mr. Woods was declared to have received 86 votes and Mr. Darbyshire 85, the former of course being returned. Mr. Darbyshire, however, questioned the validity of certain votes given to Mr. Woods, and appealed to the Local Government Board to hold an inquiry. The Local Government Board acceded to the request, and Mr. Henley, one of their inspectors, consequently held an inquiry as to the validity of two of Mr. Wood's votes. Mr. Woods subsequently appealed for an in- quiry as to. some of Mr. Darbyshire's votes, the present inquiry being the result. There were pre- sent at the inquiry : Messrs. W. Darbyshire, A. Woods, J. Hampson (Conservative registration agent), and Mr. J. C. Sutton (clerk to the Board of Guardians), who officiated as returning officer at the last election, and Mr. S. Sutton (assistant clerk to the Guardians.) The names of the persons whose votes were questioned were—James Friar, Jackson Bragg, William Wicks, George Walker, Charles Beach, Thomas Maire. Samuel Massey, George Hampson, Thomas Ditchfleld, Charles Eaton, James Burrows.—The Inspector, in opening the inquiry, read the correspondence that had taken place between the Local Government Board and Messrs. Darbyshire and Woods. The first vote considered was that of Jackson Bragg.—Mr. J. C. Sutton (returning officer) said he disallowed Jackson Bragg's vote on an objection being raised by Mr. Darbyshire to the effect that he was not an occupier, but lived at the cottage as a servant of Major Pickmere, and further that another male ser- vant of Major Pickmere resided in the same house. He (Mr. Sutton) intimated at the time that if evi- dence was given that Bragg was the occupier he should allow the vote. Such evidence was not then forthcoming; but he had since been informed that Bragg did occupy the cottage and paid 5s per week for such occupation, and that the other male ser- vant referred to was a brother of Bragg's wife, and lived there as a matter of convenience. Had such evidence been put before him at the time he should have allowed the vote.—By hr. Darbyshire: I have been informed that the arrangement for paying 55 per week was made previous to the election. I can- not speak definitely, and can only say what I have been informed.—Mr. George Fairhurst (assistant overseer for the township of Grappenhall) said the rate of the cottage was paid, the cottage being in- cluded along with the assessment of Major Pickmere's other property.—Major Pickmere, of Cedar Lawn, Grappenhall, said Jackson Bragg occupied a cottage belonging to him. Bragg had 25s per week, and witness deducted 5s per week for the cottage, which was quite distinct from witness's property. That arrangement was made at the commencement of Bragg's service.—By Mr. Darbyshire: The bar- gain when Bragg was engaged was that he should have 20s per week and house free. We had a con- versation at the time about the value of the house, and it was stated that it was worth Gs per week, but I decided to charge 5s per week, which was stopped out of his wages. The boy in the house paid 2s per week to Mrs. Bragg.—Mr. Hampson having put questions to witness, Mr. Darbyshire at this point asked the Inspector whether Mr. Hampson had a right to be present during the inquiry, and to put leading ' questions to Major Pickmere. Had Mr. Hampson a right to ask a question at all? When leading questions were being put by him he (Mr. Darbyshire) considered that he had no right to be allowed to be present.—The Inspector: He has no right to take part in the inquiry.—Mr. Darby- shire: I hope in the interest of a fair inquiry my friend will desist from putting leading questions:— Mr. Woods; It is only to save time.—Mr. Darby- shire: I shall object to it.—Jackson Bragg gave corroborative evidence as to his wage and the con- ditions on which he held his house, and in answer to questions said, with regard to the boy who lived in his house, that Major Pickmere paid 2s a week to his (witness's) wife for the &ad's washing.—The case of George Walker, Cliff-lane, Grappenhall, was next taken. He stated that not knowing how to fill up the voting paper, he sent his wife to his employer's (Mr. Long's) office, and the paper was marked with pencil where he was to sign it, and he afterwards wrote over the pencil marks in ink— Darbyshire You considered it was perfectly legal to cover the pencil marks ?—Witness: Yes.— Mr. Darbyshire: So do 1.--Mr. Woods contended that that was an illegal filling up of the paper by an agent ; this was an interested party, and had shown themselves so at that election.—Mr. Darby- shire objected to the Word "agent" as used by Mr. Woods. There had been no agent in that election except their friend sitting there (Mr. Hampson). He (Mr. Darbyshire) had had no agent. —James Friar, farmer, said he had not filled his paper up himself, but gave instructions to his daughter to do so for Mr. Darbyire. In reply to Mr. Woods he denied that.he had stated to some one at Stockton Heath potatoe market that he filled another person's voting paper up.:-Charles Beach, a farmer, living at Grappenhall, said that he signed the voting paper produced, and initialled it.. He could not say whether a certain cross which the Inspector called his attention to was on the paper when he signed. He could not say whIS7 the cross had been put on the paper, and to the best of his knowledge he did not place it there. By Mr. Woods; The initials "C. B." were not written in his house by anyone else. The "C" looked something like his; but the "B" he was doubtful about.—lt was explained that in the case of• William Wicks, the facts were similar to those in Bragg's case.—The other cases, which had regard chiefly to Mr. Wood's votes, were also gone into and evidence taken by the Inspector, to be laid before the Local Govern- ment Board. At the close a vote of thanks was prc- posed to Mr. Stevens, who, in acknowledging the same, said that although no fresh cases could now be taken on either side, it was possible he would have to make some further inquiry hereafter as to some of the cases on which he had already takt.n evidence, and for that reason he would formally adjourn the inquiry. Ile-hoped before long the de- cision of the Local Government Board upon the question would be ascertained, and that one of the two gentlemen would be finally declared elected.

div.p: SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1886.

WHATEVER hostile comment may be justly passed on Mr. GLADSTONE'S speech it cannot be fairly said that he showed any lack of dignity. There is nothing of the iritation of defeat in this utterance. He treats his op.. ponents with that old-world courtesy which it would be well if some of them would imi- tate, and he makes the most complete allow- ance for the conscientious motives of the Unionist Liberals. They cannot complain now that he does not appreciate their purpose and that he has not fully acknowledged their influence. He ascribes his defeat entirely to their "great ability and immense and un- bounded energy." He pays Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN a high compliment, and of the exertions of the Unionists he speaks decisively in a sentence which may well become historical. "Truly, no greater triumph was ever witnessed by a small party in the past." After this, is it too much to hope that the Unionist Liberals in any future controversy will treat Mr. GLAD- STONE with respect? It will certainly be a great advantage to all concerned, and to the interests of truth and justice, if we have no , more insinuations that Mr. GLADSTONE has deliberately allied himself with the party of disorder and assassination. There are some people who, in spite of their great capacity, can see in the Irish agitation nothing but the base manceuvres of foreign ruffians, bent on a policy of plunder and blood. The lofty spirit in which Mr. GLADSTONE deals with the whole question, whether he be right or wrong, is surely worthier of emulation than the nar- row and passionate prejudice which refuses to admit that the majority of Irishmen are animated by a sincere desire to manage their' own local affairs, and are quite competent to do this without involving their country in ruin. The writer of Letters from Ireland" in the Times thinks he has settled the whole question of the competence of the Irish for self-government when he repeats the idle gossip of some anonymous enemy of Home Rule. Says this person: "I think PARNELL would very likely seize the opportunity to re- tire into private life, having got what he had promised. If not, he would be swept away by more extreme men. We should have them coming over in shoals from America; the country would be bankrupt ; and it would be simply pandemonium." Here is an admission that Mr. PARNELL, at all events, is a man of moderate aspirations, and not the revolutionary demagogue who preys like a night-mare on the minds of Irish Tories, So Mr. PARNELL is Coolly relegated to private life, and it is assumed that if he does not retire soon enough, the Irish-American ruffians will sweep him away and destroy the country. This sort of read--- ing is familiar to every student of great ' popular movements. Men who can never in any circumstances place any trust in the people, whether of their own or of any other country, alway assume that overwhelm- ing ruin must follow the concession of politi- cal power to the masses. In 1830 English- men were believed by many to have imbibed

the principles of the French Revolution, and it was seriously argued that Parliamentary reform would lead the country straight to perdition. There is no historical doubt that events in France at that time exercised a remarkable influence on English opinion; and it was actually feared in some quarters that an attempt would be made to establish a Republic, with the assistance of certain revolutionary spirits from the other side of the Channel. Bankruptcy and pandemonium were all that some extremely sober politicians could see in the future of England then ; and their descendants are just as prophetic, and with quite as much reason, in their assump- tions as to the consequence of Home Rule. The chief interest of Mr. GLADSTONE'S speech is historic, and this, of course, is un- welcome to politicians who cannot see that the history of the Union has anything to do with the present condition of Ireland. Mr. GLADSIONE'S point is that, as the Union was pasEed agAnst the wishes of the Irish people, and as it never has had, and never can have, any moral validity without the sancticn of the people, it is incumbent on British statesmen so to remodel the relations between the two countries as to make Ireland content. What is the use of contending thit the circumstances in which the Union was passed are mere musty history when we are still face to face with the results of that colossal blunder? We have suf- fered for eighty-six years from PITT'S mistake in supposing that the Irish would ever submit to be deprived of their national Parliament. There are some acts which make themselves felt from generation to generation. No man would dream of telling a doctor who inquired into the physical his- tory of his family that it was perfectly imma- terial to his own health whether his grand- father suffered from some transmitted disease. When we took away the symbol of Irish nationality we inflicted a mortal offence which none of our efforts at reparation have condoned. We have disestablished the Irish Church, and strenuously endeavoured to cure all the evils of the land question, but the people will not forget that they were robbed of their Parliament, and will never cease to believe that a Legislature in Dublin would show a better appreciation of Irish affairs than the House of Commons in its most enlightened mood. Mr. Gladstone's strongest argument is that history proves that we have clung quite long enough to disastrous error; and when he is told that to trace the course of this error is waste of time, and that .the iniquities of 1800 have nothing to do with the politics of 1886, he need not condescend to tell his opponents that the politician who does not master the elementary truth, that as we have sown so we shall reap, had better turn his attention to any subject except public affairs. Sooner or later our statesmen will be forced to recognise that the restoration of the Irish Parliament, with whatever safe- guards and limitations may be deemed necessary, is the only means of healing the chronic discord between England and Ire- land. Such a Parliament will not bring the millennium. It will probably carry many disappointments in its train. There will be struggles in Ireland that are inevitable inci- dents of the reformation of political society. Other countries have gone through the ordeal, and we cannot cherish the illusion that Ire- land will eseape from it. But wherever there is any faith in the democracy, there will exist a firm belief that in Ireland, as in many a community whose early training in self- government has been watched with anxiety by friends and with mocking scepticism by foes, there will be enough manhood and enough discernment to found Irish institu- • tions broadly and solidly on sense and justice.

THE discontent of the old Tories with Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL'S new attitude does not diminish. Some of them decline altogether to discuss the subject. They can- not believe that they are actually called upon to renounce every theory they have held dear, and adopt theories and arguments which they have consistently held up to odium and scorn. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, as many people have suspected, is much more disposed by temperament to Radical measures than to the stagnant policy which most Tories have always been content to pursue. But with Lord RANDOLPH it is an affair of temperament purely. Of settled convictions he shows no sign. Many eminent politicians have beep obliged by the development of events to change their opinions, but no one —not even Lord BEACONSFIELD—haS ever turned his coat so often, and with such cynical promptitude and completeness, as the ' new master spirit of the Tory party. A con- temporary has compiled a useful record show- ing the contiast between Lord RANDOLPH'S present opinions and those which he has expounded within the last four years. It is a startling table, and must make even the staunchest Tory partisan extremely uncom- fortable. It has long been the favourite Tory complaint of Mr. GLADSTONE that he had no stability, and that nobody know what extra- ordinary revolution he would propose next. But if it is not enough to say that Ur. GLAD- STONE'S career is a consistent process col evolution, it may be safely said that no change of opinion in the course of his long life was ever so startling in its suddenness, and so completely unwarranted by any opera- tion.of principle, as Lord RANDOLPH'S con- version on some of the most important subjects of contemporary politics. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER now avows that the great object of his policy is to sup- ' press the Irish party by maintaining the com- pact of the Parliamentary Unionists. Four years ago he declared in the House of Com- mons that ".nothing could be more disastrous than a union of the two great parties of , the State to suppress the Irish party. ' No course could be more calculated to ' lead to the establishment of an Irish Par- liament ,or even to. Irish independence. Irish opposition to the English Government, even if it was obstinately obstructive and cal- culated to bring the Legislature into con- tempt, might he an evil; but it was an evil which must be borne with, unless we were pre- pared to concede freely the demand for Home Home." It may be that this opinion will prove in the long run to be much better founded than Lord Randolph's present as- sumption, but she contrast between the two judgments is sufficient to show that Lord Randolph is never likely to be embarrassed by any fixity of ideas. On the gross incon- sistency between his advocacy of the closure, pure and simple, and his bitter opposition to it in 188 z we have previously commented, and it need only be remarked that as the closure presents itself to Lord RANDOLPH'S mind now as a natur.al and legitimate expe- dient, solely because it may be used to sup- press the Irish party he bids fair to play a very conspicudus part in the fulfilment of his prediction that such a policy must lead straight to Home Rule. Br mkee, tailor, Waterloo- road, Widaes —A boy named Boardman proved seeing the prisoner take the coat from a nail in the shop, put it on, and walk along Victoria-road.—The prisoner, who protested his innocence, was sentenced to 21 days' hard lab mr.
