Hart to Annie Ravenscroft ; the Camden Hotel, Surrey- street. from Joseph Smith to Wm. Davies; the Cornwall and Devonshire Arms, Church-street, from Edward Page to Woe. Doyle ; the Dog and Partridge Inn, Halton-road, from Thomas Johnson to James Robert Critchley. A PENSIONER ON THE SPREE.—Bernard Kennedy, a res- pectable io•king man, was brought uo at Runporn Police Court, on Monday, charged with being drank and disor- derly.—The prisoner pleaded guilty.—Tbe Police Clerk proved the drunkenness, and Mr. Dutton, the market in- spector, said the man came to the market place and took possession of a fish stall. He said he would have his rights. When the woman in charge interferfered he "deliberately thrashed her," and then threw a quantity of fish on tne floor.—Superintendent Hollingsworth said the prisoner was an army reserve man, and drew his pension at Northwich on the Ist inet.—A fine of lOs and cots was imposed. RUNCORN GROCERS IN TROUBLE.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Houghton was cjiarged with selling bread otherwise than by weight. Mr. Lake appeared for the defendant, who pleaded guilty. Superintendent Hollingsworth said he bad received complaints that bread was not weighed in the town, and he had thought it well to put the act in force. In this instance the loaf was not weighed, and was three ounces under weight.—Thomas Rey• nolds, of Shaw-street; Charles Williams, Bold-street; Ma- tilda Ellison, Parker-street ; Matthew Timperley, Ashbridge- street ; and Ellen Mannering, Portland-street, were sum- moned to answer similar charges. The loaves were all antler weight to a slight extent. E lei' defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined is and costs us. STEALING DAMSONS AT NORTON.—Before Mr. A. Thomas, at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday. George Hayes and William Hayes, young men, were charged with having, on the 19th September, stolen one quart of damsons from the garden of Sir Richard Brooks, Bart.—Benj main Pickles, the gardener, who lives at Haddock's Lodge, Norton, deposed to seeing the prisoners up a damson tree, at 4,30 on the Sunday named. They were plucking the fruit. They ran away when he appeared.—Both prisoners denied that they were near the spot at that time, and George called Emma Rue- sell, of Spring Gardens, Runcorn, who stated that she saw him asleep on the sofa at three o'clock and about bait-past five.—A fine of 2s 64 and costa, lie 6d, or in default seven days' hard labour, was imposed upon each prisoner.—The prisoners pleaded guilty to appearing at the Petty Sessions, on Monday, in a state of drunkenness, and were each fined 5s and costs, 7s. A WIDNES FOREMAN CHARGED WITH DRUNKENNESS.— At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Patrick Tansey, a fore- man at Messrs. Gaskel', Deacon, and Company's works. was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Water. street on Saturday afternoon. Mr. Knowles appeared for the defendant. P.C. Cummins said about a quarter to five on Saturday afternoon, he saw the defendant, who was mak- ing a great noise and disturbance, in Water-street. A crowd of people had gathered round him, and the street was in an uproar. He asked him to go away, but he became worse. He had ultimately to take him into custody. He was drunk. —Several officers gave evidence as to defendant's state. Mr. Knowles argued that his client was well enough to take'care of himself, and that he was only guilty of disorderly be- haviour, and a summons should have been taken out accor- dingly. Mr. Tansey should not have been locked up.—De- fendant was fined 5s and costs, or seven days. A YOUNG THIEF AT WIDNES. On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Thomas Moores, 11 years of age, son of Thos. Moores, 37, James-street, was charged with having on Sat- urday afternoon stolen £1 Ils 9d, a purse, and three pawn tickets, from a dwelling-h wee in James-street, the property of John Carmen. The prisoner was playing with the prose- cutor's little girl in his house on the day in question, and Mrs Carmen went out for a short time, leaving them by themselves. When she returned the prisoner was gone, and she missed her purse. containing £1 lie 9.1 and three pawn tickets. The prisoner, it transpired, after taking the money, gave 25s of it to a boy named Malone, who handed it over to the police. Search was made for the prisoner. and P.C. Worsfold apprehended him in St. Helens market the same night. He had a new cap, 2 new pipes, an ounce of tobacco, a box of matches, and two pigeons in his possession.—He pleaded guilty, and having been convicted before of theft, was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment, and then ordered to be sent to a reformatory for four years. HOLY TRINITY . RuNconer.—The members of this association inaugurated their 13th session, on Monday evening, by a miscellaneous entertainment held in Holy Trinity schoolroom. Between six and seven o'clock refresh- ments we-e served to those present, and at half-past the musical part of the programme commenced with a few speeches. The chair was occupied by Mr. Philip Speakman, who, after Mr. H. West, the secretary, had read the annual report, made a few observations on the advantages and uses of Young Men's Christian A.ssociations. The Rev. T. P. Bell also delivered a speech, and then Mr. C. Pownall gave a capital rendering of " The gate of heaven." Miss Sim- kins received a well-merited encore for her singing of "Auntie," and in the duet "Two merry hearts "she and her co-singer, Miss Ainsworth, were similarly honoured. Messrs. Moore and Fox gave the duet "Love and war" in a man- ner that elicited a warm recall. "Waiting," by Miss Howard, was a pretty piece of vocalisation, and the manner in which Miss Preston sang "The old lock" was much ap- preciated. Mr. Fryer also gave a song. Mr. Adams, of Liverpool, and Miss Tyrie were highly successful in a couple of recitations. A pianoforte solo by Miss Isheiwood called forth a hearty encore. At the conclusion of the pro- ceedings the Rey. %kr. Preston moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman, of whom he spoke in terms of praise. Mr. Speakman, he said, was ever ready to do anything which tended to the prosperity of the town. The motion was seconded by Mr. Hankinson, and carried. THE HALEBANK FARMER AND THE Ex-POLICEMAN.— Messrs. Pilkingtcn and Brock were occupied a considerable time on Thursday, at Widnes Sessions, hewing a case in which Mr. William Turton, aged seventy, an extensive far- mer under Colonel Blackburne at Hale, was summoned by Edward Clay, an ex-policeman, who is now a carter, firstly, for assaulting him on the 4th inst., and secondly, for heat- ing a horse belonging to him with stick. Clay was like• wire summoned for doing damage to Mr. Turton's isccupa- ;Jon road to the amount of one shilling, and also as ^Jilting him. Mr. Husband appeared for Mr. Tartan. Clay stated that several people paid Mr. Turton a guinea a year for usin; the road, but he had refused to accept such payment from his employ r, Colonel Newbu-n. Witness was going on the road which led from Hal shank Stetion to. Hale, when Mr Turner charged him with trespassing. He told him to stRIIIDODS him, when Mr. Turton struck his horse with a a very heavy stick (produced) on the nose and of the back of the ear. Defendant's son John also tried to pull him over the side of the trap, and defendant tore his vest badly, beat him with the stick, and, lastly, put him over some wire fencing with the object of throwing kiln into an adjoining field. Witness admitted having been warned not to used the road.—The Bench sal lit was a matter for regret that Mr. Turton could not arrange with Clay's employers ro as to let them me the road, and he had no right to assanit Clay, but should have summoned him. However, as Clay had persisted in going that way r fter be- ing warned, they had decided to dismiss all the sommenses. —Mr. Husband remarked that an arrangement had now been made for the use of the road.

VACCINATION AT LEICESTER. --Ttle vaccination " dead-lock " at I eicester is becoming serious. lathe pa3t twelve months the number of infants success- -Lilly vaccinated has only been about 25 par cent of the whole number born, and it is stated that at least 2,000 parents have neglected the obligation imposed upon them by statute. The Board of Guardians have decided to stop prosecuting defaul- ters, and it is difficult to see how the law is to be enforced. Dr. Johnson in his address to the Medi- cal School of King's College, London, last week, specially warned the people of Leicester that they would perhaps abandon their present attitude when they were invaded by smallpox and -witnessed a ter- rible "massacre of the innocents "—a calamity which, he predicted, was certain to occar.

AT.7.111 OLD BIRDS OF THE CHURCH.—" Modern So- ciety" says :—The Bishop of Carlisle, by commis- sion, has been sitting upon an old rector in his dio- cese who has enjoyed a family living for half a century. Although the old pastor, who has shot .ed the flock all these yea— to a pretty good tune, defended himself well against the charges of doing nothing or next to hothing in the face of a growing population, the report of the commission has been against him, and the bishop has decided that he must employ a second curate. There is an Act for the retirement of these ancient fogeys when incapacitated, on not less than a third bof the in- come of the benefice as a pension, but it i 3 unfortu- nately permissive. In order to meet certain cases it ought to be compulsory. There is another old bird of this class in the diocese of Liverpool. It is a very large parish with a magnificent church and a very big income. He has Wen advertising for a year or two for a curate, but the place is so well known that the people des- pair of ever seeing the Church's work done in the Church's way. Now, why does not the Bishop of Liverpool sit upon this antiquated speci- men of a loaves and fishes grabber, and either billet three curates upon him, or else drive him resign?
PENKETH WESLEYA N MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.—The fifth session of the above society

was opened on Wednesday evening, in the Wes-- leyan Day School, when there was a very large number present. The President,. Mr. Garnett, Hall Nook, took the chair. After business had been dis- posed of, the President delivered his inaugural ad- dress, which was listened to with great pleasure, and frequently applauded. The session promises to be one of the best, an excellent programme having been prepared. There is also an increase of mem- bers. The following gentlemen spoke in commenda- tion of the address :—Messrs. C. E. Parker, Hob- son, White, Dobson, D. Garnett, D. Watson, &c., the meeting terminating with the benediction. SUCCESSFUL FLOATING OF THE NEW MANX LINE. —The official announcement of the closing of the lists of the l‘lanx Line appears in another column. The new Isle of Man. Liverpool, and Manchester S;eamship Company, Limited, has been very favour- ably received by the investing public, the shares having been taken up even more rapidly than was expected. Mr. William Pierce, M.P., a member of the eminent Glasgow firm who built those famous "greyhounds of the Atlantic," the Etruria, Alaska, and Arizona, has alreadybegun work upon the boats for the new line. - A more favourable time for this undertaking could scarcely be chosen, the present especially low pilces of materials and construction , being very advantageous. The new steamers will be among the fastest, very probably may prove to be the fastest, sa"ing out of the port of Liverpool, as they are to attain at least a speed of 21 knots an . hour. They will be luxuriously fitted up, and are to be ready n May, 1887. MUNIFICENT TREAT TO SCHOOL CHILDREN.— To-day (Saturday) the school children of Widnes, Farnworth, Penketh, and Sankey are to have a trip to the Liverpool International Exhibition. Mr. E. Bolton, the managing director of the works of the Widnes Alkali Company, is generously defrayinr, the cost, and M. G. H. Danby has had charge of the arrangements. Two trains have been chartered. The first train leaves Farnworth at 8-55, and will convey 100 children from the Widnes Church schools, 100 from Farnworth Church schools, and 400 from the Widnes Board schools. A second train is to leave Sankey Bridges at nine o'clock and convey the Penketh and Sankey schools (400 children), Father Clarke's schools, Widnes (200 children), and Father Finegan's school (100 chil- dren). There will therefore be a total of 1,300 children whe are to enjoy the prsvilege on account of their proficiency and good conduct. Immedi- ately on the arrival of the scholars at the Exhibition they will .be photographed in one group. The return journey will be commenced at 7-30 in the evening. DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.—A meeting of idle members of this Board was held in the Sessions House, Daresbury, on Thursday afternoon, Mr. Edward Greenall in the chair.—A letter was read from Mr. Thomas Hadfield, of Overton, complaining of loose sharp stones on the roads. About Frodsham, Frodsham Bridge, Sutton, and Halton the loose stones were especially abundant.—The Surveyor said he had been over the roads named, and, with . one exception, they were in excellent condition, and be wondered how such a letter could have been written.-4 was decided to instruct the surveyor to report tol.the clerk on the condition of the roads. —The Distribt Auditor having, made a surcharge of .£1 in the accounts of the surveyor, as paid to Mr. William Long, as compensation for widening a high- way in the parish of Grappenhall, and making a fence to the same, the Board decided to instruct the clerk to write the Local Government Board that the ir embers of the Highway Board considered it to be an improvement, and that the account ought to be passed.—The Chairman: This is simply a matter of red tapeism. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Long : And a piece of unnecessary meddling; as if we had not ti ‘ 3 ability to say what is an improvement and what is not.—The Finance Committee reported that all the calls had been paid, the balance in the trea- surer's hands being £1,614 2s Sd.—This was the principal business.

were quite as bad as those from the Glycerine Works. In addition to the smells there were some low pipe acting as chimn s for the conveyance of saioke, and in his opinion an intimation ought to be given that the Board could only consider them as temporary structures; because, where they had a large population close adjoining, it could be easily understood that when the wind brought the smoke into the dwellings of por people it must be very offensive. —Mr. Grine asked were the smells og Bundav to be clearly identified with the works at the corner of Greenway-read. It was not a smell that he could recognise as coming from any works in Runcoirt and neighbourhood at all. He could see no fumes arising from the

works, and the smell might have arisen from a canal boat that was carrying an offensive cargo. The proprietors of the works were anxious to carry on their bueinese without rendering themselves ob- noxious to the inhabitants.— Mr. Lightburn said there was no doubt nuisances did arise occasionally and the Health Committe had not been unobservant. He thought when there was a nuisance such as that described it had arisen from an accident, and that gas escaped, which it was very much in the interest of the manufacturers to retain. The nuisance, however, should not be attributed to one partica- hr place until they had clear means of identification. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Shaw said he wished to correct Mr. Grice. He was net there to apologise for any particular works, nor was he there to make complaints except for the public good. Mr. Grice was not very well acquainted with smells or he would not have cued that a sulphur smell. It appeared to him toebe a smell as if from burning bones, and he also knew where it came from. He saw where it pro- ceeded from —Mr. Grice replied that he was not apologising for any works; they were quite able to do that themselves. The smell of burning bones came with a south- east wind, and it did net come from any Runcorn or Widnes works.-51-. Shaw: That is another apology.— Mr. Grice : It is rot an apology. It is a distinct state- ment.—Mr. Hankinson said the smell was as described by Mr. Shaw. It was all very well for people to pass by and just get the scent of it, but to people who had to live in it and breath it, it was abomin4hle. He and his wife took a walk over to Widues on Sunday to get out of the stench.

(Loud laughter.) The smoke from those works, when the atmosphere was heavy, beat down into their very houses until it could scarcely be borne. The chimneys were not high enough. Wherever the nuisance proceeded from, it was the duty of the Health Committee to sift it out and remedy it.— Mr. Imieon said there was no doubt about the fact men- tioned by Mr. Shaw. It was an abominable stench, some- thing like ammonia. If there was a small nuisance on cot- tage property a notice would be quickly served upon the owner, and he thought the Board ought to fly at higher zame (hear, hear) and make larger people con- form to the rules. He had heard of people being caused to vomit by the stench.—Mr. F. A. Lake sr id the smell was too plein and palpable for them to be thrown off the sent by Mr. Grice trailing a red herring in Cie shape of a canal boat before them. (Laughter.) The place whence it proceeded was easily iden- tified, because, he was going to say they could see the smell. (Laughter.) He should call the attention of al. ge works to a nuisance just as readily as he would a small cottage occupier.—Mr. Lightburn said there seemedlo be a very sudden upheaval of feeling on this question, as though this nuitance had never arisen before. From the general tenour of the observations one would suppon'that the Health Com- mittee had got some reason for refrainitg from taking ac- tion against the larger birds while trying te catch the small ones. He could assure them there was no such feeling. The commitee deal evenhanded justice all round, but would take care not to harass anybody unnecessarily and make then-selves a nuisance. The law Clerk asked why should not the attention of the general manager be called to the nuisance. He had sug- gested that the R.mcorn Rural Sanitary Authority should draw his attention to anything of that- deecription, be- cause he could not always on the spot.—M. Shaw : I think nothing would have been said if it had not been for Mr. Grice trying to wriggle out of it.—The Chairman thought they might now be satisfied as the Health Com- mittee had promised to deal out even-handed justice.

div.head: MEDICA.L DISPUTE.
div.p: THE MEDICA.L DISPUTE.

At the St. Helena County Court on Wednesday afternoon, before his Honour Judge Collier. the representatives of Dr. J. E Hiffernan' at present an inmate of Rainhill County Asylum, brought an action, as a test case, against George Boardman, of Lowe-street, to recover £5 17s in respee' of professional attendance given in circumstances stated below. Mr. Beaumont, solicitor, appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Swift, barrister. Liverpool, represented Dr. O'Keeffe and Mr. E. Wilson.—Mr. Beaumont said this was one of a series of , actions which had come before his Honour's colleague. In Ithis case the representatives of Hiffernan sued a patient for medical services while he was in practice with a Mr. Wil- son, Hiffernan ara4 a duly-qualified man. but Wilson was an unqualified man, who had acted as assistant first to Dr. lO'Keeffe, then to Hiffernan, and again to Dr. O'Keeffe. The attendances in question were made upon Mrs. Boardman while he and Wilson were practising together. Accounts had been sent in on behalf of both Hiffernan and 0 Keeffe, and the defendant refused to pay either party. Advertisements had been inserted in the local papers by both parties, each warning patients not to pay the other, and consequently the patients paid neither.—Mrs Board- man, the defendant's wife stated that when she went to the surgery she saw Mr. Wilson, whom she told to rend a doc- tor to her house. Mr. Wilson visited first, and Dr. Hiffernan came frequently afterwards. She had received a bill from Dr. O'Keeffe in respect to Hiffernan's attend- ances. and she had paid him a part of the money due.— Cross-examined by Mr. Swift : She never employed Dr. Hiffernan in her life. On one occasion when be came to see her, in consequence of what he asked her, she paid for him half a glass of brandy. He asked her if she had an old pair of shoes she could give him. She remembered Hiffer- nan telling her that he had left O'Keeffe and was going into practice with another.—Mr. Wilson said he was an un- qualified medical man practising in St. Helens as assistant to Dr. O'Keeffe. Between 1834 and 1885 Hiffernan was also an assistant to Dr. O'Keeffe. During that time O'Keeffe's name was taken down and Hiffernan's name put up instead. Witnesses name was also up.—Cross-examined by Mr. Swift: He agreed acting on behalf of Dr. O'Keeffe to pay Hiffernan £2 104 a week, in addition to a portion of certain fees. Hiffernan had no interest whatever in the Practice beyond that of a servant. Hifferuan was at pre- sent an inmate of Rainhill Asylum, where he had been over twelve months.—Re-examined by Mr. Beaumont: When he made the agreement with Hiffirnan, O'Keeffe's name was not mentioned. Without waiting to bear the defend- ant his Honour nonsuited the plaintiff and ordered him to pay costs.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS:
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS:

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road. on Thursday. Mr. P. Speakman' the chair- man, presided, and there were present Messrs. S. Taylor, W. Fisher' W. Farrell, J. W. Lightburn, W. Hankinson, 11. J. Grice,J. Dobson, R. Shaw, E. Imison, W. Whittaker, F. A. Lake, H. White, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor). DOCTOR'S REPORT.-DEATH TRAPS.

The Medical -Officer of Health reported that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amount to 42. One was an inquest case, and of the remain- ing 41 deaths 22 were due to diarrhcea, two to whooping cough, two to inflammation of the bowels, two to congestion of the liver, two to disease of the brain, one to kidney disease, two to premature birth. one to pleurisy, one to con- sumption, one to debility, one to heart disease, and one to inflammation of the living membrane of the brain. The above 42 deaths show an average death rate for the twelve months of a.fraction over 29 per 1,000 of the estimated population. He had inspected during the month a series of nuisances arising from defective sewerage arrangements, and from dilapidated ashpits and closets in Show-street, and English- row, and Zion-place. The nuisances were receiving atten- tion from the Health Commissioner.—Unatakorisd Struc- tures in Yards: This was a grave and growing evil, and should be dealt with in a summary manner. Constant com- plaints were made about these dangerous encroachments. He advised the immediate framing of rules with regard to milk houses arid dairies. He again drew attention to the great danger to health arising from a direct communication between slopstones and the common sewers of the town, without the intervention of a trap. He found there were still in existence some of these pernicious death traps. Immediate steps should be f aken to disconnect the slopstones from the sewers. He had also inspected the common lodging houses during the month, and found there was a general disposition to conform with the requirements of the Acts of Parliament. He was glad to be able to report that the town was singularly free from infec- tious diseases at present.—Mr. Shaw said the surveyor should see that these suggestions were carried out. His own impression was that builders were putting up property at the present time and connecting the pipes of the slop- stones with the sewers. It would be very much better if steps were taken for having this practice stopped, while at the same time old property was altered as circumstances required.—Mr. Farrell said he bad not one of those connec- tions in his house.—Mr. Shear: I am very glad, Mr. Farrell. —Mr. Fisher said there were a great nutiober of those con- nections, but if the property owners were asked, he had not the slightest doubt they would make the alterations.—Mr. Lake asked whether a certificate was granted before a new hoase was inhabited.—The Chairman replied that when the plans submitted to the Board were approved, that was con- sidered as a certificate.—Mr. Lightburn added that the sur- veyor exercised supervision over new property.
A PESTILENTIAL NUISINCE.-IIIPORTANT DISCUSSION.

Upon the minutes of the Health Committee being moved for approval, Mr. Shaw asked what steps the committee had taken with respect to the nui,ance in Greenwav-roz 1, of which there had been great complaints for several months. On Sunday last, when people were coming from the places of worship, most sickening fumes were proceeding from the works at the bottom end of Greenwav-road. He felt sure that if the attention of the proprietors was called to what was a serious nuisance very detrimental to health, they would abate it. The smells that had arisen from thesa works

div.head: FREE LIB,IARY IsE PENSION.

Mr. F. A. Lake asked the Chairman of the Finance Com- mittee what was being done to meet the requirements of the Free Library, or whether the matter was deferred definitely. The reading-room was becoming ieconvenientiv crowded.— Mr. Fisher replied that the subk.ct had been adjourned until after the election. Of course they would now be able to gct the thing finlshed. He understood that the plan ap- proved was simply to extend the rooms on the east side, as it was considered Ills extension would meet their require- ments for some time—The Cbairinan concurred, and added that rooms for science and art cla..ses might be ob'ained by agreemeet with the School Board. Science and art classes should take deep roet la Runcorn, and if they could off o facilities in allowing their rooms that they had occupied very seldom upstairs, he thought it would be a good thing. —Mr. Shaw suggested that science and art classes should be -held not in that building but in the Board School. This was the usual course in other places, and a very moderate sum was fixed for holding all kinds of classes. Now they bad these whorls in Greenway-road, they had any amount c accsmmodatioa unused in the evening.

div.p: PUBLIC B&THS.

Mr. Liehtburn announced that t was the intention of the He.lth Committee to consider the question of public baths in the course of next month, and it would be well if the members of the burd were te think about the subject. so thlt they would not be unprepared for any motion. He stated that frequently on a Sunday moraine more persons from Runcorn used the Widnes baths than persons who re- eidrd in Widnes did.

Mr. Lake introduced a discussion on this subject, and eventually the committee of seven - gentlemen previously elected to deal with the matter were re-elected.

Mr. Imison inquired whether anything had been done about a subway at the station.—The Chairman replici that the matter was under consideration.
WIDNES __REVISION COURT,

The revision of the list of Parliamentary voters for the Widnes district of the Widnes Division was commenced on Thursday evening at the Sessions House. Whines, before Mr. J. T. Foard, barrister. Mr. H. B. Shores represented the Liberal party, Mr. .1. T. Lynskey, solicitor. Liverpool, the Irish Nationalists, and Mr. W. B. Woodnorth, solicitor, Liverpool, the Conservatives. Mr. John Goff, the assistant overseer for Widnes, and Mr. Houghton, the assistant over- seer for Dittos, were present. The court was well filled with persons having to make claims or refute objections.

div.head: IMPORTANT 'LODGER CLAIMS.
div.p: IMPORTANT 'LODGER CLAIMS.

William White. of 35, Vine-street, claimed a vote for two furnished rooms which he occupied at that address. He paid es ed to Mrs. Davies, the landlady.—Mr. 'Shores : What is the assessment of the house ?—Mr. Goff: Lii 53.—Mr. Shores: I submit that is not enough.—Mr. Woodnorth : There is no one on for the house.—The Revising Barrister: Is Mrs. Davies any relation ?—Claimantr. No.—Tha vising Barrister: I don't think it is a good claim, but as he is no relation I will allow it.

The Rev. David Davies, Welsh Wesleyan minister, eleimed, through Mr. Shores, as a lodger in respect to 5, V.ne-street. He paid Zs per week for two furnished rooms, and this payment covered the use of coat —Mr. Goff said the rateable value of the house was ZIA 58.—The Revis- ing Barrister: How many people live in the house ?—The Claimant: Four.—The Revising Barrister: How many rooms do the other people occupy ?-01aimant : Two.— The Revising Barrister : I don't think it is good enough.--,-Mr. Shores pointed out that he had just allowed a claim where fld per week less was paid, and this with an exactly similar claim. Mr. Davies had the exclusive occepation of the rooms, and he was no relation to the per- Bonin the house. He had also a specific contract for the use of the rooms only, and he submitted this was a better claim than the other one.—The Revising Barrister said it was equation whether the use of furniture and coal and gas was not worth more than 3s per week, and if so it re- duced the claim below the required rateable value. Then there was another element in this case, which did not exist in the other cr6e. There was a yore already in respect of this house, and therefore the rooms could not be worth an addition to the householder's interest of SlO clear annual value.—Mr. Woodnorth said as the entire house was rated at Lll 5s it was impossible to clear it.—The Revising Bar- rister: That is what! say. It is perfectly impossible.—Mr. Shores contended that the fact that there was already a vote given te the occupier of the house did not affect the ques- tion.—The Revising Barrister asked Mr. Shores if he could show him that there was, after deducting the other rooms of the house, with an assessment of al 101, that this man could occupy two rooms which were of the clear annual value of £lO. Could he by any reasoning convince him of that.—Mr. Shores said the claimant paid 3s lOt for rooms, and that left 3s 1d fir furniture, gas, and coals, which he contended was quite ample.—The Revising Barrister : No. I don't think it is. Mr. Shores said the gentleman was a minister in the town and occupied the rooms at their market value—as cheaply as he could get them.—The Revising Barrister said if he paid more than the actual rental value of the premises be was paying for some- thing which the law did not recognise.—Mr. Woodnoith said his Honour had stated that if a house was rated at £lB he (the Barrister) would not allow two on for it.—The Revising Barrister: That is a general rule; always subject to what he considered bona fide claims. He regarded this as an honest bona fide claim. It was a question r.,f 'fact ; were these rooms worth £lO. He did not dispute Mr. Davies' statement tbat he paid that amount, and be there- fore allowed the vote. The Rev. R. G. Hughes, Congregational minister, claimed a vote as a Liberal for the sole occupation of two rooms at Farnworth. He paid his landlord, Mr. H. Clarke, 14s per week. He considered the rooms worth half a guinea, and the rest be gave for attendance Food was net included. —His Honour allowed the claim. There were no other cases of interest. On Friday morning the court opened at 10 o'clock. Mr. Shorog again reoresen'ed the Lib.rals, and M oodnorth the Conservative..

STILL IT DIED.—A woman came forward to claim a vote for her husband, named Needham, who lives in Victoria- street. About five minutes was spent in tracing this family into four successive houses during the past 12 months, to find at last that during the qualifying period the family had occupied apartments as lodgers.—The Revising Barrister: We have taken a long time attempting to cure that vote, and after all it died. (Laughter.) There were no other cases of interest or importance. The revision has so far been highly satisfactory to the Liberal partr who have, without doubt, made a substantial gain. Mr_ *Shores, the Liberal agent, is to be congratulated upon his energetic and successful labours. Much satisfaction is felt that he has be,,n instrumental in securing the rotes of the priests at the Catholic Presbytery in Luysdale-road.

LAIN'S schemes Lord RANDOLPH lIONV speaks with profound respect, but a year ago he used these very schemes to illustrate "the intense dishonesty and the flagrant immorality of the modern Radical party." He is in favour of land law reform now, but last year he told the country that we had only to wait for the beneficent results of Lord CAIRNS'S Settled Lands Act, and we should see that any further reform was needless. He is all for licensing reforms now, and yet it is within easy recollection that he denounced the Liberals for desirin7 to " tyrannise over the liberty of, and further restrict the few privi- leges and luxuries enjoyed by, the working classes." As for Radicalism generally, Lord RANDOLPH has repeatedly sneered at the comprehensive programme of the reformers, and has declared his belief that "the Eng- lish people, with the common-sense that has always distinguished them, will prefer the subsiance of Tory reality to the illusion of Radical promises." Yet the Dartford speech is one long "illusion," and the Tories who really believed that Lord RANDOLPH was heart and soul with them, are astounded by the revelation of his imposture. Will the common sense that has always distinguished the English people sustain the fortunes of this cynical gambler? The first consideration, of course, concerns Lard RANDOLPH'S position with his own party. Will they follow the new Evangel, or will there be a revolt? How is the old county member who has spent his life in denouncing Radical innovations to adapt his mind to the new policy, and tell his constituents that afLer all there is a great deal in what Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN and Mr. COLLINGS propose? The stronghold of Conservatism has always been the fixed belief of a large class that change is unwise and dangerous; and when the coun- try has not been very eager for any particular change, this class has mainly influenced the public judgment. If there were an election now it is highly probable that many Tories would refuse to go to the poll. We are aware that party ties are often stroneer than the most cherished prejudices, and that Lord RANDOLPH'S • success will be for many Con- servatives the measure of his morality. .Others will persuade themselves that the present concessions to Radicalism are only temporary, and that when the Irish tyranny is overpast, Lord RANDOLPH will decline to march any further on the road to revolution. These and other considerations will dispose a large number of Tories to accept the new regime. But there will remain a sufficient force of discontent in the party to make every move in the game extremely perilous; and any miscalculation may reveal to Lord RANDOLPH that he has as much to fear from mutiny in his rear as from the enemy in his front.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

WIDNES 1.0.G.T., GOOD SAMARITAN LODGE.—Brother Galilee presided at the wieldy meeting of this lodge, when a capital programme of songs, recitations, and readings was gone through. W.C.T. Sister I emb closed the proceedings in due form. . FARNWORTH PARISH CHURCEG—The annual harvest thanksgiving services in connection with this church were commenced on Friday evening, when the Rey. S. Wilkinson, of St. Paul's, Warrington, occupied the pulpit. On Sundae' morning the preacher was the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton. Holy Trinity, Warrington; and in the evening the Rev. G. Bond, the vicar, officiated. The sacred edifice w s charm- ingly decorated for the occasion. SALVATION ARMY ARTILLERY AT RUNCORN.-0.1 Tees- day, Runcorn was visited by the flying detachment of the Salvation Army in the shape of six officers, who travel through the country on tricycles in order to visit the vari- ous stations. The detachment is known by the name of the "Iron horse artillery." Special meetings were conducted by the officers at the Barracks, High-street, and in the evening the building was crammed. On Wednesday, the officers left Runcorn on their „ icycles for Northwich. RAILWAY COLLISION AT HALTON JUNCTION, NEAR RUN- • ORN.—At half-past eleven o'clock on Friday night a collision occurred at Halton Junction, some two miles from Runcorn, between two goods trains. It appears that one of the trains was proceeding to Chester and the other to Run- corn from Crewe. On reaching the points the two trains collided through one having overrun the signal. Both veins were going at a slow rate at the time, and little damage was done. Three wagons were thrown off he line, and a delay of some two hours was one of the most serious coneequences of the accident. The traffic for Liverpool pro- ceeded via Warrington. HASTE TO THE RESCUE LODGE I.O.G.T.—The members of this lodge held their weekly session in the room, Major Cross-street. The usual business was transacted, after which a tea was provided for 30 members and friends by the following brothers and sisters :—Brothers Widowes, Smith, and Galilee, and Sisters Smith, Galilee, and A. Lamb. Tea over, the following programme was then given with Brother W. Galilee in the chair :—Violin solo, Bro. Andrews; recitation, Brother T. Galilee ; song, Sister A. Lamb; song, Brother E. Smith; recitation' Brother W. Galilee ; song, Sister E. Smith; song, Brother G. Owens. The proceedings terminated by singing the doxology. A vary pleasant evening was spent. NORTHWICH DIVISION PARLIAMENTARY LICENSED VIC- TUALLERS' ASSOCIATION.—The first annual meeting of this association has been held at the Crown Hotel, Northwicb, under the presidency of Mr. T. Skidmore. Messrs. A. Hough, S. Armstrong, W. Hankinson, and J. Stubbs were present from Runcorn. Mr. J. W. Lightburn, of Runcorn, was elected a vice-president, and Messrs. Armstrong, Water- worth, and Coward were appointed a district committee for Runcorn.oSubsequently a dinner was held, and a lengthy as gene through. Mr. W. Hankinson, Quarter- responded to the toast of the "Army, navy, and reserve forces" in a capital speech. The toast of the evening," Success to the Association," was given by Mr. A. E. Fletcher, who paid a compliment to the fair- minded dealings and the even-handed justice of the magis- trates in the Division, and said the licensed victualle-s would have no difficulty in maintaining their position their cases were properly represented to the magistrates. STRANGE RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR WIDNES.—In a third-class compartment of the express leaving London for Liverpool at 7-30 a.m. on Tuesday, there travelled a gentleman named Charles Brown, who lives at 35, Clare- mont-square, Islington, London, and is employed as a com- mission agent in the paper trade. When the train had just passed Halebank Station he stood up and leaned against the door for the Purpose of looking through the window at the surrounding country. Immediately the door flew open. and he fell out on to the permanent wav head first. His head and face were very badly bruised and his wrist was broken, whilst be was also much shaken He was shortly afterwards found in an unconscious state by a platelayer named Joseph Grace, and he was conveyed to Widnes by the first train. His wounds were afterwards dressed by Dr. O'Keeffe, and late in the afternoon he proceeded to Liverpool in company with his brother, who had been telegraphed for. There was an extensive rumour that the man had jumped out of the train, but that statement is understood to be untrue. THEATRE ROYAL, RUNCORN —The popularity of the per- fornaances by Me-srs. Williams and Bowyer's company has been continued during the past week, when the drama "Shadows of Life" has been presented each evening. The lead role of Gerald Wynferd was taken by Mr. Edward Quigley, who plays a difficult part with natural ability. As the unscrupulous alyenturer, La.monde, Mr. James Buchanan was eminentlY successful. Miss Elith Lysla dis- played skill and taste in her pourtrayal of the wife of C rald Wonford, and Miss Julia Listelle as the vindictive Madame Zera, made a powerful impression by the force of her interpretation of the character. Miss Vera Kingsley was veie'r happy and bright as Polly Heathcote, the Vicar's daughter. Miss Allwood created much amusement as the London landlady. The cemic element of the piece was admirably sustained by Mr. Brien McCullough, who is a natural wit and humourist. On Thursday, the performance was under the patronage of the Licensed Victuellers' Asso- ciation, and the Runcorn and South Bank Bowling Clubs, and there was a capital audience. DROWNING FATALITY AT RUNCORN: BATHS ADVOCATt.O. —At the Railway Hotel. Lowlands-road, on Tuesday, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy noromer, held an inquiry on the body of James Ellis, nine years of age, son of Thomas Ellis, captain of a steam tug, who lives at 58, Bentinct- street. On Saturday afternoon the boy was sitting on the edge of the " gut " on No Man's Land, attempting to reach a piece of wood with his foe', when he fell into the water. He was carried away by the strong tide efore aid could be obtained, and was drowned. His body was found in the river on Sunday morning, bY a man named John Darby- shire.—A verdict of accidental'y drowned was returned.— The Coroner remarked that if some benevolent gentlemen would start baths in the town they would be a great benefit to the inhabitants. Boys would learn to swim, and these deaths by drowning in the river would not occur so fre- quently.—Mr. Yarwood, the foreman, coircided with the coroner. There was one of the newly elected Commis- sioners present; he hoped he would do all he could in order to get leeths.—Tne Coroner aid he should be glad to sub- scribe to baths.—Mr. Eankinson promised that he would do his utmost in furtherance of the movement for ' baths.

The Watch Committee of the Town Council have passed the following resolutions:—" That a gratuity of £95 be granted out of the superannuation funds of the borough to the widow of the late Inspector Berry, being the maximum amount allowed by law:" and "The committee wish to express their g:eat regret at the loss sustained by the death of Inspector Berry, and their sympathy with his widow and family on their sad bereavement. The committee regarded Inspector Berry as a most efficient and praiseworthy officer, and they feel that the borough has sustained a great loss by his death."

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. DIONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies., Councillor Greening, and Messrs. Sutton and

Frarcomb. ASSAULTING A BROTHER.-30h0 Cosgrove was charged with baying on the Friday previous assaulted Thomas Cos- grove, his brother. Complainant said that soon after seven o'clock in the morning defendant CAM to his mother's house, where complainant bad been spending the night, and cemanded to know what he was doing there. Defendant ordered him out of bed, and then assaulted him.—After the Bench had considered Use case, the Mayor said he thought it would do defendant good if he was sent away for a month, and sentenced him to prison for that period. DRUNEENNESS.—WiIIiam Toole was fined 54 and costs for being drunk and disorderly in St. James-street on the pre- vious Saturday night; and Patrick Berke, for being guilty of a similar offence in Cockheclge-lane on Battirdav night, was fined 55 and costs.—John Dagnall was fined 1.03 and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-strest.— Thomas Troy and Ann McCoan were charged with drunken- ness and disorderly conduct. Constable Bixendale said that when be was taking a prisoner through Scotland-toad to the Bridewell, Troy jumped on his back; both he and the female prisoner were drunk. Troy was sent to prison for fourteen days, and McCoan, who had not before been in trouble, was discharged with: a caution.—Thomas Garritty was sent to orison for a fortnight for being drunk and dis- orderly in Winwicir-street on the previcus Saturday —Mary Jane Ell es, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Irlam• street, was discharged with a reprimand.—Michael Dowd was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Old-road, Latchford, on Saturday niaht.—Maria Shields and a girl named Conway were each sent to prison for fourteen days for being drunk and disorderly in liattersby-lane.— Patrick Burke was fined 51 and costs for b•ing drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket•street.—Daniel Neale was fined 51, including costs, fer being drunk in Cairo-street.—Edward Crosby, for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket- street on the 28th ult., was sent to prison for fourteen days. A LAZY CASUAL.—Michael McDonon4h, an Irish lad, was sent to prison for seven days for refusing to perform his task of work whilst a casual inmate of the vagrant ward at the Union Workhouse. Fighting.—Jonas Dagnall and Alexander Tompkins were each ordered to pay costs for disturbing the peace by fight- ing. KEEPING A DOG WITHOUT A LICIFNSE.—James Coln was fined 15s cod costs for keeping a dog without a license. AN OnsTnrcrioN.—John Cross, junior, was summoned for allowing sides of pork to project over the footpath in St. James-street, Latchford, on the 24th ult., and was fined is and costs. _ _ .

ScHoot ATTENDANCH CASES.—The following cases were brought before the magistrates by Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer :—Thomas Ball, forgeman, Silver-street, fined se; Michael Cryan, agent, Farrell-street, fined ss; George Ryder, carter, Reger-street, fined 53 ; William Yates, carter, Roger-street, fined Se; William Higham, forgeman, Stamford-street, fined ss; John Harper, forgeman, Albert- street, fine 4 ss; Elizab-eth Openshaw, Be arsey-road, fined 5; Peter Garland, forgeman, Bewsev-road, fined ss; Joseph Ellison, forgeman, Philip-street, fined ss. 'WEDNESDAY—Before Alderman Pickmere (in the chair), Alderman Chandley, Councillor Greening, and Mr. John
WIDNES POLICE COURT.
SATT7RDAY.—Before Mr. T. S. Tiromis.

DRUNKENNESS.— Fd ward Walker, of Winsford, was charged with having been drunk at Widnes, on tie previous evening, and was fined 53 and costs, or seven days. BEGGING.—For this offence Jane Hardy, of Widnes, was committed to gaol for 14 days. MONDAT.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. T. S. Timmis.

DRUNKENNESS —The following persons were fined for drunkenness :—Martin Dunn, 7s 61 and costs, or ten days ; Patrick Murray. 5s and costs, or seven days; James John- son, 5s and costs, or seven days; John Starkey, who made his 36th appearance, £1 and coats, or a month ; Jowl Doyle, 15th appearance, £1 and costs, or a month; John Mannion, sth appearance, 103 and costs or fourteen days Julia O'Brien, 14th appearance, 103 and costs, or fourteen days. BEGGING.—John Smith and John McCarthy, strangers, were charged with begging in Gerrard-street on Sunday morning. Prisoners, who stated that they wanted money to pay their fare over Runcorn Bridge, were committed to gaol for seven days.—An Italian, named John Hinostan,was charged with begin g in Church-street, on Monday morn- ing, and, on the evidence of P.C. Coates, was c)mmitted to gaol for seven days. DRUNK AND REFUSING TO QUlT.—Owen Lewis, a young man, was charged with having on Saturday been drunk and refused to quit the licensed premises of J. Bell, the Black- borne Arms, and with doing wilful damage to the amount of £2 to a pla:e-glass window belonging to the same person. Evidence proving that defendant would not leave when requested, and that he smashed a window when put out, was adduced. The prisoner was fined Sc and costs, or seven days, for the drunkenness,anci 10s and costs and the damages I£2, or 14 days', for breaking the window.

Fairclough. A VIOLENT MILITIAMAN.—james Larkin, a militiaman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on the plat- form of the Central Btation oe the previous night. He was also charged with assaulting two railway officials. Prisoner endeavoured to enter a train that was in motion, and was told by an inspector to get off. He then struck the official, and afterwards assaulted a station constable. It was said that it took the services of five men to convey prisoner to the police station, and that his feet had to be tied together. The Bench imposed a fine of 5s and costs, or seven days' imprisonment, for the drunkenness, and 20s and costs, or a month's imprisonment, for the assaults. THURSDAY. Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. ALLEGED WIFE ASSAULT.—John Stokes was brought ep on a charge of aseaulting his wife, Hannah Stokes, but as that person did not appear he was remanded until the fol- loping morning. KR gFING A DOG WITHOUT LICENSE —TllOllla3 Pember- ton was summoned for keeping a dog without a license. He admitted the offence, bat said he had had" poor lack" this year, and had not been able to get a license.—He was fined 5s and costs, and ordered to take out a license at once. The alternative was seven daya' imprieonment. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Rlynolds and Dr. Gornall. ALLEGED WIFE ASSAULT.—Joha Stokes was brought up on remand charged with assaulting his wife, who did not appear to support her complaint. He was ordered to pay is, the costs. ALLEGED CRUELTY.—Henry Meers *as summoned for ill-treating a horse on the 16th of September, at Latchford, and John Connor was summoned for causing it to be ill- treated. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence.—An in- spector of the R.S.P.C.A. said that he saw Meers driving two horses in a 'bus. One of the horses was suffering from an enlarged knee, and under the. flanks was a mass of bleeding warts.—Mr. Robinson, veterinary surgeon, also gave evi- dence, and sail that the horse had !a very bad broken knee. It was not fit to trot, although it might be !used in a field. —For the defence, Mr. Browne called Mr. Dixontveterinary surgeon, who said that the warts were not painful; the horse had a shambling gait, but was not lame. Witness did not think there was any cruelty in working the animal.— The magistrates dismissed the case. THEE-E.g.—William Smith, a youth, was charged on re- mand with stealing a black worsted coat, value 10s, from his father's house in Bostock-street, on the previous Mon- day, and he was further charged with stealing a pair of boots, the property of James O'Brien, on the Wednesday previous. He was again remanded. DARAGE.—Charles Berries, a lad, was summoned for dam- aging the walls of house property in Battersby-lane, belong- ing to William flestock, to the amount of ss. He was or- dered to pay the i! image, or be birched. ALLEGED DESER:I9N.—Robert leherwood was summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon him to contribute to the maintenance of his wife, whom he was alleged to have deserted. Mr. Lon:4ton defended. As the complainant did not put in an appearance the c ise was dis- missed.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WaDiszsDay.—Before Mr. Peter Stubs and Mr. John Hy] ands. Dnurrizzr-liEss.—Patrick Murphy was fined 5s and costs for being drunk on the highway at Burtonwood, and Henry Taylor, summoned for being drunk and disorderly at Croft on the 10th September, and also on the 27th September,was fined 10s and costs.—Annie Harrison pleaded not guilty to a charge of being drunk and disorderly in Manchester road, at Rixton, on the 25th ult. She was dismissed. UNJUST WElGllTS.—lienry Ball, grocer, Winwick-road, Orford, and William Knowles, shopkeeper, Orford, were sum- moned for having in use weights that were incorrect, and were against the purchaser. The cases were proved by Su- perintendent Weir, and the defendants, who pleaded ignor- ance, were each ordered to pay the cests. A SLEEPY DBIVER.—James Clark, a boy, was fined is and Costs for being asleep while in charge of a horse and cart at Wootton on the 24th tilt. THEFT —Charles Holding was charged with stealing a coat, value 10s, the property of Thomas Booth, from a field at Orford, on the 14th ult. Prosecutor placed the coat on a sheaf of corn about forty yards from the road, and it was alleged that Holding took it. He was discharged with a caution.

Up to n call of time the home team were penned in their own quar- ters, never once having a chance to score. The visitors were declared the winners by one try and foar minors to nil. For the winners, Lomax nbayed his usual safe game at full-hack; the three-quarters. Lineard, Blackmore, and Hanberley, showed good form ; Vhalley and Shaw at half- back played a grand game ; whilst the pick of the forwards were Lowe, Barker, Rafferty, Critcbley, and Whittaker. SALFORD v. RUNCORN.—Thig match was played at Sal- ford, (el Saturday. About 2,500 spectators assembled to witnees the game, the reputation of the visitors having ex- cited considerable interest. Salford won the toss, and Lewis, for Runcorn, kicked off at 2-25, attacking the race- course go.l. After even play, the Salford forwards, beaded by Eagles, got to the Runcorn 25. Weods and Speakman relieved, and the visitors looked dangerous till Williams and Walmsley, by fine tactics, neutralized, and Eagles, fol- lowing.up in briliient style, seized the leather, and. dodging ' the opposing backs, ran behind ebe posts. Slater failed at goal. A free kick by Mainwaring gained a little advantage, and from a scrimmage in Runcorn ground Slater made a bid at goal, a minor only resulting. After the drop out, Walms- ley made one of those dodgy runs for which he is famous, and, beating all his opponents, gained a clever try sear touch, the place kick being again unsuccessful, and the minor point for Salford was registered through Varley's instrumentality, and at half-time Salford had scored 2 tries and 2 minors to Runcorn nil. Change of ends brought no ehange of luck for the visitors, for, despite the most strenuous exertion!, they could not force their way through the splendid defence of the home team. After Ottiwell's kick- off, Faulkner made a grand dribble, but what this gained was quickly lost through the dexterous efforts of Walmeley land Buxton. Twice the Runcorn full back ran the ball out ' from behind the line, so determined was the attack ; then Broady became prominent by a beautiful kick, and the hearty assistance of the forwards put the Salford line in ; danger, and severe scrimmages in the home quarter were finally relieved and the Runcorn half visited. Slater bad another kick at goal, missing very narrowly, and then Fagles got possession and put in a good run, but, holding the ball instead of passing, got tackled, and a good chance of scoring was lost. A most pleasant and fast game ended in a victory for Salford by 2 tries and 3 minor Points to sßuncern nil. Teams :—Salford: Mainwaring, back; Sleter, Walmeley' and Varlev (captain), three-quarter backs; Bux- ton and Clegg, half-backs; Eagles, Williams, Roberts, Smith, Skew, Ottiwell, Vickers, Jones, and Hughes, for- wards. Runcorn: Wood, back; Lunt, Speakman, and Davies, three-quarter backs H Hughes (captain) and H Andrews, half-backe; W Hughes. Lewis, Barnes, Wainwright, Faulk- ner, Broady, Clarke, and Gatley, forwards. WARRINGTON " A " TRAM v. HULMB IST.—This match was played at Warrington on Saturday, in the presence of 1,000 spectators, the weather being very fine. The home captain having won the loss, J Smith kicked off for Halme against the wind, Nevins returning to centre. Walsh ob- tained possession, and running smartly was neatly collared by Dovan near the goal line. From a scrimmage which ensued Whittle secured the ball, and passed to Boardman, who made a smart attempt to drop at goal, a deasl ball re- sulting. After a few !:minutes' hard play, Whittle again secured the ball and passed to Appleton, who followed Boardman's example with like result. Not to be deterred by his previous performance, Appleton from a pees by Whittle, dropped a splendid goal, amidst vociferous cheer- ing from the spectators, and immediately afterwards Whit- tle handed him the ball, and he followed his success by a grand try, Walsh failing at the place. From the drop out some very fast play was witnessed. The home team, how- ever, in the end overpowered their visitors, an from a scrimmage Whittle gave Appleton another chance, which he took advantage of and gained his second try, Walsh again failing at the place. On resuming Doyen obtained pesse;sion, and made a run half the length of the field before he was brought down by Craghan. From the scrim- mage Walsh passed to Appleton, the latter transferring to Antrobus, who secured the best try of the day, having to evade numerous opponents. Walsh, however, again failed to improve the point. Half time was now called. On re- suming Whittle kicked off, and Pickerieg mulled the ball. The home forwards, headed by E. Dillon and Molyneux, dribbled to the line, Doyen saving grandly. Ashurst was the next to cross the goal line, but failed to ground the ball, and being tackled by Pickering a maul took place, in which the latter came off victorious. The chances of scor- ing now by the visitors were very poor, and indeed through- out the second half they acted on the defensive. Molyneaux, Neyine, and Antrobus also crossed the line during this half, but tries were not allowed. On time being called the score stood as under :—Warrington, one goal, three tries, and eight minors, to Hnlme nil. With regard to the play, the visitors were out-matched from the commencement, and in the first half at least the borne team practically did as they liked. In the second half the visitors played an excellent defensive game, but while Whittle's followers were often within an ace of scoring, the home line was never even threatened. The visitors were overpowered in the scrim- mages, and completely out-played by the home half and three quarter backs. Teams :—Hulme. : Doyen, full back; J. W. Smith, Pickering. and Lloyd, three-quarter backs ; Heywood and Kellsall, half backs: W. Storer,' W. Brown, Beard, Walker, Howson, Bishop, Wilson, and J. Smith, foiwards. Warrington Bandies, full back; Boardman, Appleton, and Antrobus, three-quarter backs; Walsh and Whittle (captain), half backs ; Molyneaux, Dillon, Telford, Jones, Nevins, Craghan, Littlewoed, Asharst, and Bashford, forwards. WARRINGTON V. MR. T. R. SUTTON'S PICKED TEAM. This match was played at Warrington on Thursday last. Sutton's team were not very well represented, and Warring- ton were without the services of Graham, Rigby, and Hough. The home team ran up a score of 3 goals, 2 tries, 3 minors to their opponents nil. Eagles kicked off for the visitors, Barnes returning to touch, Warrington soon showed their superiority in the scrimmage, and soon afterwards Fair. Turner came through with the ball at his toes, a dead ball resulting in favour of the home team. Play now for some time took place in the visitors' 25, until Fair. Turner made a tremendous rush over the line, scoring the first try. Speak- man failing at goal Massey next got in a good run, but Barnes lost a little ground by running. Rimmer now came through, Plumpton finely returning. The same player shortly afterwards received a tremendous round of applause for a splendid ran from half-way to the line through the thick of the players. The visitors' forwards, however, re- moved danger to the 25, but Speakman passed splendidly to Barnes, who dropped a magnificent goal. Winterbottom from the kick out obtained a free kick, but Ashton replied with a nice dribble. The visitors' forwards, headed by ' Maclean and Eagles, now made a grand rush, which was splendidly stopped by Plumpton. Barnes, after some scrimmages, got in a nice run and kick to touch, and Jolley shortly afterwards looked like scoring, but was well tackled b 7 Appleton. Eagles now removed danger to the 25 flag, and Maclean aided still further by a dozen yards. The War- rington forwards, headed by Frank Turner and Povey, took the ball to the visitors' 25, where Plumpton made a huge drop at goal, a minor resulting. Barnes shortly afterwards had a drop at goal, another minor resulting. Some good scrummages now took place, and from one Speakman kicked wide to Maesey. who ran over the line, Plumpton failing at goal. Shortly after half time was called. On the resumption of play Frank Turner kicked off, Appleton's re- turn being replied to by Davies and Barnes. Plumpton next took another drop at goal, the ball falling short, a minor being the result. Fair. Turner next took the ball back to the line, when Hayes struggled over, and Speakman kicked lama gwa rse,sacienydwogebol riaal nu spdF, rppooml sasyst shssei settling akn ngodu dt co towhnnefi nv fei nsdi thetpolras3' h, oft oomr ewb as2lrd 5f ;swfhaoyule t. Tt ton replying Ashurst now came through with a nice dribble, and the for- warns, chief amongst whom were Eagles and Maclean, fur- ther aided his efforts and took play to the home 25, Plump- rssh forwardsfowith faryd,rsobgpesi again n(g) halfownolryk worked d stoppeda yt.heFbhaayilrl .t thloeUhfr sun llefl r back. in : n The visitors e iasioa Slagg being very conspicuous in stopping the advance. div.head: FXAMJNEA. SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1886.
div.p: THE FXAMJNEA. SATURDAY, OCTOBER 9, 1886.

On behalf of Warrington all the backs played well, Plumpton being a treat to witness ; Barnes also playing a magniticent game fully up to county form. The forwards one and all showed rare combined form, Fair. Turner, Ash- ton ;rnd Dillon being the Flick, The visitors' backs were rather weak, Winterhottocn and Witiaile being the‘pick. The forwards were Over-matched, McLean, Eagles, and Harrison being best. Ashton !Ind Applaton played a splendid game for the visitors.

Teams :—Warrington : Baer, Pliarnpton ; three-quarter, Jolley, Barnes, Massey ; half, Slag, Speakman ; forwards, Heyes, Nevins, F. Turner, Turner, E. Dillon.. W. Dillon, Povey, Davies, and Ashton. Sutton's team: Back, Wardle; three-quarter, Mallinson, Appleton, and Jew Winter ; half, Smith and Clegg ; forwaros, Ash urst, McLean, Eagles, Hardy, Fife, Ithrgingbottom, Chantler, and Harrison. In the evening an admirable dinner, prepared by "mine host" of The Roebuck, was partaken of by the players.

RUGBY RULES.
STAMFORD RANGERS V. WARRINGTON ExcgLsrorts. This match was played on the Rangers' ground, who were victorious. Scare : Rangers, 1 try, 10 minors; Excelsiors, 1 minor.

FARN WORTH (2ND TEAM) V. ST. PAUL'S (2ND TEAM), SEA.- comEs.—These teams met at Seacombe on Saturday, the game resulting in a win for Farnworth by 1 goal, 4 tries, and 19 minor points, to nil. SAXON OLD BOYS, WARRINGTON V. SUTTON FRES WAN- DERERS —These clubs met for the first time on Saturday, on the ground of the former. The result of a Very pleas- ant game was a win for the borne team. LION RANGERS, RUNCORN, T. WESTON TAM-O'-SHANTERS. —Played at Weston, on Saturday, and a capitally contested game resulted in favour of the Rangers by two tries and two minors, to one try and four minors. Molyneax and Web- ster played a grand game for the visitors, and each crossed the line.

WIDNES V. MOSSI.EY (2ND TEAMS.)—These teams met at Widnes, and like the first team the Widnes 2nd had to put up with defeat, by one dropped goal to two tries and three minor points. Widnes were very unfortunate in their at- tempts at goal. In the general play Widnes had a slight advantage, as is evidenced by the score. RUNCORN RECREATION V. TUEBROOK (2ND TEASES). A match was played between the above clubs on Saturday last, on the ground of the former, resulting, after a fast game in a victory for the Recreation. Score : Runcorn, two goals, one try, four minor.; ; Tuebrook, one try, one minor. The tries for Rancor's were obtained by J Lunt (2) and R Jones (1) ; goals kicked by Crompton. FARNWORTII (IST TEAM) V. ST. PAUL'S (SEACOMBB).— Ibis match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and after a most pleasant game resulted in a vic- tory for Farnworth by two goals, six minor points, to one minor point. The tries were obtained by li Broome and Holt. The try by Broome was got after a splendid run in. All the home team played well, the best of the visitors being Broady, Bunting, and Clark, backs; and Vicary and B Davies, forward. WIDNES RECREATION (IST TEAM) T. WIGAN Rome. —At Widnes, owing to the late arrival of the visitors, it was five o'clock before play commenced. Two " thirties " were Ow time allotted, and at the conclusion of the time, Widnes Recreation were the winners by one goal, two tries, and four minor points, to nil. For the home team, Parkinson and Bradshaw were the best of the backs, whilst for the forwards 'Norris and Brannon worked hard, especially the latter, who I obtained two tries in splendid style. For the visitors, Donoghue and Leyland were most prominent. RUNCORN RECREATION T. TUEBROOK,—PIayed at Liver- pool on Saturday, in fine weather. The Recreation winnieg 'the toes, took the choice of goal, and Tuebrook kicked off. The Recs. failing to return, a scrimmage was formed near , the line, Pearson carrying the ball over. The Recs. an- ; pealed for handed forward, which the referee disallowed. I The remainder of the game was very well contested, and re- ; sulte4 as follows :—Tuebrook, I try and 2 minor Points; I Recreation, 4 minor points. learns :—Recreation: W Wish- lade, back; J Clare, S Abrams, and H Pendleburv, three- quarter backs; G Pendlebury and S Booth, half backs; J lActon, S Worrell, J Green, J Pennington, W Johnson, F ; Couth, T Bite, D Massey, and Peacock, forwards. Toe- brook: F Bayley, back; A Vickers, H Edwards, and J Bay- ley, three-quarter backs; R Lech and G J Mahon. half I backs; Pearson, Slee, W Holloway, S Holloway, Lines, Fletcher, Robins, Western, and Pearson, forwards. i THE WIDNES INTER-WORKS FOOTBALL COMPETITION.-- I WID!IES ALKALI (No. 1 TEAM) V. HUTCHINSoN'S.—These teams met to play off their tie in the second round of the , Widnes Inter-Works Football Competition on Monday I evening. Two "twenty-fives " was the time allotted. Hut- ! chinson's won the toss, and elected to play down the brow' 1 The first half was well fought, and altheugh the Alkali had , the services of Farrell, of the Widnes F.C., and Speakman, 1 of the Runcorn F.C., they had their work cut out for them. 1 At call of half-time the Alkali had scored a goal, kicked by , Farrell, from a try by Bentham, to their opponents' two mi- nors. In the next half Hutchinson's, although they pressed ' their opponents on several occasions, were unable to score, while the Alkali put on three more ' minors. The match ended thus—Alkali one goal and three minors, to Hutchin- • son's two minors. Farrell and Speakman played well for the Alkalites, and Smith, Broom, and the full-back for Hut- . 1 chinson's. The latter saved several times in grand style. , I The umpires were Messrs. Albert Brown and Herbert Cooper land the referee Mr. W. Reay. WIDNES V. MOSSLRy.—On Saturday the " Chemicals " , I journeyed to Mossley to play the club of that town. Both 1 teams were fairly representative, but Widnes were without , Farrell, and Mosslev without Newby. A grand game ended I in a win for Mossley by one goal (dropped by Lawton) one I try and six minor points, to Widnes one goal (dropped by 1 Plumpton) and four minor points. Soon after the corn- ! mencement of the game Plumpton by a tine kick, landed a I goal for Widnes. This seemed to be the winnime point 1 until within a few minutes of" no side," when amidst an indescribable display of enthusiasm, Lawton cleverly drop- ped the ball over the Widnes bar, thus securing the victory for his side. The Widnes men showed a wonderful im- provement upon their performance of the previous Saturday, land gave great satisfaction to the 4,000 spectators present. ! Teams :—Mossley : W Winterbottom (captain), back ; Joe ! Winterbottom and S Lawton, three-quarter backs ; A Ash- worth and G Billings, half-backs ; J Wood, J Mayhall, M , Rowan, T B Mitchell, James Winter'oottom, J Walker. H i Coxe, J Firth, T Rvlance, and J E Aleakin, forwards. : Widnes: S Bingham, back ; D Harding, Morris, and Plumpton, three-quarter backs ; Howard and Barker, , half-backs ; Kiddie (captain), Smith, Hardman, Fogg, 1 Meagher, Pervin, J Bingham, Hughes, and IN ilkinson, for- wards. I RuNCORN (2ND TEAM) V. LIVERPOOL ATHLETIC.— ' Played at Runcorn on Saturday, before a goodly number of I spectators. The game was of an interesting nature, being I very fast throughout, but the home team completely over- played their opponents, and won by two goals, three tries, i and six minors to the Athletic nil.
