div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The Runcorn team, although defeated at Salford on Saturday, have left behind thorn amongst the Mancunians an enhanced reputation as sterling scientific football players. The score is far from representing the state of the game. Salford made all their score, with the exception of a touch- down, in the first quarter of an hour, and afterwards Hughes' lads not only kept their redoubtable opponents at bay, brit made numerous and dangerous incursions into the home territory, in fact they were very unfortunate not to score, and they were frequently rewarded with sympathetic and encouraging cheers from the spectators.

The ttuncorn front division always play up with dash and vigour, but on Saturday they surpassed themselves, and veritably played a "demon game." The back division were, however, too light to stay the strong rushes of the opposing team, which threw a still heavier task upon the forwards, but they proved equal to the task, and all without exception are deservinc, of the warmest praise. Woods, the fullback, " mulled " the ball on several occasions, and Lunt who had numerous chances given him, picked up very badly. Speakman played a capital game, and made a beau- tiful attempt at a arop goal, bet he WAS charged down. The captain and Andrews played well at half back. To-day the team journey to Rochdale to meet the Hornets, and a stub- born and fast game is anticipated. There will be several alterations in the hack division.
Mr. J. Peers writes to complain that the Warrington True Blues arranged two dates with St. Paul's Football Club, but have now cancelled them.
For.some.time an agitation has been current In EN gby
rootball circles for an —alteration in the roles under which

the game is played. At present a goal, dropped or ettisr- wise, is a winning point above any number of tries, a rule which has often been felt to be most arbitrary and unjust. A club may have the hest of the game all through, and may plant the ball behind the posts any number of times ; and yet if their opponents excel in place kicking, or can drop a lucky goal, that point will give them a win over any number of tries got by such superior play. At a meeting of the Lancashire Coanty Rugby Union, on Friday night, this matter was brought forward for consideration, and certain preposels were adopted which will be discussed at the approaching meeting of the Rugby Union. The dele- gates from Lancashire county were instructed to support the following proposition :—" A. match shall be decided by a majority of points. A goal obtained from a try shall equal three points, a goal obtained in any other manner two points, and a try one point. If the number of points be equal, or no goal be kicked or try obtained, the match shall be drawn. When a goal is kicked from a try one goal only is scored." A long discussion took place with respect to the proposed new rules against professionalism. The first rule, "That professionalism is illegal," was agreed to; but when the meeting began to discuss a clause which precluded a club or any member of it frJrn making a payment to a player for loss of time some difference of opinion was manifested. Mr. Taylor (Oldham) proposed that a club should be allowed to compensate a player fir less of time incurred by reason of any accident sustained in a match. Mr. Wigg (Rochdale) expressed his willingness to go far- ther, and, in the interests of working-men players, thought that slubs should be allowed to compensate their players for actual loss ef wages.—An amendment to this effect was, however, at once rejected by a large majority, and the pre- position of Mr. Taylor adopted.

div.head: TOUR WITH THE WARRINGTON
div.p: A TOUR WITH THE WARRINGTON
TEAII IN THE FURNESS DISTRICT.

For a considerable time the chief topic of conversa- tion amongst the members of the Warrington Foot- ball Club has been about their tour in the famous Furness District. Saturday last was the date fixed for their meeting Barrow, one of the most famous teams in the north of the county. About 9-3 o the team began to gather at Bank Quay Station, together with a strong gathering of their friends sad suppor- ters to witness their departure by the train leaving at 9-57. Through the kindness of Mr. Ashurst, a saloon had been procured for the comfort of the team, and punctual to the time we steamed out of the station as Heyes trmed it, on our jonruey to the "Icy North." Besides the team, the following gentlemen also under- took the:journey to see how the boys acquitted them- selves, namely, Mr. J. Kneen (of Bridge-street), Mr. J. Bramhall (late umpire), Mr. A. Simpson (an ardent supporter), and Mr. W. Ford (captain of the specta- tors). The journey to Carnforth was quickly got over, some amusing themselves by playing cards, others by chat about the match, and the rest admir- ing the various objtcts of interest on the way. On our arrival at Carnforth we were met by Rigby and Graham, two of our players, the former an old War- ringtonian who has taken up his residence here, but who is always willing to assist his old club. An adjournment, at the invitation of Mr. Kneen, was made to the refreshment room, the whole party being regaled at his expense with refreshments. On leav- ing Carnforth, all eyes were turned on the beautiful scenery of Silverdale, Arnside, Grange, &c., Mr. Kneen and one or two others, who were well ac- quainted with the district, pointing out all the objects of interest in the district. After passing "Reyes ploughed fields," and the viaduct over the Leven (both places of note to all of us), we soon arrived at Barrow, being met by Forshaw, a noted three-quarter of the Barrow Club, and escorted to the Imperial Hotel, the headquarters of the home club, and soon Messrs. Asheon and Barnes were making arrange- ments for our comfort during our stay here. After partaking of a slight luncheon, we were driven to the scene of action, and soon play was raging fast. I will not say anything of the game, as it will appear in another part of the paper, suffice that it was a splendid exhibition of football, and very pleasantly contested. After the match we were entertained by the home team to a good substantial repast, admirably served up under the superintendence of the proprietor (Mr. Hincks), and a very enjoyable couple of hours were spent. Some good speeches were made by Messrs. Harley. Houghton, and Ashton, the home team congratulating the visitors on the excellent form displayed, and more especially for their winning the cup of the W.L.B.T.R.U. Mr. Houghton also spoke in high terms of the kindness of the Warrington Foot- ball Club on the occasion of their visit last season. During the latter part of the evening the various places of int,,rest in the town were visited, the guides being Messrs. Slater and Forshaw, and we must not forget to mention Mr. R. Rogerson's Bowling Saloon, where the giant knocked down all the pins at one sweep. At eleven o'clock bedtime arrived, and then ensued a rather lively scene, the captain of the Spec- tators fairly enjoying his little self on Sunday. In the morning the docks, and Walney Island were visi- ted, and in the afternoon Mr. Kneen, iMr. Councillor At - kineon, a well-known Barrow gentleman and an en- thusiastic supporter of the game of football, took 114 to Furness Abbey to inspect the grand old pile of ruins, an outing we all enjoyed. The evening was quietly and enjoyably spent. On Monday morning Mr. Kneen proved that we had obtained the right gentleman to accompany us, as he had a free pass to see through the Barrow Hematite Steel works, the largest in the kingdom, and also a letter from Mr. Harley ta visit the shipyard, and another letter to visit the large flay and jute works,lthus showing us that he is a gentleman who was respected in the Furness District. As time would not permit of our seeing all the three places of interest, we chose the former, and were well repaid by seeing right through the works, as Mr. Nichols, the manager, did all in his power to make the visit as interesting as possible. The department where rails were made was the chief cen- tre of attraction. Although a vast amount of interest was taken in the working of a vast steam hammer and other things, the journey to Askam was made at 2-40, the team arriving a little before three, the kick- off being fixed for five. The game was pleasantly contested, the home team securing the verdict. This may be accounted for by the home club having a lot of new members, and some of the best in the Furness district, viz., Todd and Bellany, of Dalton, and Ken- dall, of Gleaston. After the match we were entertained to dinner by the home team, and were earnestly pressed to stay until the last, but as the saloon could not be attached to the mail, it was decided to make the journey by the train before. We therefore left Askam and its jolly crew behind, and soon arrived at Carnforth, staying with Rigby for upwards of half an hour. Another halt was made at Preston, but even- tually we arrived home a little before twelve, where we were met by a crowd of friends. Every one, thanks to Messrs. Ashton and Barnes for looking after our comfort, and to Mr. Kneen, for acting as our guide, being delighted with the out. WARRINGTON V. BaRROW-IN-FUItNESS.

The cupholders journeyed to Barrow to meet this power- ful organisation, on Saturday last. Although they bad such a long journey they still managed to retain their re- putation as one of the leading clubs in the county by beat- ing their opponents by 1 goal, 2 minors to 1 try, 1 minor. Some 1200 spectators had assembled to witness the match. Frank Turner kicked off with the sun in the eyes of the visitors, the ball being badly returned. The first scoring took place in the home quarter, the Warrington forwards

playing strongly together. Good runs and passing were next seen on the parts of the Barrow backs, Walton, Barley, and Forshaw figuring prominently. Gregory next obtained possession, but was well stopped by Massey. H. Ashton now came through with a rush, and being aided by Ferny and Frank Turner, play for some time raged furiously in the home quarters; but eventually Little and Baines carried through and relieved the pressure, play being now confined to half way. Good form was next displayed by Forshaw and Walton on one side and Jolley and Massey on the other, very little advantage being, however, gained; but soon after a brace of good runs were seen by Gregory and For- , sine:, and a free kick to Barrow further improved matters. The Warrington forwards, not to be denied, rushed the ball to half way and Hough carried it to the home line, Graham, from a pass by Speakman, having a shot at goal, a minor resulting. Rigby charged the kick out, play again taking place in the home 25. The ball coming up the field fell into the hands of Gilbert, who kicked to touch. Walton now came to the fore by a piece of smart following up, thus causing play to be confined to half way, and Gregory ob- taining possession further improved matters, being only stopped by Hewitt when a try seemed a certainty. Fair. Turner, Povey, and Jolley, however, carried the oval back again, and shortly afterwards half time was called, with the ball in the home 25. Score, 1 minor to.Warrington. Har- ley, on the resumption of play, kicked off for Barrow, Jolley returning, Kinnisk helping the oval to touch. Hough first showed up by a strong wriggling run, being brought down in the home quarters, Woodburn saving nicely. Jolley next got in a good run, but Harley replied with one equally as good. Boucher now intended to give a pass to Forshaw, but Harley stopping the progress of the oval, it fell' into the hands of Graham, who scored the first try, from which Speakman kicked a goal, to the great delight of the Warrington supporters. Walton kicked off and followed well up, but not soon enough to prevent Hough from returning. Play. however, soon settled down in the visitors' 25, a dead ball shortly afterwards being registered to the credit of the home team. Jolley returned the kick from the kick out, and the battle raged furiously in the home 25 until Forshaw came to the rescue by a dashing run. Hewitt missed the ball, just lifter Jolley had fumbled it, Little getting over and scoring for Barrow, Gregory failing at gaol. Frum•now until the end play was very exciting, War- rington in the end running out winners by the score as above stated. The visitors' forwards played well, especially Hough, W. Turner, and Povey, as also did the backs, with the exception of Hewitt, Massey being the pick. The Bar- row forwards were over-matched, although Baines, Leek, and Kinnish played a good game. The two halves were all there, as well as the three quarters, Woodburne at back playing a grand game. Warrington were without Barnes, Dillon, and Buxton ; Barrow, on the other hand, being capitally represented. WARRINGTON V. ASKAM-IN-FURNESS

Fresh from their victory over the Barrow Contingent, the sup holders jonrneyed to Askam on Monday to try conclu- sions with the club 9f that name. They felt pretty confi- dent of success, but in this they were mistaken, as the home team in the end proved one too many for them. This may be accounted for by the visitors perhaps overtiring them- selves by looking about the neighbourhood of Barrow, and more so by meeting such a poserful team got together to do battle against the cup holders. A lot ef new players have joined the Askam Club, two especially playing who are noted in the district of Furness, viz., Todd of Dalton, and Kendall of aleeston. On account of a stiff breeze prevail- ing it was arranged to divide the game into four quarters of 15 minutes each way. The first three were unproductive of any scoring if we except minors. In the last quarter the wind increased considerably, and the Askamites taking ad- vantage of this, pnt in some long points, and from one of these Kendall followed up, and Jolley failing to gather the ball, it went on to Hewitt, who also failed to pick up, and thus the first player got over and scored the only try of the match, McDonald failing at goal. The Askamites showed up very prominently in the pack, especially Woodend Todd, and their captain MacDonald, being much heavier players than their opponents. Kendall played a superb game at three-quarters, as also did Sharp and Crawley. The War- rington forwards seemed to have the best of it on the loose, all playing well under the circumetances, none figuring more prominently than W. Dillon, Fair. Turner, Ashton, and Pevey. Davies had his first attempt at half back, and canoe off with flying colours, at times passing with good judgment and accuracy, besides repeatedly stopping dangerous rushee. Gilbert, his partner, also played well, and Graham at three- quarters played finely until hurt. Massey played a good game, but Jolley was faulty in picking up. Hewitt did not play up to expectation, his kicking and picking up being rather weak. Buxton, Barnes, and Speakman were absent from the Warrington ranks. Score :—Warrington,l minor; 4-skarn, 1 try, 3 minors.
LIBERALISM IN NORTHWICH

div.head: SION.
div.p: SION.

PRESENTATION TO MR- . J. T. BRUNNER. A. most interesting gathering took place on Satur- day at Winnington Old Hall, near Northwich, the residence of Mr. J. T. Brunner, J.P. Liberals as- sembled from all parts of the division, in numerous instances being accompania by their wives for the purpose of showing honour and respect to Mr. Brun- ner, the Liberal candidate, at the last election, who was to be the recipient of a token of confidence and esteem, At the disposal of the Runcorn Liberals,Mr. Brunner had placed a steamer and a boat, and in these upwards of 200 persons had a charming sail up the valley of the Weaver, to Wilmington. The Wins- ford Liberals were similarly favoured. On arrival at the Hall, the visitors were served with refresh- ments in a marquee erected in the Park, and imme- diately afterwards the proceedings commenced in the open air. Although formally the meeting should have been only of members of the Council, tickets had been freely distributed to friends of the °alike' and upwards of tpooo persons were present. Mr. E. H. Moss, the president of the Association, occupied the chair, and he Was supported on the platform by Mr. and Mrs. Brunner and family, Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., and many of the leading Liberals in the division. Mr. W. Handley, of Runcorn, the Liberal agent, read letters of apology for non-attendance from Mr. James Torn- kinson, of Wellington Hall, Mr. T. Gair Ashton, of Hyde, Mr. P. Speakman, of Runcorn, and others. The presenta- tion to Mr. Brunner consisted of a beautifully illuminated address in album form, supplied by Messrs. Smith and Dell, of Liverpool. In one corner of the page on the left is a small sketch of Winnington Old Hall, the remaining space being filled up with the letters of Mr. Brunner's full name, richly illuminated and interwoven with floral designs. On the opposite side is the address artistically engrossed, sur- mounted with a capital portrait of Mr. Brunner and his arms and crest. A handsome border encOmpasses the whole. The exterior of the address is brown morocco. The address I was read by Mr. W. Handley as follows : "To John Tomlinson Brunner, Esq., J.P., Winnington Old Hall, Nerthwich. _ _ _

"The Council of the Liberal Association for the North- wich ,Division of Cheshire desires to express its unabated confidence in you as the Parliamentary candidate selected to do battle on behalf of true Liberalism in this constituency, and its appreciation of the valuable services you have ren- dered as the first member of Parliament for this division. "The Council recognises in you a politician who has never swerved from the Liberal principles you profess. No personal ambition or selfish purpose has influenced you in your public action. When Liberalism was struggling to as- sert itself in this county, long prior to the passing of the last franchise acts, it had ne stronger or more earnest sup- porter than yourself. You have never been affected by the social and political influences which have so often prevented men of wealth and position in this county declaring their Liberal allegiance. You have throughout been firm in the assertion of the rights of the people as against the privileged classes, and your name more than any other in this consti- tuency is associated with the cause of true and sound politi- cal progress. _ _

"'Phi; Council of this association has never had any to regret its choice of you as its candidate, your ex- position of your political faith has been so clear, so ample, and so straightforward as to leave no doubt on thA minds of those whom you have addressed as to your political con- victions; your Parliamentary action has fully justified the confidence reposed in you. A difference of opinion on a ques- tion of national policy has brought about a temporary repre- sentaiion of this division which the association cannot regard as satisfactory, and this Council asserts its belief that the candidate of its choice will at no distant data be returned to Westminster by an overwhelming vote of • the re-united Liberals of this admittedly Liberal constituencf.—Signed on behalf of the Council, " EDWARD: HOWARD MOSS, President. "October 2nd, 1886."

The Chairman then handed the address to Mr. Brunner, and said the duty of doing so was a personal pleasure to himself. They all knew low ably ani well he had fulfilled his duty as their member. (Hear, hear.) The reasons why he did not occupy that position that day were well known to them. (Hear, hear) But however high an opinion they had of him as their member, his conduct since that cruel de- feat had caused him to rise far higher in their esteem from the quiet manly way in which he took that defeat. (Cheers.) He (the sneaker) was sure that the first feeling in Mr. Brunner's mind was not personal, but first and foremost the loss to the Liberal cause—(cheers)—and how grievous was the reply to the momentous question of our grand old chieftain. (Cheers.) He then asked Mr. Brunner to accept that address with their best and heartiest good wishes. (Loud cheers.) Mr. Robert Shaw, who had a cordial reception, spoke as chaibman of the council. He said he was gratified toat Mr. Brunner bad not only been the member for that divisios, but that he had very wisely deciaed to stand by them and fight their battles again. (Cheers.) In Mr. Brunner they bad a eandidate who represented the feelings of the great mass of the population of Northwich Division. (Hear, hear.) They felt that he was prepared at all times to assist in carrying forward those measures which should be of the greatest peace and happiness to the largest number of the population—(cheers)—and he could conceive of no legisla- tion lasting long—be could conceive of no Government re- maining in office long, that would rest upon anything lower than that. (Cheets.) And though they had in a measure suffered defeat by a combination of influencies— by the Conservative party and the weak Liberals—yet they had no doubt that the principles they then went in for and for which they contended would ultimately come to the front and succeed. (Cheers.) They had nothing to regret in being for a time a defeated party when they considered that they fought for justice to

the oppressed population of Ireland, that they sought to establish something that should he a lasting beneLt and a strength not only to that country, but to this country also. (Cheers.) They were told it was separation that they went in for, and he believed that statement, though it is:we un- true, had a great deal to do with the result of the election. The Liberal policy was not separation ; it was to bind to- gether the people of the United Kingdom in bonds far stronger than existed to-day. (Hear, hear.) The Irish people would never be with them until they did there, jus- tice, and made it 'possible for them to live in their own country. Notwithstanding all that had taken place, he be- lieved that victory was near them. The cause of justice would succeed, and that soon, and the people of Ireland would be united with us as one nation, feeling that we had enabled them to live in the land of their birth in comfort and peace. Feeling that Mr. Brunner was the only gentle- man he knew who could wrest the Northwich seat again, and be their member, he hoped, as long as he lived—(cheers) —he had very great pleasure in supporting the presenta- tion. He was satisfied that it would not be long before they met again under happier circumstances than those Voice: "The sooner the better.".-.. cheers) when they could feel that their principles had triumphed, and that their laborers had not been in vain. (Cheers.) The Rev. IT. Gelley said he could most heartily subscribe to every statement contained in the address. He had known Mr. Brunner for three years, and the more he knew of him the better he liked him. (Cheers.) He had known him as a neighbour, and he was a neighbourly kind of individual. (Hear, hear.) He had known him as a capitalist, and be dared say his reputation had been fairly‘on an average with that of his brethren of the district. (Hear, hear.) He had known him as a philanthropist, and he thought his charac- ter in that respect would bear favourable comparison with that of any of his neighbours. (Cheers.) 1 he address ex- pressed enabeted confidence in Mr. Brunner. He knew of nothing that would justify them as men of judgment and sincerity and integrity in withdrawing their confidence in Mr. Brunner. (Cheers.) All the great principles that be (Mr. Brunner) had pledged himself in the Drill Hall to support he supported, and lie also supported things that he. was not pledged to measures that were calcu- lated to promote Liberal progress and Liberal principles. Mr. Brunner had never swerved from the political princi- ples he professed. He was a man with a backbone— (laugh ter) —a political backbone in him—(cheers)--and however deeply he deplored the issue of the last election, he must frankly state that he would rather have him sitting there as plain Mr. Brunner without the M.P., but with his principles and character untarnished—(loud cheers)—than he would have him with the M.P. obtained by violating his principles and 'telling bis party. (Great cheering.) One of the principles that Mr. Brunner had never swerved from was that of giving to Ireland the largest possible measure of Home Rule. (Cheers.) He was glad that Mr. Brunner was the choice of the Council of the liberal Association, because he regarded that Council as the fah and legitimate mouth- piece of the Liberal vote and voice of that constituency. Therefore, if Mr. Brunner had the confidence of the Coun- cil, he was the representative of the great bulk of the Liberal thought and opinion in the division. (Cheers.) The Coun- cil was composed of the cream of the Liberal party, men who had never swerved from their political principles,with a candidate who had never swerved from his political opini- ons, and if there was a God in heaven their cause was sure to triumph. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner then rose to address the meeting, and was received with enthusiastic cheers and the singing of "For he's a jolly good fellow." He said : Ladies and gentle- tien,—You have been merciful to me in giving me a mo- ment or two in which to swallow the heart which was com- ing into my mouth. (Laughter.) Believe me it is with a very full, a very warm, and a very grateful heart that I have heard the kind words that have been said of me to- day. It is sow, I think, nearly two years since I deter- mined to devote myself unreservedly to your service. Dur- ing those two years, to quote a celebrated statesman, "a good mealy things have happened." It is very nea.ly two years now since I took a very active part in determining, as far as my work could manage it, that the redistribution of Cheshire should be effected in accordance with the spirit of what I believed to be tbe words of the Legislature. We have a number of our friends here to-day from Ruscorn,. and very good friends to the Liberal Cause they are- -(cheers)---and do you know, my friends, that if the pre- sent member for Northwich had had his way, no friends from Runcorn would have been amongst you. It was his wish that Runcorn should not be put in the same division with us, but that it should have been cast out, into what weal that time, in our ignorance, considered to be the bowling desert of Eddiebury. We know better than that to- day. We know that Eddisbury is thoroughly Liberal; but, gentlemen, we value our Runcorn friends, and we owe no thanks to the man who wanted to keep them away from us. (Cheers.) Later on, but only a very short time after that, there came the formation of the Liberal Association, in which, and for many a day before, I had taken a very warm and hearty intetest. Then came that memorable day referred to by my friend Mr. Gelley, when it was discovered that there were two Richmonds in the field. (Laughter and cheers.) I am happy and proud to believe that one of the men whom you Ilea before you that day bas not fallen in your estimation. (Cheers.) Well, then, there came the electoral campaign, and as this address says, I declared be- fore you my Liberal principles and my hopes and my wishes on your behalf and on behalf of my fellow countrymen and women. It is perfectly true that there never was for a moment any wish in my heart to shirk or conceal anything with regard to the faith that was in me. We talked of many things, and many a question was addressed to me, and those subjects which we discussed toather, and on which I believe we were absolutely one in mind, are coming up again for our consideration. Gentlemen, you did me the honour to. elect elect me as your representative in Parlia- ment, and with all my might and with all my soul I endeavoured to do my duty by you. (Cheers.) I did what I believe very few members of Parliament ever think of doing—l tried to bring you into direct touch with the Houses of Parliament. I have tried to interest a very large number in the work that was going on there, and very i suc- cessful have I been in obtaining help from many an intel- ligent man and sympathy from many a warm heart n the work I was doing on your behalf in Loadon. (Cheers.) Gentlemen, I attended early and late. and I don't think I ever went to sleep over your business. (Laughter.) I have spoken a great many times in the House, but almost always after 12 o'clock, when the newspapers take very little notice of speeches from new members. I spoke, gentlemen, only on subjects about which I knew something. (Hear, hear.) I spoke on Free Trade, and I spoke on a bill inten- ded to amend the Public Health Act, 1875, in regard to what is called private improvements. The object of this latter bill was that wherever a private improvement was made by a local authority the cost of it should be charged upon the surrounding owners, not as had been dose up to to-day, that each property owner should pay in proportion to the length of frontage that he had upon the new street, but in proportion, as near as possible, to the benefit he re- ceived. A man has a long garden wall abutting on a new street. The new street he does not want ; it will be no con- venience to him ; but he has a very large proportion of the cost to pay. Another man has a large timber yard and only a doorway into the street. His timber yard is trebled in value, and yet he only pays in accordance with the width of his doorway. A frienu of mine told me a few days ago of a hardship he and his neighbours suffer through this law. A speculative builder bought a tract of ground near Liver- pool, along one side of which were the garden walls of some very pretty houses. This speculative builder had made roads all round the four sides of his ground, and upon it he has built a number of cottages. He is enabled to compel the owners of the houses whose garden walls come alongside his ground to pay half the cost of the road which is made for his benefit, although those owners didn't want it, and he has compelled the railway company to pay half the cost of making a road along one strip, although it does not do the railway company one pennyworth of good. That is an in- justice which we tried to remove, but, unfortunately, the bill had to go to "another place,"l mean the House of Lords, where it had to be dropped, because the Lords put into it a clause which absolutely destroyed its value, and my friend and his neighbours are suffering the injustice to-day. That was a matter I understood, and I talked about it. Well, as this address states, I gave my influence as your member and my hearty sympathy as a man he to t cause of the suffering people of Ireland. That subject has been so well dealt with to-day that I shall say very little more about it. We had an election, the seat question in which was this question of Home Rule for Ireland. The North- wich constituency has given its decision, but whether the decision that was given by this constituency. and by a majority of the constituencies of this country is to be to the people of Ireland what has been called an irrevocable "No" or not remains in the womb of the future. I have my hopes that not many days will pass ere the great map who has led us for many happy years will at last have his great heart filled with happiness at the result of that when von and I will have done justice. (Cheers.) So far as to the work that I have done for you, and in which I have always been supported by very great kindness from you. The address that has been presented to me to-day is a very full and a very ample reward for all the work that I have done for you. (Cries of "No, no.") Gentlemen, I tell you that the man who devotes himself to the public service must look for no other reward than the good will of his fellows. (Cheers.) This address claims meas your servant as hitherto. (Cheers.) This address is, if I read it aright, not only a claim uponme, but it is a repudiation of that hollow mockery that we have heard called Liberal Unionist. I was very much struck with the absolute hollowness of the mockery when I heard that one gentleman with a great names who came to oppose me as a Liberal Unionist, had taken service under a Tory Secretary of War. I don't know that I need name him, because I should be very sorry to cast blame upon any man of his name. This address tells me that you do not approve of the conduct of the man who has suc- ceeded me. (Cheers, and a voice: "It is not likely.") Mr. Verdin is known to you, and very well known to you. (Laughter.) He is known to you as, perhaps, the most wide- awake man in the Northwich Division when he is looking after number one-(laughter and cheers)--but curious to relate, when he goes to London to do our work, he is known as the 37 soundest sleeper in the House of Commons. (Loud laugh- ter and cheers.) Do you know I like a good sleeper? I am a good sleeper myself. (Laughter.) I will back my- self to sleep any man of my own age, size, and weight— (laughter)—but I have always made it a rule to sleep in my own .time and not in my master's. (Loud laughter and cheers.) For what is it that You claim me as your servant? I take it that you want me to do true Liberal and Radical work. (Cheers, and a Voice : "That's just it.") Despite the lapse of a good many whom we looked upon as leaders until lately, despite the absence of the ringing voice of Mr. Chamberlain, you and I, I trust, mean to insist upon it that

the Government of this country shall give due attentilan English affairs, and lam not ashamed to talk of Imperial affairs. I believe the work of a true Liberal ía principar4,l to abolish ail unjust privileges—privileges in Church, vilegee in State-to bring about abate ate era uel;te between man and man before the law; that the magistrates shall not he chosen from one class exclusively. Delighted was I, a feer days ago, to read that Len! Rosehery, the coming ma- (cheers)—told his his neighbours in Scotland that he felt that as Lord-Lieutenant he had not fulfilled his duty in net making working-men inagistratee. (Cheers.) I don't knoll whether you temember how I called your attention to the fact that Mr. Glaeistone's last Government was the first that had ever made a working-man a magistrate. That can be done in boroughs, but it can't be done in English counties. Gentlemen, if we are to have unpaid magistrates I don't approve of them very highly (laughter) but I say fair play all round, and let ns have working-men there too. (Cheer) I hope that you and I together, before we are very much older, will have something to say of the Game Laws. That is another unjust privilege el the ri di. (Cheers, and a Voice, "It is a bad 'on, toe-- Another Voice: "It is a rum 'an, for I know something about it."—Loud laughter.) I never was; taken up for poaching myeelf—(laughter)— but it will go very hard with me if ever I have to convict a man for it. (Hear, hear, and a Vole-3 : "That's proper."—Laughter.) I want equality before the law in another matter. I have spoken time and time again about the homestead law. Get this fact into your mind, that no creditor can touch my furniture, for it is net mine, but belongs to my wife and to my children. There are very few rich men in this country whose. house- hold furniture is not protected against their creditors-There are very few rich men whose grounds can be taken, because they are pmtected by the law. Gentlemen, what the rich have I want the poor to have, and I want this to be brought About, that by no process of law shall a man's household be broken up when he has honestly get it together. This is &- law that obtains throughout America, the freeest country im the world, and Germany, the most aristocratic and most autocratic coun ry in the world, and if it can be done irr these countries I say that English working-men should be protected as they are in those two quarters of the globe, I want this brought about for many a reason. I want it for the sake of the men, because it will make them thrifty, home-living, and self-respecting. I want it for the dear women and for the children that have been born unto Your that they shall never, as long as their fathers and husbands are honest, be turned into the street and be kept by you out or the parish rates. (Cheers.) Gentlemen, you and I sorne day will deal with tithes. (Hear, hear.) I remember or' tering a very emphatic declaration on the subjeet of tithes, creating a good deal of unfavourable comment. The well-known County Court judge, Mr. Homershaw Cox. made this suggestion with regard to tithes a few days ago "Take away from the parson the right to distrain." I want no man to be allowed to distrain upon another man's goods for a debt. I want all to be put on the same footing and go to the same Court to recover a debt that you and [have to 'go to. I want equality between man and man before the Jaw in this respect—that one man shall have Out one vote. The last election was carried by 74,000 votes, and there are a great many more equires in England, Wales, and Scotland than 74.000, and every one of them has two or three votes. The Tory majority in the House of Commons is the result of the duplicate votes of these squires. This is an inequalitV. before the law that you and I someday will aid in putting an end to. (Cheers.) So much for the destructive part of the work that you and I have before us. We want to do more than destroy what is bad. We want to build up what is good. (Cheers.) Above all things do we want this—we want to co-operate together in order, through free education as good as we can get it, to obtain from the individual talents of each the highest result possible for us all. Whatever talents anyone of us have ought t) be, by the aid of all, so cultivated to the highest pitch as to obtain for society the best possible results. The poor man's child must have as good a chance as the rich man's child. (Hear, hear.) We want an honest Liberal policy ill Imperial affairs, and what does that mean ? It means that the same fair play that you and I practice in a transaction between each other shall be the rule with nations having to deal one with the other. If a man attempts to introduce a little Christianity into the management of public affairs people call him a sentimental fool, and no set of men, I very much regret to say, have opposed the introduction of Chris- tian action into public affairs more sternly or steadfastly than those who profess to be the most religious amongst us. Gentlemen, I want more Christian feeling introduced into dealings between nations. Those are the leading points of the work that it seems' to me you wish me to do for you. Now I have only to thank you for the much too kind words, the much too flattering words that have ben used towards me to-day, and I assure you that with all my feeble strength I mean to work as unselfishly as it is possible for me to do, and if you will hold up my feeble bands. and God helps, the result would be good. (Lelia cheers.) Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P. for Merionethshire, who wes warmly greeted, said he had had the good fortune to be sent to a place where ha could notice,with some interest, bow his own party and bow the party of the enemy worked. And this was the first fruit of his experience—that in the House of Commons Liberals were not nearly so Liberal as they were when they were in the constituencies—(laughter)— and what was still more melancholy was this, that Tories were far more Tory in the House of Commons than they were before the constituencies. (Laughter.) They sate. therefore, that the prospect was very dark, but the present House of Commons had got a feature which made the pros- pect still darker—it had within it a party of Liberal-Union- ists who at one moment called themselves Liberal and at the next moment acted as Tories. Now, it seemed to him the situation there was to get to know exactly what a Liberal- Unionist was. (A Voice :"A quack.") (Laughter and cheers.) Now, after such a pithy answer as that, he thought it would be quite unnecessary for him to enter at any leeg b into the doings and professions of a Liberal-Unionist. (Laughter.) This, however, he might say in all seriousness, that when a Liberal-Unionist was sent to the House of Com- mons, and there failed to give one single L‘beral vote, then they had something worse than political quackery. (Cheers.) It was political dishonesty for a man to call himself a Liberal, and then by word and by deed, by omis- sion and coulmission, act as a Tory. (Cheers) It was in order to get rid of a state of things in which Liberal-Union- ists voted for Tory measures that they looked forward to the next general election. (Cheers.) On the motion of Mr. H. BRATT, seconded by Mr. DAVID- SON, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Moss for presiding, and the proceedings concluded with the singing of the National Anthem.

SUICIDE OF MOTHER AND DAUGHTER.—OR ThursdaY morning Hetty Robinson, aged 66 years, and Edith Ann Hirst, a.r,ed 21 years, mother and daucrlater. were found drowned in the canal at Windhill, near Bradford. The younger woman, who was married only three weeks age, left a note for her husband stating that as she was unable to make him happy she and her mother had resolved on suicide.

FIGHT BETWEEN ENGLISH AND FRENCH FISHERMEN. —For some time past there has been a fierce feud be tween the English and French fishermen using Ramsgate harbour. An outbreak of violence on Monday was followed on Thursday by an affray between an Englishman and.a. Frenchman, which culminated in a serious disturbance le the town. The Frenchmen were at length taken under the protection of the officers of customs and the coastguards and got safely on board their boats.

A sunstroke.—A photograph. Those who toil and Spin.—Bicycleriders. The best thing yet discovered for sea-sickness.—Port. Great point of resemblance between farmers and their poultry.—Both delight in full crops. What is the difference between a traveller in the tropics and a chiropodist ?—One feels the heat and the other heals the feet. At an examination a boy was asked, 'What are the warmth-producing foeds?" His reply was, "Cayenne pepper and Jamaica ginger." 'What doeS S.P.Q.R.' on that Roman banner stand for ?' asked a yonthful " super " of one of greater expe- rience. "Why, 'Salaries paid quite regularly," replied the latter promptly. CAUSE AND EFFECT.—A certain University was once said to be a learned place from the fact that- most per- sons took some learning there, while but few brought any away with them. So it accumulated. Aw ExrLonnp Ennon.—lt is a mistake to suppose that women have stronger attachments than men. A man is often attached to an old hat; but who ever heard of a woman being attached to an old bonnet ? - HOW AN APPRENTICE EXPLAINED IT.—A shopkeeper's apprentice;being asked what his master was, like, said, "He's all right; but, he's got a funny way with his weights and • measures. He always putting down drams and laying aside scruples." Art-auctioneer: We have here, ladies and gentlemen, a most superb marine view.—Assistant, in a loud whis- per: Hold on! It's a, picture of a sheep.—Auctioneer: As I was saying, ladies and gentlemen, we have here a picture of a most superb merino. . What am I offered on a bid? A little seven-year-old was taken by his mother to see an old uncle who was very deaf and who had an ear- trumpet, Tommy said finally, "Mamma, why does uncle try to get music out of that horn with his ear, when he has tried hundreds of time and knows he can't do it?" Young Smallwage : I desire to purchase a ring for my janeee.—Obliging jeweller: Yes? How long have you been engaged ?—Young'Smallwage : Nearly three years. —Obliging jeweller, to assistant: Ah, yes! James, show this gentleman some of those imitation garnets. A MAN WHGCAERIED HIS POINT.—It is stated that an Ohio widow owned a large gravel bank which a certain railroad company were very anxious to secure. Several propositions were made and rejected, and the president finally sent his private secretary down with instructions to offer up to 14,000 dollars. The young man returned after a couple of eays, and, when asked how the business had turned out, replied, "I will accept your offer." "You ?" "Exactly. I married the widow and own the bank." . CUSTOM Alm CusTom.—After the first instalment of a novel of his had,appeared in the Revue des Deux Mondes Edmond About went to ask for his money, only to be informed that it was not the custom of the Revue ever 'to pay for the first article of any author. "Very well," said About quietly, "if it is not your custom, no matter ;" and he went on his way. But, when they sent to him for the manuscript of the second instalment of the story, he refused to send it, saying that it was not his custom ever to send the second instalment of a story until he had been paid for tire. first. *- - CrALLANTRY.—A professor was delivering an exceed- ingly pleasant series of 'lectures on his last year's travels in Italy before an attentive audience of students of a certain college. Behind the professor sat his pretty niece, who had accompanied him on his tour in Italy. The professor was advancing his view—quite a revolu- tionary one, by-the-way--that the amount of beauty of all sorts that is to be seen in Italy had been greatly ex- aggerated. "It is far from being a land where all is beautiful," said he. "Indeed, I will tell you what may surprise you—l did not see,a single pretty woman during all my travels in Italy." This remark was followed by a chorus of slight coughs that arose from different parts of the room. The professor was about to proceed when the chorus of coughs grew louder and stronger. He began to think that something. was wrong, and then re- called what he had said, glancing around at his niece at the same moment. "During all my sojourn in Italy," he corrected, "I saw not a single beautiful woman who was a native of the country." This remark was followed by applause, and the professor went on with his lecture. How A YOUNG DOCTOR DIIGNOSED.—Young doctor, to patient: "Let me look at your tongue: H'm—troubled with dyspep—" Patient: "Not a bit. I can eat sole- leather." Young doctor: "Let me feel your pulse. 11'm—wakefulness at night." Patient: "Sleep like a top." Young doctor: "Let me see your tongue. H'm— dizziness and pains in—" Patient: ":No." Young doctor: "Let me feel your pulse. H'm—easily tired, with an indisposition to mental exertion of any—" Patient: " No. ' Young doctor: "Let me see your tongue. H'm—headache and stiffness of the—" Patient: "Haven't had a headace in twenty-five years." Young doctor: "Let me feel your pulse. H'm—you are using too much tobacco." Patient.: "Never touch it in any shape," Young doctor: "Let me see your pulse --er—l mean your tongu6. H'm—too much confined to your desk. • You need fresh air and—" Patient: "I'm a letter-carrier." Young doctor: "Let me feel your tongue—that is,. I should say, your pulse. Irm— you have a tired feeling come over—" Patient; " Never !" Young doctor: "Let me see your—never mind; your tongue--feverish at times, with a desire for water ? ' Patient: "No, beer." Younc, doctor: "Do you drink beer ?" Patient: "Oh, yes !" 'Young doctor: "To excess?" Patient: "No." Young doctor: "Tell me how many glasses a day?" Patient: " Sometimes more and sometimes fewer." Young doctor: "I thought so. We members of the medical profession are seldom deceived in our diagnosis of a case." Patient: "Am I in any danger, doctor ?" Young doctor: "No immediate danger; but it's lucky you called me in!"

DEATH OF MR. G. W. LA TRAM. Mr. George W. Latham, of Bradwall Hall, Che- shire, who represented Crewe Division in the last Parliament, but retired at the recent election on ac- count of continued ill-health, died at his residence late on Monday night. As was well known, Mr. Latham had long suffered from a painful disease ' which a few months ago compelled his retirement frora active life. Mr. Latham was long a tower of strength amongst Cheshire Liberals, and his loss will be greatly felt amongst them. The de- ceased gentleman was the eldest surviving son of Mr. John Latham, of Bradwall Hall, Sandbach, his mother being Elizabeth Anne, daughter of Sir Henry Dampier, formerly Judge of the Queen's ; Bench. He was born in 1827, and was educated at Brasenose College, Oxford. He was called to the ' bar in 18.52, and went the North Wales and Chester ' Circuit. He was a magistrate for Cheshire, and for the borough of Crewe. In 1856 he married Eliza- beth Sarah, daughter of the Rev. Henry Luttman Johnson, of Binderton House, Sussex.. Mr. Latham's political career has been a stirring one. No fewer than three times did he contest the old division of mid_cheshire. His first contest was in March, 1863, on the retirement of Colonel Cornwall ' Leigh, when he was defeated by Colonel Eger- ton Leigh. At the general election of 1880 he was once ruore to the front, and with Mr. V. , Armitage as his colleague again fought a losing II U S I C I A N S. battle against the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton and 93, Bilstoia-otreet, Wolverhampton Air' piers E. Warburton. Again in 1883, on the sue- March 2, 1862. ' . cession of the Hon. W. Egerton to the peerage, he To Mr, R. U. Lowe.—Dear Sir,—' have the greatest plea. entered the lists, this time against the Hon. an de sure tin recommending your PiliE, which I have used tor the Egerton. When Cheshire was divided up he was g3aarese;rtaanindrlen all cases of cold and indigestion, have found wthoe naturally selected as the Liberal candidate for the remedy. I can also recommend them to Crewe Division • ' musicians who are accustomed to bl ,w wind instruments as ' in-vision of Cheshire, and last year gained II after a hard day's work, much relief is gained by takijag ;I, comparatively easy victory over his opponent, Mr. dose. 0. L. Stephen. Soon after the election Mr. Latham's health broke down, and for some time he was un- able to take his seat. Though he was at last able to do so, be never really recovered his natural ' health, and was not permitted to take an active !part in political strife. At the last general election , he was most wiwillingly compelled to decline the iinvitation again to contest the seat, which he would I assuredly have carried with ease. From that time , to within a few days of his death he has been a con- stant sufferer. Mr. Latham was an authority on , the land question, which he had studied deeply, and i I was one of the founders of the Farmers' Alliance. He was an able speaker, and never spoke better I than when discnssin" points connected with the land. Amongst other public offices held by Mr. Latham, he was vice-president of the Farmers' Al- liance, and manager of the Bradwall Reformatory School. Ile would be described amongst politicians as an advanced Radical, and wfw byno means afraid of that description of his views. His place in the political life of Che-hire will not easily be filled, whilst in all personal and social relations he enjoyed the respect and esteem of all who knew _ _

IRERRENWORTH, THE LATE KING OF
BAVARIA.'S ISLAND CASTLE ON THE HERRENCHIEDISEE.

1 Since his tragic death the mad King Louis of Bavaria's follies have been exciting universal attention, and the following interesting .description of one: of his seven residences taken from recent numbers of the Gartenlaube Will be :,1, ptidpOs just snow :—Between the stations of Endorf and Preen a glimpse ortmagnificent scenery may be obtained from the railway train, which, on the way from Munich to Salzburg, rushes forth from a gloomy wood into i, wide and grand landscape. In the back- ground stretch the Alps; under them lies the lake called • Herrenchlemsee, studded with little islands. On one of those little islands are the ruins of an abbey, and on • another stands the island castle Herrenworth. From the shore of the lake to the castle two landing-stages extend, built a few years ago to transport the costly art treasures for the building and decoration of the celebrated edifice. It is a dazzling picture the sun shining on the lake and on the long white façade of the castle. The old abbey stands high on a hill; and surrounded by splendid trees, and with extensive views from every side, it is more imposing than the castle itself, with its , long front almost hidden by trees. The west side is the first to attract •attention, it being the side from which terraces lead to the wide canal which has been dug from the lake to the castle. From the lake steamer the eye at once falls on the castle, with its glittering balustrade reflected in the water. The roof is flat, and is orna- mented With a long row of statues and trophies. Three richly gilt trellised gates open into a vestibule, com- manding a good view of the lake east and west, but in this part all the rooms, except the King's swimming- bath, are unfinished. The bath-room. is unique. It con- sists of an oval hall containing a marble basin about eight or ten metres in diameter and three metres in depth, and it is entered by marble steps. The walls and the: arched roof are decorated with a large richly coloured fresco —a - marine picture repre- senting Nereides and Tritons sporting on a rocky coast. The window curtains are dark red, and the whole room is filled with a magic red light. Adjoininr,.• is a little dressing-room. Besides a richly-embroidered bed, it contains scarcely any furniture, but the charac- teristic ornaments of this apartment consist in the mirrors, which are so skilfully arranged that whichever way one looks the persons entering are multiplied a hundred-fold, and the little room itself seems to be drawn out into an endless flight of rooms. A narrow winding staircase leads to the royal. bedroom. Here the superb bed, in which the King has only slept four nights, holds the eye. It is a masterpiece of art and industry. The sides are composed of blue silk and white panels with a gold border and other ornaments. . The gigantic canopy and the curtains are of .dark blue velvet em- broidered with gold. The corners of the canopy are decorated with bunches of white ostrich feathers, while under a golden crown glitters Louis's moeogram, with a genius on each side of it, one holding a palm branch and the other a lily. On the bed-head there is a large beaming sun, and above it a coloured piece of art embroidery representing the crucifixion. Gold ears also shine from the roof of the canopy. A gilt bas-relief forms the' foot of the bed. At the right side of the bed stands 'an oratory, before which the King said his prayers immediately on rising. The washstand is no less splendid than the bed. The room also contains a marble bust of Louis XIV., whose costly residence at Versailles the unhappy King sought to excel at- Herren- worth. In another part of the Castle there are rooms just as handsomely furnished and decorated, and all exact copies of those at Versailles. Each apartment seems more magnifiCent than the last until we reach the Salle de Parade, to excel which it would be quite im- possible. Another celebrated room is the mirror-room, which, with the Salle de la Guerre and the Salle de la Pain, occupies the whole of the west front of the Castle. Opposite the" twenty-arched windows of this hall there are as many mirrors of the same size; the doors are also composed of mirrors an inch thick. On this side of the building stands the Fortune fountain, the waters of which have only played three times when the King was present. Another flight of steps leads to the Latona fountain, but here, too, the waters do not play, while the steam-engine, 70-horse power, is probably being ruined by rust. The noble building fills the spectator, with melancholy. Below it the clear lake reflects the golden light of the evening sky, while the unfinished royal palace here and there already shows traces of damage done by frost and rain storms. The metal basins of the fountains are beginning to (Tumble away, delicate moss is taking root between the marble steps, and weeds are growing on the walls which the builder had begun to erect for the new south wing.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, TlitiltSDAY.

A strange thing has happened in political history. On Saturday, Lord Randolph Churchill delivered a speech at Dartford. On Monday, .Mr. Gladstone spoke at Hawarden, and lo! the oration of the:whip- -per snapper of the Conservative party has played the part of the lean kine in Pharaoh's dream. In respect of public interest it has swallowed up Mr. Gladstone's speech, and while everybody is still talking about the Dartford sp ;ch, the Hawarden address is passed by almost without comment. it is not quite correct to say that everyone is talking of the speech, for silence broods over it in the very 1 quarter where it might have been expected com- ment would have been most garrulo as. The Con- servative press, more particularly in London, have been stricken dumb by the amazing oration of the' Chancellor of the Exchequer. Tnere is in the speech matter sufficient for a dozen successive leading aiticles. On Monday the usual leader was forthcoming, it being impossible, of course, to ig- nore a lengthy speech by the leading personage in the Conservative party. But since then a grave- like silence has fallen upon the Metropolitan -Press, which, with a single exception, has hitherto cheered on Lord Randolph, in some cases not be- cause they distrust him less, but because they hate Mr. Gladstone the more. The speech was sufficiently remarkable to ac- count for this unique phenomenon. As doubtless all your readers are familiar with it, it will suffice here to say that Lord Randolph Churchill, appearing; as the spokesman of a Conservative Cabinet, de- liberately announced the intention of himself and his colleaghes to adopt the full and undiluted pro- gramme of the Liberal party. All the things of which, since he came to the front, Lord Randolph Churchill has been the noisy and vindictive oppo- nent he now calmly appropriates. He will, carry the closive in Parliamentary debate; he will fur- ther extend Mr. Gladstone's Irish Land Bills; he will deal with the educatis- question in response to popular demand—that is to say be will make education free. He will adopt Mr. Jesse Collings's scheme for blessing the agricultural labourer with three acres and a cow. He will appropriate Mr. Mundella's Railway Rates Bill; he will deal with the question of local government in Ireland, that is to say he will concede Home Rule, which can be done only .upon the lines of Mr. Gladstone's Bill. Tais is certainly enough to take the breath away, and to strike abie Conservative editors dumb. It is really comical to meet a friend from the Conserva- tive camp and talk to him on the political event of the day. Up to yesterday afternoon Conservatives were like their journals, inclined to take refuge in sullen silence. But last night the "St. James' Gaz- ette" gave the cue, and now they are all saying that they will wait and:see whether Lord Randolph Churchill's views really represent those of the Cabi- net. There need not be any such delay. No one who knows anything of the noble lord, of his ordin- ary method of procedure, and of his relations with his colleagues, can doubt that amongst the most amazed readers of his Dartford speech were the members of her Majesty's Ministry. That is a con- sideration which will probably give Lord Randolph the keener satisfaction in his Berlin expedition. There is about him a certain elfish humour which will be tickled at the picture supplied to the imagin- ation of Lord Salisbury readingthe Dartford speech, of Viscount Cross rubbing his spectacles in the hope of. dispelling illusion `t and of Sir Michael Beach grinding his teeth in impotent fury. With a certain dramatic effect not unworthy of Napoleon, or at least of Mr. Disraeli, Lord Randolph Churchill posted off to Berlin the day after he had delivered his speech. The details of his journey were carried out with fascinating mystery.. He disappeared at a London rail- -way station, and where he reappeared no one at -this moment can say with definiteness. A certain ." Mr. Spencer," who put up at one of the hotels in Berlin last night, is suspected to be the Chancellor ,of the Exchequer. But on this there is no trusi:- worthy evidence. It is very funny to think of Lord Randolph travelling on the Continent under an alias, as if he were a fugitive monarch or a prince of the blood. It smacks of what Lord Randolph him- self would call tomfoolery. But it is excellent fooling, and catches the public eye as it was in- tended to do. The "Standard" this morning ex- presses some apprehension of the practical results of this new escapade. "We should,' says the most enlightened of the Tory organs, "feel same uneasi- ness if we thought that he carried in his pocket the policy and the foisunes of England." But as the "Standard" goes on to show, there is no dassger of Prince Bismarck making any mistake as to the pre- cise importance and bearing of this mysterious and picturesque visit. Ldrd Randolph is a clever young man, but he is not everybody; is in fact nobody at all unless he carries with him the sanction of the House of Commons. Ssill the visit will, from his point of view, be a success, since if it cloes nothing else it is sure to make Lord Salisbury squirm. )t must be a hard thing for the proud head of the Cecils, the veteran warrior in the Conservative rank, to be thus lightly thrust aside into a back seat by this audacious young man. The notion of the Jubilee Colonial Institute does not grow in popularity. It suffers in the first place from the connection of its immediate promoters with the exhibition at South Kensington. There is a strong impression that that colossal undertaking is largely carried on for the personal profit of a small coterie which has come to be known as "the South Kensineton gang," Night and day the vast building is filled by a paying public. Year by year the popu- larity of the show has gone up. This year the number of visitors is .considerably more than it ever was. Yet it is said there is no money surplus, and it is even hinted that the balapce is on the wrong side of the account. This, though smprising, is of course quite possible, only it would be better if the facts were set forth in the familiar and irrefragible form of a balance sheet. This has not yet been done, though I fancy the undertone of growlinv i which goes on whcsever the subject s spoken of may presently reach a pitch which will compel the Commissioners to meet public curiosity on this point. With respect to the Jubilee Institute, the letter to the Lord Mayor in which the Prince of Wales submitted the scheme was too suggestive -of an undertaking to be privately exploited. Of course there is no charge against the Prince of Wales; but H.R.H. is surrounded by a clique whc, it is said, know how to utilize his influence for their own benefit. When on a recent occasion the Prince came forward tcr direct the subscriptions to the Gordon Fund to the creation of a hospital in remcte Egypt the absurd proposition was received in the first instance in civil silence. Then objections began to be put forward, till finally, thouglt not till a fatal blow had been dealt at the fend, the propo- sition was withdrawn. Something of the kind threatens to nip in the bud the proposal of the New Colonial Institute. It is, however, not too late for reasonable objections to be met, and doubtless the .good sense of the Prince, if he can only disembarass himself of the influence that hampers him, will find a way out of the difficulty. A plot of ground which is almost histm lc and has certainly been written about has just charged hands, and will soon be the scene of the builder's labours. The Cock ta.vern has long ago been pulled down, though the sign, which Tennyson immor- talised, has been as carefully kept as the pictuse David Cox painted for the Royal Oak at Betty's. The ground was too valuable. to be the site of a chop- house. The only question was who was to get it, and to what purpOse it was to be put. The ques- tion is answered; for the. Bank of England has bought the site. The neighbourhood of the New Law Courts is, of course, what made this corler of London so specially valuable. The East En-I rises and the West End falls. The London West End

A SUICIDAL DISTRICT.—Thomas Smith, master • blaek- smith, committed suicide at Thurmaston, en Monday. He got up, walked straight to his shop, where he took a baiter, walked over to a storeroom, and a few minutes afterwarls was found hanging dead. He had had a slight difference with some friends. This is the tenth suicide in the district within a short period. BOARD OF TRADE RETURNS.—The Board of Trade returns issued on Thursday that during September the imports decreased £965,283, while the exports increased £307,311, compared with the corresponding month of last year. For the first three-quarters of the year the imports decreased £23,643,681, and the exports decreased Z 1,172,261, corn- pared with the similar period of 1885. FATAL HASTE.—Yesterday, a young married woman named Ellis proceeded to the railway station at Dorking, with the intention of booking to Reigate. She hurried, but missed the train, and sat down to wait for the next. She had a baby in her arnas and two other children with her. Suddenly sbe fell forward, and when carried to the waiting. room it was found that life was extinct. GOoD TEXPLARY—The weekly seseion of the Hope of Earlestewn Lodge of Good Templars was held on Mon- day night, when there was a good attendance, and Brother J. Macdonald, W.C.T., presided. The evening's programme was "Roll call." and the roll of members was called. Arrangements were made for visiting absentee members, Jze., after which a selection of odes were sung. FUNERAL OF Ma. LATHABL—The funeral of Mr. Latham, formerly member of Parliament for the Crewe Division of Cheshire, took place at Sandbach Heath on Friday. The funeral was a public one, and the procession extended for a considerable distance from Bradwall Hall, deceased's real- dencr. In the con:ege was a large deputation from Man- chester, Mr. M'Laren, M.P., Mr. Leadam, Mr. Tomkinson, and representatives from Congleton Board of Guardians, Arclid Sanitary Authority, Crewe Liberal Association, Cr.we Liberal Club, Winsford, Middlewich, Northwich, and Sandbach Liberal Clubs, Free Gardeners, and various friendly societies. The shops of Sandbach were closed as the procession passed through the town. The service was performed by the Vicar, the Rev. S. H. Armitstead, and the Philharmonic Society assembled round the grave and sang, very feelingly, "When our heads are bowed with woe." Expressions of regret and sympathy were mani- fested throughout the district.

rents have gone down this year, though the level is considerably above what it had reached five years I ago. But it is in South Kensington that the fail has I been sharpest. There is no doubt but that the I ' series of successful shows, beginning with the ' Healtheries has considerably ' damaged house pro- , perty round about Onslow-square. Aristocratic I districts have been vulgarised by being scored with lomnibus routes, and the small shops that suggest a poor neighbourhood are now spiinging up. These , for the most part have but a six months existence, I . opening with May and closing with October. But I if the show should be permanent, and "An Impe- rial Institute" created, we may look to a permanent I depreciation of property. In the long run, indeed, things will right themselves. Sites that are useless for houses are useful for shops, and shopkeepers on the whole pay a higher rental than residents. But Onslow-square that twenty years ago when TI ackerav lived at No. SC, and had Ae-niral Fitz- roy f3r his next-door neighbour, and Millais not far I off, Onslow-square that used to be Brompton, and \of no great account., and then became South Ken- .sington and aristocratic, is already dwindling in value, and all on account of the Exhibitions.

Sir,—With regard to the reference to a bill of mine made by Mr. Copeman, the defendant's solicitor in the action of Husband v. Hemingway, reported in to-day's "Examiner," allow me—as I was not concerned in that action nor present at the trial—to say that the bill was made rut by items in the usual way, and came to £7 103 103. How- ever, as I was acting for a building society, and as the property was of Eomewhat small value, ?nd also as Mr. Husband appealed to me to be ;enient,l voluntarily, and in the first instance, made and tent out my bill for £3 17e 63, to Mr. Husband's satibfaction ; at the same time setting out the proper charges amounting to the larger sum na ned. I may say the mere coaies made and perusal of the draft , exce Is £3 17s 63. I was, therefore, as you may judge. greatly surprised to read that the defendant's advocate had stigmatised me as charging" on an exorbitant scale." lam glad to find that that sentiment found no echo in anything said either by the judge or Mr. Husband. In fact lam told explanations were made in court, which, however, are not published. Reference to the report will also show that the course taken by the judge was not governed by any- thing affecting me.—Yours, &c., Widnes, Oct. 2nd, 1886. • T. J. PETERS.

WESLEYAN METHODISM AND THEATRE GOING. Sir,—l was always led to believe that Wesleyan Metho- dists discountenanced theatrical performances, but at the convers%zione held on Wednesday last I was surprised at two pieces being introduced in the presence of four minis- ters, one from "Henry VIII.," the other a dramatic scene from "William Tell." The only difference from a theatre was dress and scenery; everything else was real, in tact the acting was, as expressed by one, "just like life," the actors being highly complimented by two of the ministers. 'The Wesleyans have recently been pretty well tllked to from the pulpit upon theatre going, dancing, card playing, and all questionable amusements. It will be hard after this for them to know where to draw the line. It seems theatricals are good when played in a Sunday school, under the patron- age of the ministers, but I should like to know whether it is the piece or the walls that makes a theatre. If the minis- ters do not wish their people to go to theatres, they are go- ing the wrong way about the matter, for they certainly are creating a desire in the minds of the young for such places, and they are not leading their flock to fulfil the scriptural requirements that Christians "should flee from all appear- ance of evil," and "Come ye out from among them, and be ye separate ;" but are approaching as nearly as possible to the fashions and customs of the ungodly. It seems to me too many ministers are fingerposts, and I am puzzled to reconcile matters, and Oink they'require an explanation.—l am, yours, ecc., W. E. S.

div.head: URINAL QUESTION.
div.p: THE URINAL QUESTION.

Mr.—Kindly allow me space in your next issue to take objection to the remarks made by Councillor Mackie at the last meeting of the Town Council. His pet theory of en- deavouring to tamper with existing urinals—which are most certainly necessary conveniences—has led him into utterances that when looked at in a calm and philosophical light, certainly cast serious and uncalled for reflections upon myself. Referring to the urinal recently erected. on the nest side of the Mirket Hall, to which he strongly objects on the ground, I presume, of its being opposite his old haunts—his private office of 15 years' standing, as be de- lights to call it—now yclept the "workman's club "—he says "there was one connected with the Blackburne Arms, which they had compelled to be closed, when they ought simply to have compelled it to be kept clean and in proper condition, as by the previous tenant." Well, if I had been a Yankee I should unhesitatingly have exclaimed, "I guess that is a tarnation cool p;ece of impudence." Almost in the same breath Dr. Mackie inquires if eight yards is far enough fer a urinal to be situated from a dwelling, and is met with cries of "No" Here comes Dr. Mackie's incon- sistency. He is quite content for a urinal to be divided by only a brick wall from the shop of Mr. Smith, whose win- dows overlooked it, and which was only about •three yards from my door-way. He would inflict upon the public a real nuisance, and dispense with the new structure which must prove an incalculable boon to those who visit the dancing classes and other amusements provided at the Workman's Club. To enlighten Councillor Mackie, for in this matter at least he is undoubtedly enshrouded in dark- ness, allow me to inform him that the writer of this letter may be placed in the category of the "previous tenant," seeing that my father was such, and that I residld with him during his occupancy and until his death. Further allow me to inform him that the urinal which has been I closed had no direct connection with the Blackburne Arms, that it was a public urinal, and that neither myself nor the "previous tenant" had a right to keep it clean, or to stoop to act as scavengers for the benefit even of an embryo mayor. Whether the new urinal is an eyesore or not is no business of mine, but it is certainly my business to protes` against a "stab in the back." In conclusion it is rather singular that Dr. Mackie enjoyed 15 years' neighboarly ex- perience—with only a brick wall dividing—of the "nasty place," and yet never became acquainted with the fact that it was public.—Yours, &c., Blackburne Arms. THOS. CROMPTON.

Sir,—Already there are very distinct rumblings in the air that the year 1887 is to be a notable one. Her Majesty will have completed the term of years popularly suppcsed to call for a season of thankfulness, and all classes will be expected to give some token, or outward and visible sign of their loyalty. For myself, I de not feel very loyal. I cannot help see- ing around me much that is deplorable. Working-men, by whom the greatness of England is sustained, are in a state of incipient rebellion against the class distinctions which are gradually, yet surely, forcing them deeper into poverty. This being so, hew can one possibly feel jubilant at the exaltation of one family? Heaps.of money will. I suppose, be contributed towards raising funds to enable the people to testify to her Majesty how pleased we all are that she has reigned over us for 50 years, and that in all this long tern of years, we are pleased to say, she has mpst assiduously looked after her own business, and left the welfare of the nation in the hands of the people. Many a man, all, and many a woman could have done the same at a much less cost, and would, perhaps, have spared the nation the iLdiction of so costly a family con- nection. Towards ht r Majesty, as a woman, I have noth- ing to say. She is certainly no better, perhaps no worse, than thousands of her fellow mortals. Upon her and upon her deer German cousins much of English wealth has been poured, and very little of it finds its way back to the people, so that the existing causes for thankful- ness are of a negative kind. I have no desire at the p:esent moment to figure as a kill-joy, but rather to suggest that the occasion should be made one of usefulness. To many 1887 will be a memorable year. Self aggrandisement will receive its finishing touch, honours will, most likely, be scattered abroad, and many will have cause for thankfulness that in the Town Conncil they had a majority of friends, and that through their aid they were enabled to step to the front, full blown members of the Order of Knighthood. When the year has gone by, and our chief citizens are wearing their honours worthily, I wish our town of War- rington to have something of a pleasurable character to look to. London is taking steps, at the suggestion of the Prince of Wales, to form a permanent Exhibition, and 'Manchester has already a large guarantee fund for erecting something similar. What shall we in Warrington have ? Shall it be said that while other towns were spending their money wisely and well, Warrington spent her's in something that left no trace behind It? What better could we do than peti- tion the coming Mayor, whoever he may be, to place him-

self at the head of a strong and substantial committee for declaring our public library a Free Library ? Such an event, accompanied by a banquet to which representative men might be invited would do more to commemorate the year than any amount of wasteful lavishness. Each one around the festive board would feel
" Ihe net of feeding, PS you understand, Is butt frgetlon of the work in hand."

I have heard a suggestion made that working-men, through their various lodees, should now commence to make arrangements for contributing small sums of money. so as to be prepared to take pat in any demonstration that may be set on foot. I think. any such step will end in dis- aster, as all lodges, whether of a friendly or of a trade character, need all their monies at the present time, more especially when we remember how cool has been their action towaids a scheme (the Ship Canal) that might have benefited them. If a special effort is made by the:working- ' men of Warrington to rai.e a tom', let the object be towards benefi log the town in the direction I have named. The time is gone by when the nation's money can be wasted in fireworks and senseless foolery. Nor yet are we a nation likely to lose our heads in the worship of Royalty. We are rather iteking to grow out of it, and place ourselves out- ..side the possibility of running the chance of seeing placed on the throne such immoral characters as Thackerav has depicted. The interesting reminiscences Caroline Bauer recently gave to the public should do something towards keeping the people in their minds during the year 1887. CLIFFORD DIX.
