div.head: GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD.

A monthly meeting of this Board was held in the new Board schools, Great Sankey, on Tuesday. There were present Messrs. W. B. Kerfoot (in the chair), W. 1). Houghton, and J. Cooke; Mr. S. Sutton (clerk).—The Clerk reported that there was a balance of £415 78 2d in the hands of the treasurer in favour of the Board.—The Clerk read the following letter, which had been addressed to the chairman by Mr. R. ' Garnett, on behalf of the Penketh Element,,ry School :—" I have often proposed to bring before your Board one or two matters which mutually concern us. Some years ago we found considerable difficulty and some friction, both in the Sankey School and Peneeth School, from children who were badly governed at home, playing one school against the other, or in other words going 'from one school Is the other, with or without parental consent, or on ..ria slightest punishment being awarded. We took steps as far as our school was concerned to prevent the reception of Sankey scholars, unless there was amply sufficient reason given for the change, and this on enquiry at borne was found to be confirmed; and on ap- pealing to the vim we have reason to believe he gave such ditecjons as to diminish, if not entirely to correct what had become an annoyance to both schools, and an injury to the scholars themselves. As it is now a good many years since this understanding was arrived at, we think it a good time to suggest, undr the new order of things, that some mutual understanding bf this kind would work well for both schools; possibly you may think it well that our school fees should be adjusted, so that there should be no material diff.rence on that point. We learn, with sotne surprise, that it has nowbecorte the custom of the teachers in your school to provide all re quisites, in the shape of books, ,tc., for home and set 00l use (except, perhaps, slates and pencils), free of cost. We assume this to be done by the wish of the Board. If so, we may reinariz it is not the custom in Warrington, and it is not ours, and it bears with it, by implication, that it is a sort of premium on attendance. I name this in fair- ness to oareelves, as we cannot see any point gained in competing for children. For nearly 30 years we have en- deavoured to give a good sound education in Penketh, and we feel sure the gent' men forming your honourable Board have only the same object in view, and it cannot serve your purposes, or ours, ultimately, to offer any special attractions to enrich one school at the cost of another. I venture to point these matters out as involving some consideration which, possibly, they have not had .hitherto." The Chairman otrerved that there had been no alteration made in regard to the Great Sankey schools.—The Clerk said tbe question was whether they intended to make any alteration, and what goods, if any, the Board desired to charge the scholars for.—The Chairman : The schools seem to work well, and I don't see why we should make any alteration.—Mr. Houghton was of opinion tbat that Board should not consider the Penketh school for a moment, as they had nothing to do with it. They had the management of their own school at Great Sankey. and their duty was to provide the best possible education they could at the most economical rate possible. It was not their duty to lift up or pull down the Penketh school in any way; and so long as t'aey gave satisfaction at Great Sankey it was a secondary question entirely whether their action was approved of by the residents of Penketh, and ought not to concern them for one moment. If the children came to the school they could not refuse them.—The Clerk said a great proportion of the children who attended the school were f 'OM the neighbourhood of Great Sankey. The more children who attended, the greater the grant would be.— Mr. Houghton thought it was their duty to educate the children of Penketh and the outlying neighbourhood if they could do so. and they could not adapt their rules to suit little private schools in the neighbourhood —Mr. Cooke said if children liked to come from Penketh he did not eee why they should not be allowed to attend.—The Chairman proposed that the Clerk write to Mr. Garnett to the effect that there had been . o complaint about the management of the Great Sankey Schools., and the Board could not see their way to alter the existing arrangements.—Mr. Houghton said the schools were being satisfactorily carried on. The fees were increasing very considerably, and the education was far superior to what it had been. It would, therefore, be a great pity to adapt themselves to the requirements of other schools in the neighbourhood. Besides, as he understood the letter, it was not so much for the good of the child- ren, as for the purpose of keeping open the Penketh schools. —The Chairman's motion was carried, and the meeting terminate.i.

div.head: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.

On Wednesday an ordinary general meeting of the members of this club was held at the White Bull Inn, Warrington; to confirm the minutes of the committee meeting on 22nd September, and to transact other business. The president, Mr. J. Marsh, occupied the chair, and there was a large attendance.—The CHAIRMAN moved the adoption of the committee's minutes containing resolutions re- questing surrounding landowners and titheowners to grant remission of rents and tithes, and also an expression of sympathy with Welsh farmers "in their opposition to the continued payment of that special class tax tithe.'" Referring to the great reduction in the price of agricultural produce, the 1 Chairman said that a few years ago they looked to their early potatoe crop to make something hand- some. But now the Jersey potatoe came into the market earlier than theirs, the consequence being that last season Jersey potatoes were selling for 7s. per 112 lbs. whilst they could not get that price for a load Of 252 lbs. That was a very great blow to this neighbourhood. (Hear, hear.) if they took milk, he would give them his own case. The differ- ence of price which he received for that article this year as compared with last made to his income a difference of Os. a day. With regard to corn he did not think they had experienced such low markets for 20 years. He certainly did not remember corn to have been so low. He thought, therefore, that they were justified in asking for a remission in their rents. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. T. STELFOX, in seconding the Chairman's proposition, gave some instances of the fall of prices. In 1878, he said, his August potatoes aver- eged from 12s to 14s a load. This year, in the month of August, they averaged 7s a load. Since August they had got down as low as 4s a load. (A Voice: "3s Od a load.") Wheat in 1878 was sold at 6s a bushel, to-day they were offered 3s 10d and 4s. Eight years ago oats were 3s 6d and 4s, and now people would be glad to receive 2s 6d. His hay and clover were sold at Od per stone in 1878; the price to-day was—hay 6d and clover 6i,d. His summer's milk in 1875 was 2s id, and the winter's milk, 2s 8d a dozen; this year the summer's milk was is Bd, and the winter's milk from 2s to 2s 3d a dozen. He thought they cYi show their landlords such a case as to convince them that the lowest reduction they were entitled to was 30 per cent. Unfortunately, however, they had often not to deal with the land- lords, but with agents, some of whom, he was sorry to say, were paid a percentage on the rent, and, consequently, when they lowered the rents they had so much less percentage to draw. He ur-ed that if they could not get the agents to reduce the rents farmers should take. their books to the landlords themselves and let them compare present prices with those of former years.—Mr. KNOWLES said that in Manchester mar- ket the Rochdale " -operative Society paid more for foreign pota.oes than. the English farmers could get for theirs. If they could induce the members of these societies to look carefully after what was being done in this respect he thought it would be a benefit to the farmers.—Mr. J. DARBY- SHIRE advised the members of the club not to allow themselves to lx) vaitten down by newspaper editors and other persons. He also spoke strongly against the imposition of tithes.—Mr. DEAN sug- gested that their application to the landlords should be accompanied by a schedule of prices. He also thought that land!ords should note the advice given by Lord Randolph Churchill to railway directors, that it would be well "to agree with their adver- saries whilst in the way with them." (Hear, hear.) —Mr. PERCIVAL said he had come to the conclusion that the best thing to be done was to get out of farming as quickly as possible.—Mr. HouGu and Mr. BAGULEY also spoke, after which the proposi- tion of the chairman was agTeed to.—A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the proceedings to a close.

div.head: LATEST _NE WS.
div.p: LATEST _NE WS.
EXTRAORDINARY DRATIL—An elderly gentleman named Emerson Martindale was found dead in his lodgings at Car- lisle on Friday morning with an ordinary darning needle eta,* through his breast.
THE FIGHT BETWEEN ENGLISH AND FRENCH FISHER• MEN.—The Board of Trade will hold an inquiry at Rims- gate harbour offices to-day into the disturbance between English and French fishermen.

IRISH EVICTIONS —An eviction took place on Friday at Tromore, near Miltown, which resulted in desperate attack on an emergency man, whose life is despaired of. He re- ceived a i)low from a stone which severed his ear from his skull. The police effected two arrests and stopped further dittarbances.

FOREIGN AFFAIRS.—Lord Iddesleigh continues to be etosely engaged with Foreign Office affairs, and did not leave Downing-street until a late hour on Fr'clay evening. During the afternoon he had interviews with the Austrian and Italian Charges D'Affairei. The incidents constantly arising with reference to the Russian intrigues in Bulgaria, are promptly report LI to the English Foreign Secretary. DECOYING A GIRL. Richard Halton, described as a traveller in the wine and spirit trade, was remanded at St. Helens, on Friday, on a charge of attempting to decoy a girl named Margaret Miles, thirteen years old, a domestic Eervant. She was travelling from Preston to Chester on Thursday, and the prisoner got into the same compartment. He asked her to go to Manchester with him. and said he would make a lady of her, but took her to St. 110 ens, and went to a lodging-house, where he attempted to pass :her off as his wife. DES TRUCTIVE FIRE AT CHORLEY.—On Friday morning the cotton spinning mill belonging to Messrs. Lawrence and Sous, Chorley, was burn down. The damages are esti- mated at about .£30,000. The operatives were at work when the alarm was given, and a terrible scene ot excitement ensued. The fire spread with such rapidity that some of the staircases were enveloped in flames and prevented exit. The bands in the second and thi-d st,reys broke the windows and let themselves, by means of strapping, into the street. It is reported that two c. three persons are severely burned. There were three fire brigades present, but the mill was gutted. Four houees in Aldred-street were wrecked by the mill wall falling on them.

div.head: BELFAST RIOTS.
div.p: THE BELFAST RIOTS.

The inquiry into the Be'last riots was resumed on Friday morning. District-inspector Stritch was examined respect- ing his views of the oreanisation and handling of the police during the riots, in which be was wounded. He did not think mounted men could disperse rioters, but only armed bodies of constabulary. He declared that the firing on rioters was the only means of overawing them. The magis- trates bad not done their duty in only fining stone throwers at the beginning of the riots. These rioters did not mind short terms of imprisonment. He would treat them as garotters when convicted of stoning the police in the execu- tion of their duty. Constable Gerald said the rioters cried like wolves and stoned the police savagely. The constabu- lary ought to have been allowed to fire immediately they were stoned. He would not have hesitated to run a rioter through with his bayonet, or shoot him if be actually saw him ironing the police. Loyalist counsel having asked the constable if his opinions were general amongst the constabu- lary, Mr. Justice Day said he hoped none of the constabu- lary would have I,esitated if ordered to fire on the rioters, who were endangering their lives. Other constables testi- tied to the savagery of the rioters.

DISCOVERY OF INTFRESTJNG RELICS AT WARRINGTON. The opportunity afforded by the clearances in Bridge-street to make a search for relics on the site of the ancient Priory of the Hermit Friars of the Order of St. Augustine has been taken advantage of during the present week with satisfactory results. The search has been undertaken by the Corporation on the suggestion of Mr. Beamont. The General Purposes Committee of the Town Council, at a meet- ing field on the 27th of last month, favourably con- sidered the request of Mr. Beamont, and gave in- , structions to the Borough Surveyor (Mr. Longdin) to superintend the cutting of trenches across the vacant land in Bridge-street. The resolution stated that the object was "to discover, if possible, any relics of the Priory of the Warrington Hermit Friars of the Order of St. Augustine." It came before the monthly meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening, and was agreed to unanimously, Councillor Wright expressing the belief that some most in- teresting discoveries would be made at a trifling cost, and the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) remark- ing that he was glad that there was a prospect of something being discovered, and that he con- sidered that the money devoted to that object was well spent. The operations, so far as they have been conducted, have been watched with great interest. They have resulted in the discovery, behind the spot where the old White Bear public-house formerly stood, of what seem to be foundations. They apparently represent the south side of an entrance doorway, which shows I, base of pilasters and half circular columns. A dis- tance further on, in a westerly direction, moulded foundations have been found, and they appear to be the base of a pillar, which was evidently con- structed for the purpose of supporting an arch, or, possibly, the angle of a tower. It is surmised that as the work of excavating proceeds corresponding pillars will be discovered. In addition to the dis- coveries mentioned there have also been found a :ew coloured tiles, Which have indications of being of Roman make, but they are placed in a position that leads to the belief that they did not in their present situation form a portion of the floor. On the resumption of work by the workmen on Thursday, it was seen that a portion of the masonry had been somewhat damaged, but, fortun- ately, it was not a moulded part that had been in- jured. Extreme care is being taken that no further damage shall be done. The place has been boarded in, and a policeman is in charge during the day, and a watchman during the night. On Thursday a moulded base was discovered, and it is believed that the piece of masonry discovered is a large trancept pier. Great interest is manifested in the search, and Messrs. Pierpoint and Adams have taken sketches of the pillars, &c., that have so far been discovered.

div.head: WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMEM
div.p: WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMEM
SOCIETY.

Another session of this society was opened on Wednesday evening with the holding of a conver- sazione in Bold-street schoolroom, Wan ington. There was a large attendance, amongst those present being the &vs. G. E. Young, G. E. Cutting, J. Howell Jones, and the Rev. R. Pilcher. The fine schoolroom was very prettily decorated, and there were on view several objects of scientific and artistic interest. In the centre of the room were exhibited some beautiful pressed ferns and engravings, the former being con- tributed by Mr. Lilly, and the latter by Miss Brad- bury. On side tables there were displayed a num- ber of Japanese and Ceylonese curiosities be longing to Mr. Joseph Hunt; a galvanic battery belonging to Mr. Hargreaves; and a stereoscope owned by Mr. Beaman. A great deal of interest was also taken in some cases of insects and mosses contributed by Mr. Mounfield, .a powerful microscope lent by Mr. L. Greening, and some fine specimens of British and foreign woods. The room was very tastefully decorated with plants, supplied by Mr. F. Wright, and curtains belonging to Mrs. Horton. In the course of the evening light refresh- ments were served round. The ladies' committee, which had the management of the decorations, re- freshments, &c., consisted of Misses Bennett, Weaver, Lawton, M. Bennett, Gleave, E. Toft, and Horton. The proceedings having been opened with hymn and prayer, the Rev. G. E. Young, president of the society, gave a short ad- dress. He was, he said, very glad to be there that night, and he rejoiced very much to find that there was connected with Bold-street an association of that kind. They looked upon their young men and women with great interest, because they expected they would i take the positions in the church n the future which their older friends were taking now, and what the church and the world needed was thorough-going young men and women. (Ilear, hear.) They did not want foolish or indolent people, they did not want namby-pamby sort of people, but they wanted men and women with hearts and brains, and with a strong determination to make themselves useful to their fellowmen. (Applause.)—An excellent musical programme was then gone through, songs being sung by Mr. W. Wallington, Miss Slater, Mr. Neild, and Mrs. Massey. Pianoforte solos were rendered by Miss S. Pigot and Miss K. Lawton. Two dramatic scenes from "Richard III." were also very successfully performed, the Darts being taken as follows : —,Duke of Gloster, W. Furness; Duke of Clarence, W. Broadhurst ; Sir R. Brackenbury, E. Plinston ; Ist Murderer, Joseph Hunt; 2nd murderer, Mr. Booth. Each item of this programme was admirably dealt with, Mr. Wallington, Miss Slater, and Mrs. Massey being favoured with encores. Miss F. Toft made an ex- cellent accompanist. At the close of the entertain- ment the Rev. G. E. Young moved a vote of thanks to those who had to do with the getting up and the carrying out of that very 'successful conversazione. —The Rev. R. Pilcher, in seconding this proposal, said he had spent a most successful evening, lie complimented them very highly upon the entertain- ment provided, and upon their recitations, which showed talent of a high order.rln introducing them, he thought, they had shown spirit and bravery. They had made such rapid progress of late years in this country that he thought they were perfectly safe in introducing a higher class of entertain:ment, such as they had done that night. (Hear, hear.)— The Rev. J. Howell Jones said he was pleased to see such a goodly number present, and he trusted that that entertainment would lead to the members of their society andcongregation acquainting them- selves with their English classics. He believed there was no better, no more profitable, reading. (Hear, hear.)—The vote of thanks was then heartily accorded, and a very pleasant gathering was brought to a close.

LIBERAL CLUR "AT HomEs."—The committee of the Earlestown and District Liberal Club have lately been making arrangements for a series of entertainments and dis- cussion during the ensuing winter months, and the pros- pects of the club are of a more encouraging nature than at any former period. The gatherings, it is expected, will partake of the character of musical " At Homes," and these will be held fortnightly, while during the intervening week a discussion upon pfilLical topics will take place. Many of the principal musicians of the district have promised their see vices, and the first entertainment, next Thursday night, will be ,iven by Messrs. P. Hastie, S. Swann, J. W. Wil- liams, E. Corlett, clic. In order to provide the necessary accommodation one of the billiard tables will be removed The gatherings will not only be opened to members and friends, but ladies will be invited to attend,

FIVE CROSSES WESLEYAN CHAPEL. -- Harvest thanks- giving services were held at the Wesleyan Chapel, Fife Crosses, on Sunday, when the Rev. E. Mosscrop, of Frod- sham. occupied the pulpit in the afternoon, and the the Rev. W. Edmunds, of Banbury, in the evening. The collections, amounting to the sum of S 6 12s 9d, were in aid of the trust funds.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.—Harvest thanksgiving services were held in the above chapel on Sunday afternoon and evening, when the Rev. T. Lagar, the resident minister, preached. The choir gave the harvest anthems "Cry out and about" (P. P. Bliss) and "Oh. praise the Lord "KG. F. Root.) The chief feature in the decorations of the chapel was a niceiv-arranged stall of large fruits and veotables in the communion. The collections were in aid of tcir. cuit fund.

A FOOTBALL PLAYER DBOWNED.—The body of Banja- min Parkinson, aged 19, son of Samuel Parkinson, of New- town, Frodsham, has been found in the river Weaver under circumstancbs surrounded with mystery. It appears that he went to Warrington on Saturday last to take part in a football match along with others. They walked home, and he was in the company of his mates until arriving at Sat- ton,when it would be getting near midnight. Here he stayed behind, and his companions were under the impression that he was following them, but they did not see him again. On Sunday morning his parents began to make inquiries and a search was made which resulted in his hat and abottle being found on the banks of the river at the above place. On Monday at noon the body was very soon recovered on being grappled for.

Muirrei. IMPIOVEDIENT SOC ETY.—The opening meeting of the Frodsham Wesleyan Mutual Improvement §ociety for the forthcoming winter season was held in the Trinity schoolroom, on Friday evening, when the Rev. E. Mosscrop presided. The Chairman, in his remarks, stated that the programme, which was both interesting and instructive, would call their attention to knowledge of various kinds. Literary and sacred subjects would be dealt with ly various members of the society, and 'meld be presented in the form of recitations and readings, essays and short papers, discus- sions and extempore addresses. Amongst the list of novel- ties, they were to be favoured with the debates of a House of COPOMODS, and short extempore sermons on texts of Scripture. After the chairman's address an interesting programme was gone through. FUNERAL OF MR. GEORGE GORST.—The funeral of Mr. George Gorst, of Bradley, near Frodsham, who died sudden- ly on Thursday week whilst out driving, took place at Prod- sham Parish Church, amidst signs of the deepest regret. It appeared that the deceased gentleman was out driving and was taken suddenly ill. He had been ailing for some time, and was under the care of the family doctor. He was taken into the Bridge Inn and medical attendance was summoned. but it was of no avail, as he died in less than an hour after the attack. Mr. Gorst was born about the year 1830, and was educated at the local school, after which he was ar- tie.-ed to Mr. Purcell, solicitor, which gentleman he served for a long time. He has been on most of the public bodies, and was treasurer for the Frodsham Savings Bank, and overseer for the district. He has lefta wife and three chil- dren to mourn his lose. The funeral ecntege left the resid- ence of the deceased at half-past three, and amonest the gentlemen present were Mr. H. Linaker, Mr. W. H. Picker- ing, Mr. James Rigby, Mr. Thsmas Riley, Mr. H. Riley,and Mr.T:Lewis. A number of Oddfellows also followed,deceased being an influential member. The burial service was read by the Rev. E. Charley, M.A. The funeral arrangements were carried out admirably by Mr. Joseph Gorst, of Frod- sham.

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF HOPE.
div.p: CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF HOPE.

At the opening meeting for the winter season last Tues- day evening, a large audience assembled under the presi- dency of the Rey. James Johnston (pastor), who remarked that it was as necessary to bave temperance institutions as- sociated with every Sunday school as it was imperative to have lifeboats and lighthouses on the most dangerous parts of the English coasts for the protection and rescuing of the mariner. The arguments in favour of abstinence were a hundred to one against intoxicating drink. Morally, the influence of drink produced crime, physically it caused dis- ease, socially it resulted in poverty, and intellectualLy and spiritually its consequences were beyond calculation. They were frequently recommended to consider the virtues of moderation and alcoholic stimulants. What were the limits of moderation F Sir Henry Thompson had stated that " A very large proportion of the most painful and dangerous maladies which come under my notice are attri- butable to the ordinary and daily use of fermented drink, taken in the quantity which is conventionally deemed moderate." Moderate drinking had been described by the highest scientific authorities of the time as causing maladies and disorders and aggravating others already produced. No term was more misleading or working as much mischief in the present day. As regards the advantages of drink as a stimulant, had it not been long ago established as a fact in physiology that stimulants produced subsequent depression, and lost their force through frequent repetition. The de- pression corresponds to the temporary excitement, and the loss is unfortunately greater than the gain. If the physi- cal system is out of order, something more remedial in the form of diet, sleep, exercise, rim, is requisite to effect a vital and permanent reformation. The drinking habits of our' countrymen and countrywomen are appalling. Of the lat- ter class it has been said by Gustafsen in his "Foundation of death" that there is &more drink- ing among the women of England to-day than among the women of any other civilized country. The ravages of drink makes no exceptions in its victims. It was as destructive in the first centuries as in modern his- tory. Drink brought on the downfall of Alexrnder the Great at the early age of 32. Many of the Roman em- perors after the Augustan age ware ruined through excessive drinking customs, and their leaders were powerless to resist the inroads of the Goths and Vandals. Drink gave the advantage to William the Conquerer over Harrold at the Battle of Hastings, and equally SO to the Mahommedan armies (pledged to abstinense) over the provinces on the shores of the Mediterranean. In England, in the year 1883, there were 27,050 breweries, which yielded 990,000,004 gallons of beer. This quantity exceeded the combined pro- duction of the countries of France, Austria, Hungary, Switzerland, Holland, and, Belgium. Upon beer and similar drinks Englishmen spent the same year the sum of -Z225, 477,275, while devoting the sam of £lOOO,OOO for the spread of the gospel in heathen lands. After most careful eequiries, it is computed that 80,000 persons are slain directly and indirectly every year through drink. The Rev. R. J. Ward an Mr. R. Craven (Liverpool) afterwards addressed the meeting.

REVISION AT LYMM. On Wedaesday Mr. W. T. Parkins, revising barristtryheld a court at Lymai Sessions-room, to revise the voting lists for Lymm and the surrounding townships. Mr. -1.• E. • Paterson, with whom were Mr. E. S. Kenyon and Mr. Skil ling, appeared for the Liberals, and Mr.. F. R. B. Linselly with whom were Mr. Callender and Mr. Goodwin, for tbe - l Conservatives.

RIVAL BROTHERS. The Conservatives claimed a vote for Henry Browning, in respect to the occupation of a dwelling-house at Booth's Hill, Lytnin.—Mr. Paterson made an objection on the ground that Henry Browning was not the sole occupier of the house, which, he said belonged to several children.—Mr. Shilling said that the whole family lived in the house, which was reported to be held in trust. Mr. Browning said that he occupied the house in company with his three brothers and two sisters. He himself paid the trates, and had been considered to be the head of the family since his mother's death about four years ago. In answer to Mr. Paterson he said that he was not the eldest brother. The brother that: the Liberals had claimed for, Thomas Browning, was his elder brother.—Mr. Paterson: Did you give him half a sovereign to go away ?—Witness: I asked him last night if he would like to go to the exhi- bition at Liverpool, and he said he would.—Mr. Paterson : It appears that there are five of you living together, and the house is left in trust for you, and a certain sum is allowed for household expenses ?—Witness: My brothers and sisters authorise the payments to be made to me..—Mr. PaterSOll seibmitted that there were joint tenants in this case, and that the applicant had no prior elaim.—Mr. Liasell said that the house was put in the name of Henry Browning, who paid, and was responsible for, the rates. They all owned the house, but he was responsible. Mr. Paterson said that he had witnessea to prove that the other brother was induced to go away until the revision was over.—After hearing particulars as to the assessment of the house, his Honour allowed both claims.

A WOMAN'S CARLESINESS. - An objection was made to the name of a voter remaining on the list, on the ground that he was in arrears in the payment of his rates. The person's wife attended court, and said that the rates were all paid now, but she admitted having neglected to pay them within the required time.—The Barrister told her that the vote was lost.
Most of the business was of a routine character.
LYIVIM LOCAL BOARD.

The ordinary monthly meeting of this body was held at the Boardroom, Lvmm, on Thursday evening, when, in the ab- sence of Mr. Cameron, the chairman of the Board, Mr. Thompson was voted to the chair. Thera were also present Messrs. Rogers, Forster, Brazendale, Hall, Appleton, Gibbon, Woolley, and T. J. Ridgway (law clerk). REPORTS.—Tbe report of the Surveyor was read and adopted without comment. —The sanitary report was also read. It urged the necessity of making structural altera- tions to privies and aahpits, in order to improve them in a sanitary point of view, and to give better facilities for scavenging. It also called attention to the dilapidated con• dition of certain privies and ashpits belonging to fustian cutting shops. It was resolved that steps be taken to rec- tify the matter.—Mr. Graham, gas manager, submitted his report, which was adopted. A Sunain.—Mr. Hall asked when the work of paving in the village was going to be undertaken. Hs thought that as money had been voted for it, it should be done.—Mr. Rogers said that Mr. Hall must not be sarcastic, or he would "sit upon" him.—Mr. Hall : You are so very egetistica' in your remarks. I have asked an important queston.—M . Rozers : I am not prepared to answer it.—Mr. Hall said that paving bad been done at Statham, and he wanted to know bow the money that was intended for Lymm village had been spent, or when the work in the village would be undertaken.—Mr. Rogers: I am not prepared to answer it.—Mr. Brazendale said be ,thought Mr. Hall's qpestion a justifiable one. They should know whether or not it was intended to pave the village.—The Clerk said he thought the work would be done for less than the estimate.—Mr. Hall (to Mr. Rogers) : You Oink you will sit upon me,. but you will not.—Mr. Rogers :; I will, but you have not settee to see when you are sat upon.—Mr. Hall : I will bring you to task.—Mr. Rogers : Will yea.—Mr. Hall : I think I am capable of taking care of myself.—Mr. Rogers LTEdeed you are not.—Mr. Hail : Besides I do not consider you a. member of this Board. You only slipped in to do that which is not atraigbtforward.—Mr. Rogers : What is it I demand an eaplanation.--Mr. Hall was understood to say that Mr. Rogers was there to assist an interest that had too long been dominant on the Beard.—Mr. Rogers You will have to answer for more than you are able to answer for, in another place than this.—Mr. Hall :. I know how far to go; you will not find me go over a certain. line. lam too wideawat e for that.—Mr. Rogers You are not wideawake.—This discussion then ceassd.—This was the ptincipal business.

The proceedings were orderly. Resolutions were passed unanimously at eac% of the three platforms declaling that education should be free,.and'pro • testing against the levying of rates for educational pun- poses.

Registered under the Companies' Arts of 1862 to 1883, whereby the liabitity of the shareholders is limited to the amount of their shares. CAPITAL, £200,000, in 200,000 SHARES of El EACH.-5s on application, ts on allotment, balance to be called up as re- quired, with not less than three months' interval between each call. Original shareholders of not less than 10 shares shall have attached to their allotment notes a coupon entitling them to free passages between Liverpool and the Isle of Man during the season 1887. • TETE FXAMINER, SATURDAT, OCTOBER 99 1886 THE BANKRUPTCY OF AN ALDER- MAN. The affair e of Mr. Edward Johnson, provision dealer, St. Helens,-Runcorn, 'Warrington, Earlestown, and other towns, were again before the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court on Thursday, when the bankrupt appeared before Mr. Registrar Bellringer on his ad- journed public examination. Mr. Johnson is an alderman of St. Helens, of which borough he is also an ex-mayor. The bankrupt was represented by Mr. H. L. Riley, Mr. Cornett appeared for the trustee (Mr. 1 Mahon), and Mr. G. B. Rodway for Mr. J. T. Davies and Mr. G. C. Dobell, of this city, creditors on the estate. The liabilities are reported at £10.839 141, and the deficiency at £7,532 105—Mr. Cornett questioned tile bankrupt as to a debt of £45 due to a Mr. John Fishvrick.—The bankrupt said this debt was for goods for household use. There were one or two other small creditors for household expenses. His ; wife had a private income of between £5OO and £6OO. He did not think any of the small debts for household expenses ' amounted to more than £2o.—Mr. Cornett: Have you since the last examination discovered anything new in the tran- saction between you and Mr. Dobell ? Do you adhere to your statement on the last occasion ?—Bankrupt : No. I have since discovered the statement I then made was wrong with reference to the disposal of £15,000. It was for the purchase of the Swan -lane Colliery, including two brickworks. Mr. Rodway objected to this matter being gone into, and the bankrupt making allega- tions which other people had no opportunity of contra- dicting.—The Registrar said the bankrupt must be allowed to give his own explanation of the matter.—The bankrupt said he received £15,000 from Mr. Davies and Mr. Dobell for the purchase of the brickworks and Swan-lane Colliery. Of this sum £12,000 was to pay off a mortgage, and £3,000 was paid to Mr. Davies for moneys which Mr. Davies had lent him to meet cash accoumts.—Mr. Corbett asked for an adjournment for the bankrupt to prepare accounts showing the transactions between himself and his sons, and the moneys paid them as salaries.—The Registrar complied with the request, and adjourned the examination to the 21st inst.
